videos.full_text: Sometimes in real estate, it's the unsexy asset classes that give you the most cash flow. When I first started in real estate, I always wanted to build a beautiful building and I cared a lot about the interiors and the design. And that is amazing and I've done very well in making big bangs of profit in my projects. But to really build sustainable cash flow, I found certain niches like industrial that are better for like longer term growth. So, as an example, I just read a LinkedIn article about a billionaire that I think came from Missouri and he believed he started with one Motel 6. Having long-term cash flow is sometimes, you know, people do really well in limited service hotels or affordable housing or things that might not be pretty but are needed and wanted in the long run and that's a way I've complemented my real estate portfolio. If you ignore the less flashy asset classes, you'll miss out on cash flow. I'm Magda Balastian, I'm a real estate developer and I've successfully balanced my real estate investment portfolio, meaning I do projects that make a lot on the back end as well as having high cash flow. So, I first got interested in industrial as an asset class when I was buying land from sellers to build multi-family. And I started talking to industrial users, so that's like, you know, a guy that owns an HVAC company or an electrical company and one guy had an insulation company and he was sitting on $16 million worth of land but he had nowhere to go. And so, I started talking to him about what he really needed in terms of finding a another industrial space and it basically was completely missing in the market. And then I thought, okay, huh, there's an opportunity there. And that was how I pivoted and ended up developing about a million square feet of industrial. Obviously, I did a lot of research, I talked to brokers, I looked at the vacancy rates and ended up getting into shallow bay sort of early because I saw this need and there was no supply. That led me to industrial outdoor storage kind of in that same vein. So, when the pandemic happened, logistics and people buying everything online, you know, there's a huge demand for that. And so, it takes a lot of staging for trucking companies and Amazon and all these delivery companies to get things to where people order them, right? And that created an asset class called industrial outdoor storage that is basically like storage yards that are in urban infill locations that are zoned for industrial. Now, what I really like about this strategy is that cities don't necessarily want more of this land because it's not bringing high tax revenue and not like building residences that's going to make a community or schools. It's just sort of like an industrial use. But, that makes it very supply constrained and then demand. So, if you have an industrial outdoor storage space, it can be really nice covered land play, but it can also double as appealing to our new logistics lifestyle that people demand so much. You talk to people, you listen to brokers and it was like, "You know, I really can't find any space for me to move to. I'm an industrial user in downtown Nashville. Everyone wants to build housing here, but I have nowhere to go and I'm not ready to shut down my business." So, that was how I branched into shallow bay industrial and similarly is how I got into industrial outdoor storage, which is basically just was driven by the pandemic. There's lots of needs for logistics staging and and basically places for like junkyards, imagine, where people need to store things, but there's a better way to do it that's more commercialized. And so, that's just a way to sort of I realized like it doesn't involve a lot of development. I have a very high heavy development strategy in doing condos that's very uh intense and high risk and takes a lot of capital. And it's a really nice way that I balance my portfolios and found more cash flow is outdoor storage. So, the thing I like about outdoor storage is that I intend to build a cash flowing portfolio. A lot of what I've done in the past has been uh buy a piece of land, design a building, build it, sell it, and then you make a nice return on your investment, but then you're done with the building and you have to start all over again. As opposed to having a cash flowing strategy. And I think every portfolio should have both or every savvy real estate investor should have both. And this is the way that I've identified in my portfolio that I want to increase the cash flows. Don't underestimate the value of simple, easy to execute business models in real estate. If it's something that's simple and tried and true and can be done over and over repeatedly, that is something that can be scaled and can offer cash flow. So, don't overlook asset classes and investments that are very boring but easy to operate and sustain. I remember when I first started looking at industrial as an asset class, I thought, this is not like me, it's not pretty, it's nothing like residential, and it's so different, but it's actually much, much simpler to execute on, especially if you're just getting started in real estate. So, doing something that's like boring and you know, has sustainability is a really good way to start investing because it's a lot easier to focus on more like industrial or storage type assets than dealing with all of the million intricacies that happen on the residential, commercial side. I'm Meg Epstein, if you want to hear more advice like this, please check out my next video.

metadata.title: ANDREW SMITH: Is Industrial Open Storage (IOS) The Hidden Real Estate Goldmine?
metadata.author: SAENTYS
metadata.shortDescription:
Is Industrial Open Storage the next big opportunity in real estate? And why are investors waking up to an asset class hiding in plain sight?
In this episode of Bricks & More, host Adrian Strittmatter sits down with Andrew Smith, partner in the commercial division at Carter Jonas, to explore the rapid growth of Industrial Open Storage, also known as Industrial Outdoor Storage (IOS) and why rising demand, rental growth and limited supply are attracting investors to this overlooked sector.

Andrew explains how IOS has evolved from temporary land use into an increasingly institutional investment opportunity, supporting everything from logistics and HGV parking to EV charging and major infrastructure projects. They explore the economics driving the market, what determines the value of an IOS site, and why planning constraints and land scarcity are creating new challenges for occupiers.

Adrian and Andrew explore:
-What Industrial Outdoor Storage (IOS) is and why demand is growing across the UK.
-How logistics, HGV parking, EV charging and infrastructure projects are driving demand for open storage land.
-Why limited supply and rising rents are transforming IOS into an increasingly attractive real estate investment.
-How location, planning permission, site surfacing and services determine the value of an IOS asset.
-Why occupiers are seeking longer leases and greater certainty, rather than short-term solutions.
-How rental growth and yield compression are changing the investment case for IOS.
-Whether redundant industrial sites and former offices could be repurposed to meet growing demand.
-How the UK compares with the US and Europe, and what needs to happen for IOS to become a fully established institutional asset class.
-Why investors shouldn't underestimate the complexity of site selection, planning and development.

From the economics of open storage and the infrastructure supporting modern logistics to the potential for institutional investment and future market growth, this episode examines why Industrial Outdoor Storage is emerging as an important part of the real estate landscape, and what investors and developers need to know to seize the opportunity.

metadata.shortDescription:
Micah Johnson and I break down industrial outdoor storage (IOS) from the ground up: what it is, why the right land is so hard to find, and how the Longyards storage-yard model differs from a typical IOS lease. I also share the hard lessons from growing too fast.

Originally recorded on Real Estate Pros Show with Micah Johnson — thanks for having me! Full show: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6jzMcNItutY

Chapters:
0:00 Intro
2:24 My story: from carpenter to storage yards
5:57 What is industrial outdoor storage (IOS)?
7:09 Why the right land is so scarce
9:34 How the Longyards yard model is different
15:48 Developing a yard vs. buying an existing one
19:24 Lessons from growing too fast
23:00 Final thoughts

Learn the full storage-yard model on my free training: https://www.golongorgohome.com

metadata.title: Inside a $4.8M Industrial Outdoor Storage (IOS) Deal in Fontana | Benji Miller
metadata.author: Adding Value w/ Shy Assar | CRE & Industrial
metadata.shortDescription:
Industrial outdoor storage (IOS) has shifted from overlooked mom-and-pop truck yards into one of the most profitable, highly competitive sectors in commercial real estate—consistently outperforming traditional core asset classes. 

In this episode of Adding Value, host Shy Assar sits down with Benji Miller, founder of Negresco Property Group. Benji shares how he transitioned from working on massive institutional portfolios to launching his own firm and teaming up with Bethesda-based Open Industrial to deploy programmatic capital across Southern California.

We dive straight into our recently closed transaction at 10905 Hemlock Avenue in Fontana, CA—a $4,800,000 all-cash acquisition ($50/LSF) on 2.20 acres featuring a ±10,000 SF building and verified by-right truck and trailer storage. 

In this episode, we cover:

• The 10905 Hemlock Breakdown: Sourcing, front-end due diligence, and navigating Fontana’s strict zoning landscape.
• The 1–3 Acre Sweet Spot: Why smaller low-coverage parcels provide the highest leasing velocity versus chasing "white whale" 10-acre sites.

• Acquisition Criteria: Why sub-30% coverage, functional service facilities, and dual-street ingress/egress are non-negotiable for institutional IOS.

• Structuring Co-GP & Equity Partnerships: How emerging sponsors scale by leveraging balance sheets, LP equity, and patient capital.

• Capital Markets & IOS Maturation: Debt conditions, cap rate expectations (fives to high sixes), and how 1031 buyers view IOS today.

• Advice for Brokers & Sponsors: The "unicorn" skill set of raising equity vs. finding deals, and how brokers can win institutional business.

I went through a process speaking to a variety of different people and it's kind of like a marriage, like it's a dating process. You You talk to people, you see what they want, what you can provide, and you know, similar to what we were talking about before on Hemlock, this just kind of checked all the boxes and, you know, it's a marriage. Like at the end of the day, like that's what all of this is, whether it's your co-GP, your LP, like you are getting married to these people for the next 3, 5, 10, hopefully more years. And in some instances it's more important than your regular marriage cuz you're speaking with them >> Sure. >> on a daily basis and these are the people that you are allocating all of your time, resource, and betting your future on. So, you know, similar to what I was saying before, like my wife and I take this very seriously on who we partner with. And we love the Open guys. They're amazing. They've been super great to work with. I can see the future and we like very much see eye to eye, me and all the partners there and and and some of the junior all the junior guys. >> Sure. >> And, you know, I'm just looking forward to really blowing the top off and, you know, continuing to to buy assets but in very like meticulous way where we're very calculated about the the types of deals that we buy. >> On the topic of types of deals that you buy, so what are the what are you looking to buy? >> Sure. So, generally what we view as like the most ideal IOS sites are 30% coverage or less with by right zoning. We're not in the >> Okay, so let's let's talk about coverage. >> Sure. >> So, when we talk about 30% coverage or less, why is that important? >> Sure. So, anything that goes above that, we it's kind of this inexact science. It's kind of like this tipping point where people start to utilize rents on a per building basis as opposed to viewing it on a per land basis. And it kind of tips into more of a building deal. I There's some research we have behind the scenes that I'm not privy to or I'm not able to to share. >> Sure. But, that's kind of the demarcation line. Now, look, if we saw something that was like 32 and 1/2 and maybe had some extra sheds that you could knock down and then all of a sudden you're below that, like different game. >> But, the the institutional standard is the definition would be, hey, IOS check, 30% coverage or less. >> That's how we view it. >> And then and then I'm assuming also it also goes it comes back to the thesis that like really if you technically want to be an industrial outdoor storage side, you have to have predominantly outdoor storage. >> Sure. Right. >> So, I mean it has to match the definition. >> Yeah, absolutely. It's just that's kind of the demarcation line for us. We look for sites that, you know, generally have some sort of service facility. We will buy sites that are just paved yards, but they're going to need the high highest functioning and you know, best uses, whether it's drayage, uh trucking, and it will likely need to be closer to the port so we can feel comfortable about those logistics uses. >> And and that's the thing, it's like right now we are seeing better leasing activity >> Yeah. >> on sites that do have a building or a service facility on it. It's just because, you know, when you have just a drop yard, >> Yeah. >> that's what you're limited to. >> Right. >> Like somebody wanting to drop containers there or outdoor storage, and that tenant pool is not looking to stretch on rents. >> And I've seen deals that are leased to Fortune 500 companies that have limited improvements on the site, which will get priced to much higher cap rates had they had, you know, 20, 30, 40,000 ft. >> Mhm. >> Which is interesting. I think that a lot of the institutional equity is wisening up to, you know, IOS 1.0, anything that had additional parking was IOS. Um and now people are very much more meticulous about the markets they go into, the sites they look at, the features that those sites have, and you know, we fit in that bucket as well. >> So, we got coverage. We got a uh improvements >> and land use. >> and land use, which is zoning. >> Correct. >> And then that that thesis behind having a liberal zoning is the flexibility to lease to a variety of tenants. >> Correct. >> Such as trucking, equipment yards, construction, uh lumber, you know, just just having that kind of nuance, being able to the flexibility. >> Yeah. And you know, as I was speaking about before, I always viewed IOS sites in a very similar fashion to mobile home parks, which, you know, my like I had mentioned, my friend worked in the alternative business. They're really not approving more of them. The cities, for whatever reason, are not the biggest fans from like a pollution or traffic, noise perspective, which is ironic because there's another study that we saw where even those cities are pushing manufacturing uses because of all the jobs that they probably bring to the the the local communities, they actually have four times as much truck traffic >> Mhm. >> as IOS facilities. >> Mhm. >> So, it's kind of like six of one, half a dozen of the other. >> So. >> We got the understanding of what the acquisition criteria is. Is there a size range that you'd like to purchase, a location, a region, a deal size? Like and we understand that, you know, the focus is really you can do value add and you can do stabilize. So, is there any any more insight you can provide on kind of >> Sure. >> picture. >> Yeah, I mean, we can buy portfolios, we can buy one-off sites. Generally, like I know this is a wide range, so it's kind of a cop-out, but uh we'll buy in the three to 50 plus million dollar range, you know, where one day we're looking at a four million dollar deal, the next day we're looking at a 60 million dollar deal, and all things being equal, we'd love all of those in our portfolio. Um in some instances, the 60 million dollar deal can be a multitude of sites or could be a one-off. But as I mentioned before, we're generally not going to be buyers of large vacant sites just just because it doesn't pay right now. So, if we were to buy >> lease. >> Yeah, absolutely. If we were to buy large facilities, they're either going to need to be able to be multi-tenanted based off of how they lay out and have some sort of like longer wall in place, or else we just don't view that as worth the squeeze. >> Let's talk about what's going on on the exit strategy. Like what that world is looking like right now, because my understanding is that because industrial outdoor storage is a relatively new asset class, >> Yeah. >> it's kind of an unchartered territories as far as where how you exit a portfolio, and it's almost like every time somebody is able to successfully do so, it's like a new benchmark. >> Right. >> Like the market is maturing. >> Yeah. >> Where we at right now in the cycle as far as kind of the maturation of the asset class on like a large-scale institutional level? >> Yeah. I would say in the last six months, I've seen a fair amount of portfolios come across. >> Who who's who's been like the who coming some of the players that have been able to successfully do so? Or maybe some of the deals that have that you've seen. >> Yeah, I I would say like, you know, what happens ends up happening in some of these deals is it depends on geography. So, maybe a group comes out with like 15 properties and two are in California or Texas and a local group will buy just those. Or, you know, they'll go to the market and they'll have better um success recapping it and keeping it personally and just having new equity partners. So, there's like all these sort of menu options on the table and it really just depends. But, what's unique is you have these portfolios of 2022, 2023 vintage that, you know, if you're on a 3-year maturing loan or just, you know, a 3-to-5-year business strategy, you need some sort of liquidity event whether it comes from the debt markets or the equity markets. So, in that instance, there are going to be have to like there are people that are going to have to sell. Like, everyone, you know, each year there's this wall of maturities that comes up and, you know, there's by default going to have to be an exit strategy for pretty much all groups unless you have a much longer-term horizon where you can maybe wait out when cap rates come in a little bit. So, we're seeing, you know, more recaps, more, you know, new new debt facilities happen, and you know, it's happening all over the place and it could be anywhere from $50 million worth of deals or $200 million worth of deals and people are testing the market from both a debt and equity perspective. >> Which is a good pivot to one, where is debt on industrial outdoor storage facilities and where are cap rates on a stabilized asset? >> I mean it really just depends like >> Let's talk to Southern California. >> Sure. Southern California, debt is kind of all over the map depending on stabilized, debt fund, you know, life co, etc. But, I would say, you know, cap rates for stabilized assets can be in the mid to high sixes, mid to low sixes depending on credit. >> Which is which is not that high if you think about it because I mean, what is a 10-year treasury in like the high fours? >> Yeah, and what's interesting is people definitely, you know, if you have a 10-year lease to an institutional tenant you're going to try and come out in the fives depending on, you know, size. I think if you have a deal that you're selling as a one-off sub I don't know, 12, 15 million dollars, there's going to be a lot of action even in the fives depending on basis or high fives for like 1031 money that, you know what's interesting now is like a United Rentals is the new Starbucks. >> Mhm. >> You know, people are all of a sudden interested in some of these facilities from the 1031 perspective, but you know there are those buyers that are becoming a bit smarter from that perspective and they're saying, "No, I'm not going to take the 575. I want a six, six and a quarter, etc." but, you know, generally I would say like that's kind of the range that I'm seeing. >> You know what I really appreciate about this business is, you know, I remember when I first started that people would always tell me that it's a long-term business that these relationships take a long time to form and when we first started talking, I think it was I don't know, I think it was like five or six years ago. >> Yep. >> Uh and um finally after five or six years we did a deal. >> Yeah. And so >> yeah, I mean, like what do what do you What do you think about that? >> Yeah, I I I think it's really cool how in our business, you know, you make relationships and you keep talking. You never really know where it's going to go. You know, I bumped into you at Costco with my dad. We talked. We, you know, try and, you know, figure out new deals together. We speak. Nothing happens. I saw you at some NAIOP events. We keep in touch and then out of nowhere five, six years later, boom, like deal happens. We have other things that we're chasing together as well and that's just really cool. And and as a result of that, I was able to meet Ian as well. We've become friendly as well and you know, looking at new opportunities and you know, you just want to work with people that are fun and entertaining because this can be a slog what we do. As we were talking about the other night, you know, when you buy a deal, when you sell a deal over like a 3 to 5 year time horizon, you kind of limp to the finish line. >> Sure. >> You get there, you're pretty bloodied and you like a piece of you died >> inside. >> Yeah. >> And you know, you want to work with people that you enjoy being around that are, you know, just those that if you left the room, you know that they were saying like positive things about you because we only have so much time on this earth and you know, it can be a very stressful game. So at least do it with people that are going to be enjoyable who, you know, will have your back and you know, I I definitely have felt that sort of camaraderie from from you guys at Boyes. >> 100%. And and and and I agree. Like I said, I think that um one of the things I appreciate the most about this business is is that it's a relationship business. >> Yeah. >> And so, you know, I know I know we've touched on a little bit about kind of some some of your experiences, kind of the um the learning curve you had to go through just starting on the principal side. But in general, if there are just a few nuggets that you would share with young guys who are looking to get in because I think there's this perception and and and for everybody who looks to get into commercial real estate that like, hey, I'm going to become an investor or I'm going to become developer and I'm going to be rich. >> Right. >> Right? I mean, like that's that's you know, you hear it from young guys all the time like I that's that's how it all works. Uh and it's uh like you said earlier, it's a slog, you know, it's a lot of challenge, it's a lot of adversity and it and more than anything, you know, and I haven't been a principal. I can't speak on their behalf, but I've seen young guys or younger our younger generation get into the space. It looks like it takes a lot of time. >> Yeah. >> And so, if there are a few words of advice you can share with both okay, one side for brokers who want to get level their game up to do more institutional business and to younger principals who want to grow and become successful. >> Yeah. >> What's some advice you can share? >> Man, uh good question. I would say that and I alluded to this a little bit before, I think who your partners are cuz even if you're a solo entrepreneur, like you still have equity partners, you still have property managers, you still have accountants. Your entire team matters and like I mentioned before also, it starts at home, being in a good head space, being aligned with your spouse. >> What are all the what are all the single guys supposed to do? >> Yeah, exactly. [laughter] They got no spouse at all. >> I can't I can't help with that department cuz uh you know, I understand what that could feel like. I I was single once. Um so, beyond just being, you know, a good person and and having good partners, early on in the business, one of my mentors whittled real estate down to one sentence, which has evolved a little bit. He said, "If you want to be on the sponsorship side, you need to be able to raise equity or find deals or you can be replaced." >> Mhm. >> And that has always been kind of my guiding light. And what's interesting is if you built two concentric circles in the Venn diagram, the people in the middle are the actual unicorns, like the Victor Wembanyamas on the Spurs sort of people. >> And they can do both. >> That can do both. It's very rare that people have both of those skills, but that's always been my guiding light. I've always been someone that's been able to find opportunities. I worked worked in acquisitions, but depending on what sort of company you work at, you don't always get to flex the capital raising muscle and that is a huge part of our business. >> Mhm. >> For better or worse. >> Convincing people to invest. >> need to believe in you and you know, you need to be be able to take that seriously. Like you have to be able, whether it's good news, bad news, be open and honest, and be able to deliver that information in the middle of a tough cycle, and you also just really need to be a good partner and someone that can actually execute. So, you know, those are the two pillars on the sponsorship side that have really built everything. Now, look, that statement has evolved. You can outsource your deal sourcing, you can outsource your uh equity sourcing through debt and equity brokers, but the reality is like generally on the sponsorship side, you're going to need one of those two skill sets to excel. And that's kind of been my guiding light beyond the the partners discussion. Like, it's super critical to to be able to, you know, develop that. Develop that and be kind of an all-star MVP in that department. >> And what about on the broker side? And this is actually pretty critical because, you know, because this market the industrial yard market is relatively new to being institutional. >> Yeah. >> It comes with a new playing field. You know, I and a different level of reporting, a different level of data. >> Yeah. >> Um what are some some advice you can maybe give to brokers who want to be successful um IOS brokers who do not just do business with the private users, but do business with the institutions. >> Sure. I would say that the best brokers in our business on the IOS side will come to me with an idea that is somewhat baked. It doesn't have to be fully baked, but it could say something to the they could say something to the extent of here's a deal, here are the general lease terms, or it's vacant. I've already spoken to the city. I know that you can do X, Y, and Z, and you kind of just >> They do some due diligence for you on the front end. >> Yeah. It's just like being able to speak to the property and not just sending out someone else's, you know, other someone else's idea. I think that I've seen yeah, I that pays dividends and gives us on the sponsorship side confidence that this has been somewhat baked and I should pay attention here. It's super important. And then you alluded to kind of like reporting like I think you know, when we have conversations on the leasing side or just need to share updates with capital partners being able to share the most recent comms and what's going on in the marketplace and who the players are what the trades are understanding on a very like hyper local perspective of what's going on and and also having an opinion on based off of X, Y, and Z, I think the market's going to move in this direction. That goes a very long way. And having very structured reporting that you can share internally with your capital partners, it makes them feel comfortable that they've hired the correct firm and team within that firm that is professional above board, knows how to handle an institutional quality type of process and asset. >> Yeah, and then it sounds like what you're talking about is somebody who is is to a degree like a thought leader in that space. >> Correct. >> Right? Somebody who can as a asset manager or a leasing manager you can turn to and be like this guy knows what's going on and not just puts up a sign and is waiting for somebody to walk in and lease it. >> Yeah, absolutely. And you know, we want brokers to show off to our equity partners, too, so that they realize that we have the right people for the job and that we've you know, cuz generally a lot of people will hire the individuals who sold them the opportunity and generally those people are the best because they're you know, in the mix. >> Mhm. >> Um and it's important that they show their worth and you know, how beneficial they are to the process. So, you know, we don't look at this as one transaction like I plan on being in the business for the next 20, 30 years like we want to rinse and repeat and just utilize the same people and just keep running it back each time with >> Sure. same group if possible. >> Great. >> Yeah. >> Well, I appreciate you coming today and congratulations again. Thank you so much for doing what you say you were going to do on that deal, which is incredibly important in our business. Um but yeah, thanks again. >> Thank you. >> Thank you for listening to Adding Value with Shea Salazar. We'll continue bringing on guests with stories and insights that matter in the world of industrial real estate. If you enjoyed today's episode, please share it with a friend or colleague. And if you're a landlord, tenant, or investor exploring opportunities in the Inland Empire, feel free to reach out to us. We'd be happy to help you navigate the market.

metadata.title: The Economics of Owning a Billboard
metadata.author: Stick to Wealth
metadata.shortDescription:
So you want to own a billboard. Everyone thinks it's simple — rent the sign to an advertiser, collect the check. The real machine is stranger: a billboard company is a government-protected monopoly on attention that rents out land it doesn't own. A static structure costs $20-100K to build (a digital LED one $150-500K+), but you often CAN'T build a new one — the 1965 Highway Beautification Act plus local moratoria froze new permits, so existing billboards are grandfathered and the PERMIT can be worth more than the steel (4 states ban billboards entirely). The land is usually leased for ~15-20% of revenue. Then the digital trick: one digital board rotates 6-8 advertisers on 8-second slots, multiplying the revenue of the static board it replaced. Margins are huge (Lamar ~47% EBITDA), which is why Lamar and OUTFRONT became REITs in 2014 — legally, a billboard is real estate. The risks: Clear Channel Outdoor's ~$5B debt, ad budgets cut first in recessions (OOH fell ~45% in Q2 2020), and the ultimate one — São Paulo's 2007 'Clean City Law' erased ~15,000 billboards overnight. Fact-checked; sources pinned.

metadata.title: So You Want to Own a Billboard Company
metadata.author: Rio Explains
metadata.shortDescription:
Why are billboard companies some of the most profitable businesses you've never thought about?

In this video, we explore how outdoor advertising became one of the most protected industries in America. From government regulations and permit restrictions to billion-dollar advertising companies, you'll discover why new competitors almost never enter the market—and why existing billboard owners keep making money year after year.

If you've ever wondered how a simple roadside billboard can be worth millions, this video breaks it down.

💡 Subscribe for more business, finance, and "So You Want to Own..." stories every week.

#Business #Billboards #Monopoly #Economics #Finance #Investing #BusinessExplained #Money #Advertising #Entrepreneurship

segments.text: So you want to own a billboard company.
Rent some empty air above a highway,
slap up a sign, collect a check every
month from a business that wants
eyeballs. That's the whole pitch and on
paper it sounds almost too simple to be
a real industry. Here's the number that
should stop you cold. The out-of-home
advertising industry generated over $9
billion in revenue in 2024, the highest
volume ever recorded. One single company
controls roughly a quarter of that
entire market and it didn't do it by
outspending anyone on flashy technology.
It did it by understanding something
almost nobody outside this business
realizes.
A billboard company isn't selling
advertising space. It's hoarding a piece
of government-restricted real estate
that legally cannot be replicated. And
once you understand that, the entire
economics of this industry stop looking
like a simple sign rental business and
start looking like a scarcity monopoly
hiding in plain sight. Start with the
company that built this playbook.
Lamar Advertising began in 1902 in
Pensacola, Florida as a regional poster
and signage operator.
By 2024, it had grown to more than
displays across the United States and
Canada, generated roughly $2.1 to $2.2
billion in annual revenue, and converted
itself into a real estate investment
trust in 2014, meaning it's legally
structured the same way a shopping mall
or apartment trust is.
Lamar itself says it owns about 25% of
the entire out-of-home advertising
market. That's not incremental market
share. That's one company holding a
quarter of every billboard, bus shelter,
and airport display face in North
America. And the reason it could get
that big without a serious rival ever
catching up brings us to the actual
mechanism behind this business. Here's
the part that explains everything else.
Lady Bird Johnson pushed through the
Highway Beautification Act, requiring
states to maintain effective control
over outdoor advertising along federal
highways or forfeit 10% of their federal
highway funding. The law restricts new
billboards near roughly 306,000 miles of
federal aid highway, and on top of that
federal layer, nearly every city and
county has its own local zoning
ordinance controlling where a new sign
can legally go up.
The practical result, six decades later,
is that in most major American markets,
it is now nearly impossible to get a
permit for a brand new billboard
location. Cities like Bellwood,
Illinois, have simply banned new
billboard permits outright. This means
the billboards already standing today
aren't just assets, they're licenses to
occupy a piece of scarce
government-restricted airspace that a
competitor legally cannot recreate next
door. You're not buying a sign, you're
buying one of a fixed, shrinking number
of legal advertising locations in the
entire country, and that scarcity is the
actual source of the pricing power in
this business. Now, let's talk about
what it costs to actually operate one of
these once you own the site.
A standard static billboard face
generates a real, verifiable revenue
number.
Lamar's own chief executive, Sean
Reilly, disclosed on a 2025 earnings
call that a typical static unit brings
in about $3,000 a month. That's the
baseline. But the real money in this
industry over the last two decades has
come from converting those static faces
to digital. A digital conversion costs
roughly $200,000 per unit, and here's
the mechanism that makes that number
work. A single digital face can rotate
between six to eight different
advertisers throughout the day instead
of showing one advertiser's message 24
hours a day, seven days a week.
Reilly's own numbers show that same
$3,000 a month static face jumping to
somewhere between $15,000 and $18,000 a
month after conversion, a five to six
times revenue increase from the exact
same physical location and the exact
same government permit.
Independent analysts modeling Lamar's
economics found that after accounting
for lease costs at roughly 20% of
revenue, sales commissions around 7%,
and ongoing electricity and monitoring
costs of a few hundred dollars a month,
a static to digital conversion delivers
approximately a 43% return on capital.
That's not a rounding error. That's one
of the highest returns on invested
capital of almost any physical
infrastructure asset in American
business, and it's why Lamar has been
converting 300 to 500 static faces to
digital every single year. Here's where
the ownership structure gets genuinely
clever, and it's the part almost nobody
outside the industry understands.
Billboard companies typically don't own
the land underneath their signs. They
lease it from third-party landowners,
farmers, small business owners, families
who happen to own a parcel next to a
highway on-ramp. This means the actual
capital tied up in real estate stays low
while the company controls the far more
valuable asset, the permit itself, which
is tied to the location, not the
landowner.
As of 2025, Lamar owned about 11,200 of
its billboard sites outright, roughly 3%
of its total inventory, while leasing
the vast majority.
Lamar has also been quietly buying up
permanent easements on land it doesn't
own outright, locking in the right to
keep a sign at that location
indefinitely, even if the underlying
property eventually changes hands.
You end up controlling the single most
valuable and scarce piece of the puzzle,
the government-issued right to occupy
that exact stretch of sightline, while
someone else carries the property tax
bill on the dirt underneath it.
But this business isn't invincible, and
the industry's second largest player
proves exactly how it can go wrong.
Clear Channel Outdoor, tracing its roots
back to Foster and Kleiser in 1901,
spent the 2020s buried under a debt load
built up during decades of aggressive
leveraged acquisitions across the
outdoor advertising, radio, and live
events businesses under its former
parent company.
By 2026, Clear Channel Outdoor was in
the process of going private, retreating
entirely from public markets, unable to
keep servicing that debt while local
advertising, the category that makes up
the bulk of billboard revenue, stayed
highly sensitive to the exact same
regulatory zoning restrictions that
protect the industry's scarcity.
The same rule that makes a permit
precious once you have one, the near
impossibility of building new billboards
in most markets, also means a
debt-loaded operator can't simply build
its way out of a cash crunch by adding
new locations. Compare that to Lamar,
which entered 2026 with net debt at only
about three times its annual earnings
before interest, taxes, depreciation,
and amortization. One of the lowest
leverage levels in the company's
history, and roughly $834 million in
total liquidity.
Same regulatory environment, same
scarcity-driven asset.
One operator used conservative leverage
to compound quietly for over a century.
The other used aggressive debt to grow
fast and ended up forced out of the
public markets entirely. The permits
didn't fail either company. The balance
sheet did.
So, here's the final balance sheet
collapsed into one sentence. A
government-restricted, functionally
non-replicable supply of legal
advertising locations, combined with a
digital conversion upgrade path that can
multiply revenue five to six times off
the exact same permit, has turned
billboard ownership into one of the
highest-returning, lowest-competition
real estate plays in American business,
but only for the operator disciplined
enough to keep debt low while everyone
else in the industry overleverages
chasing the same scarce inventory.
Lamar didn't win this market by building
the most billboards. It won by
understanding over 120 years that the
sign was never really the asset. The
permit was. And once a government stops
issuing new ones, whoever already holds
the old ones effectively owns a piece of
the sky that nobody else is legally
allowed to build in.

Lamar didn't win this market by building the most billboards. It won by understanding over 120 years that the sign was never really the asset. The permit was. And once a government stops issuing new ones, whoever already holds the old ones effectively owns a piece of the sky that nobody else is legally allowed to build in.

metadata.title: The Real Cost of That Billboard You See Every Day
metadata.author: Economics Decoded
metadata.shortDescription:
How does billboard advertising turn a profit when drivers see it for free? We break down the billboard business model.

We follow the money behind a roadside sign, examining the relationship between the advertiser, the operator, and the landowner. Most people assume the billboard company owns the ground beneath the sign, but the reality is that the financial structure often involves complex leasing agreements. We look at the specific costs involved in maintaining these structures and how location, visibility, and traffic flow dictate pricing.

The conversation extends into the economics of outdoor advertising, comparing traditional printed signs to modern digital displays. While digital screens allow for dynamic scheduling and multiple advertisers, they also introduce significant operational overhead and investment risks. Understanding how unsold inventory impacts total advertising revenue is key to seeing how these companies manage their bottom lines.

Subscribe for daily business breakdowns, and comment below on what other industry models you want to see analyzed next.

segments.text: A restaurant pays to put its name on a
billboard. Drivers pass it in seconds.
The restaurant never owns the sign, and
the company selling the ad may not own
the ground beneath it. So what exactly
is everyone paying for? Imagine a diner
beside a highway exit. Its owner wants
hungry drivers to notice it before they
pass the turn. A billboard offers a
chance to reach those people at that
particular place. The diner pays for
advertising space. In our example, the
billboard operator owns the structure
but rents the land. That means part of
the money coming in already has
somewhere else to go. Now the diner's
campaign ends. Traffic keeps passing,
but the operator needs another paying
customer. That's the tension behind this
business. A useful location can keep
attracting drivers without keeping its
advertising space sold. And replacing
the printed sign with a digital screen
creates more space to sell, but also a
bigger decision about what that location
can support. Start inside the diner. The
owner has empty tables and a breakfast
menu. Somewhere out on the highway,
people are deciding when to stop. The
owner could buy advertising in several
places, but for this particular message,
the geography matters. A hungry driver
approaching the exit can act on the
advertisement almost immediately. The
same driver seeing it just after the
exit has a less convenient decision to
make. That's why two identical steel
structures can offer very different
things. One faces the people the diner
wants to reach at a useful moment. The
other may face the wrong direction, sit
beyond the turn, or be difficult to see.
The diner isn't paying for the amount of
steel in the sign. It's paying for an
opportunity to be noticed. An
opportunity is exactly what it is. A car
passing a billboard does not
automatically mean someone looked at the
advertisement, remembered it, or bought
breakfast. Industry audience measurement
tries to make these distinctions useful.
Geopath, which measures outdoor
advertising audiences, describes
measures for likely exposure, the kinds
of people reached, and how often
encounter a display. Think about a
commuter passing the same sign on the
way to work. Repeated exposure may help
the message become familiar, but seeing
the same person again is different from
reaching a new person. Ten encounters do
not necessarily mean 10 different
potential customers. For our diner
owner, even an excellent audience
estimate leaves another question. Does
this advertisement bring in enough
useful business to justify its price?
Perhaps the message is too complicated
to understand from the road. Perhaps the
food pictured on the sign looks better
than the food on the plate. The
billboard operator cannot fix the eggs.
The advertiser's own business affects
whether the campaign gets renewed. That
connects what happens at the diner's
counter to what the billboard operator
can earn beside the highway. Now suppose
the operator finds another promising
stretch of road. Plenty of traffic, good
visibility, and several businesses
nearby. Why not install another sign?
Because a promising view from a car
window is only the beginning of a usable
site. First, someone controls the land.
Our operator needs an agreement with
that person. Then there is permission to
put an advertising structure there and
keep it there. Florida offers a concrete
example. Its transportation department
describes a permit process that includes
authorization from the property owner or
other lawful controller of the site,
along with documentation concerning
local requirements and land use. A
landowner agreeing to a billboard does
not, by itself, settle those other
questions. Those are Florida's
requirements. The details vary by
location. The economic point is that
permission and a usable location have to
come together. Imagine our operator
pointing to a perfect-looking patch of
grass. The diner owner likes it. The
landowner likes the proposed rent. But
if a sign cannot legally operate at that
site, the advertising plan stops there.
Now imagine a permitted site with a poor
view of approaching traffic. The
paperwork alone does not persuade the
diner to buy it. Each condition solves a
different problem. Permission allows the
business to operate. Visibility gives an
advertiser a reason to consider it.
Neither guarantees a sale.
This also explains why the landowner and
the billboard operator can be separate
people. The landowner contributes a
location. The operator takes on the job
of turning that location into an
advertising business. Lamar, a large
billboard company, openly recruits
property owners to lease land for its
displays. So this arrangement is more
than a convenient detail in our
imaginary diner story. Return to the
original sign and follow a payment. The
diner pays the operator for its
campaign. The operator owes money under
the land agreement. The person who
receives that rent doesn't necessarily
have to find the next advertiser.
In our example, let's make the land rent
a fixed payment. That makes the division
of risk easy to see. A successful
campaign can benefit the operator
without immediately changing the
landowner's payment. A gap between
campaigns can hurt the operator without
immediately reducing that payment
either. Actual agreements can work
differently. Some leases tie part of the
payment to revenue. The contract
determines how much of the ups and downs
each side shares. Then look up at the
structure. Someone had to pay to build
or acquire it. Someone has to arrange
the advertising, handle the customer,
and keep the site usable. A printed
advertisement needs to be produced and
installed. Hardware needs attention over
time. An illuminated sign needs power.
The precise bill and who pays it depend
on the job and the contract, but the
work still has to happen.
Our operator also has a sales task. The
billboard doesn't walk into the diner
and explain why this location deserves
part of the owner's advertising budget.
A person has to make that case,
negotiate the campaign, and get the next
booking ready. That is why an
advertising payment cannot be read as
the operator's income to spend. It first
supports an operation and an asset. If
borrowed money helped pay for the
structure, there are financing
obligations too. We don't need a pretend
industry average budget to see the
problem. We can isolate one question.
How much difference does it make if the
space sits unsold?
For this teaching example, assume one
advertising face earns $2,000 for each
calendar month it is sold. These are
made up terms, not a quote for a real
billboard. We're using calendar months
consistently to keep the comparison
simple. If it sells all 12 months, it
brings in $24,000 for the year. But
suppose it sells only nine months. At
the same price, that produces $18,000.
Three unsold months have removed $6,000
of revenue. We haven't calculated profit
and we haven't assumed every expense
stays identical. We have shown what
happens to the money coming in.
Think about those three months from the
roadside. The structure is still
standing. Cars are still passing. The
location has not necessarily become
useless. The operator simply hasn't
turned that time into a paid campaign.
And once that time passes, it is gone.
The operator cannot sell last Tuesday's
exposure to a customer who calls on
Friday. The next customer can buy future
advertising. That booking does not
recover the expired time as a separate
product waiting on a shelf. Meanwhile,
under our fixed rent assumption, the
land payment still comes due. The
operator needs to protect the right to
use the site even while looking for
someone to advertise on it. This makes
the sales calendar part of the assets
economics. The price of a successful
booking tells you something. How much of
the year is actually booked tells you
something else. You can see why our
operator might prefer a dependable
campaign that runs longer over a higher
priced booking followed by a long gap.
That preference would depend on the
offers available, not on a universal
rule that longer is always better.
But cutting the price has a limit. If a
customer would have paid more,
discounting sacrifices money without
adding a booking. If the price falls too
far, filling the calendar may still
leave too little to sustain the site. So
the practical job is more demanding than
keeping a sign physically occupied. The
operator needs paying demand at workable
prices.
Back at the diner, the owner considers
renewing. The advertisement has to
compete with other uses of the same
money. The operator now has a reason to
understand this customer's business, not
just the traffic outside it. Perhaps
breakfast is busy enough and the owner
wants to promote dinner instead. On a
printed billboard, a new message means
new physical advertising material. On a
digital display, the content can be
changed electronically. That flexibility
is part of the attraction of an upgrade.
Lamar describes its digital billboard
advertisements as rotating every 6 to 8
seconds and offers electronic message
changes. One display can carry different
campaigns within a repeating schedule.
For our example, imagine the diner, a
repair shop, and a furniture store
sharing the screen at different moments.
Each buys advertising in the schedule.
Each can have a reason to value that
location, but the screen has not created
more cars on the road. It has created
more ways to divide and sell exposure to
the people already passing. The diner
also no longer occupies the face
continuously during its campaign. A
driver could pass while the repair
shop's advertisement is showing. The
operator has changed the product, not
simply made identical copies of the
printed offer. That is why we cannot
multiply the printed billboard's price
by the number of advertisers and call
the result digital revenue. What each
customer receives is different and what
each will pay has to be established.
Picture the sales conversation. The
diner owner asks whether sharing the
display is worth the quoted price. The
repair shop asks which drivers the site
reaches. The furniture store wants to
know whether the schedule fits its
promotion. The operator has more
inventory to offer, but still has to
connect that inventory with customers
who value it. There is also a
substantial investment decision. In its
reporting for the end of 2025, Outfront,
another major outdoor advertising
company, put its average initial
investment for a digital billboard
display at approximately $260,000.
That is Outfront's reported average, not
a price tag for converting our fictional
sign. It gives a sense of the commitment
a large operator describes. It does not
tell us what this roadside project would
cost. An electronic display also needs
electricity and functioning equipment. A
printed billboard can use power for
lighting too. So this isn't a comparison
between a free-to-run sign and one with
bills. It is a comparison between two
different operating arrangements. The
operator should ask what the upgrade
adds after its additional costs compared
with keeping the existing sign. That
last comparison matters. Suppose the
printed billboard already has reliable
customers. Their existing revenue is
part of what the operator already has.
It cannot all be credited to the upgrade
when deciding whether the new investment
is worthwhile. The useful question is
how much better the business becomes,
how long that improvement can last, and
how much money must be committed to get
it. Our operator would also need to
establish whether a digital display is
permitted at this site. Owning a printed
billboard does not settle the approval
question for every possible replacement.
And the land agreement matters again.
Imagine paying for a major upgrade just
before the right to use the ground
becomes uncertain. The operator would be
committing money to equipment whose
usefulness depends on staying in a
particular place. Before ordering the
screen, the operator needs a credible
plan for the site, the customers, and
the time available to earn back the
investment. Digital can be a strong
choice where that plan holds together.
Where demand is thin, it can leave the
operator with expensive capacity that
customers do not buy. The diner gives us
a useful way to understand the
difference. Adding tables creates more
seats. It doesn't automatically create
more hungry people. A screen can create
more advertising opportunities, but the
operator still needs buyers for them.
The comparison has a limit. Billboard
customers can share a repeating
schedule, and their messages can change
electronically, but the investment
question is familiar. Does the
additional capacity solve a real
customer need at a price that supports
it? Now look again at the original
billboard. Three people see three
different opportunities. The diner owner
sees a chance to reach customers before
they choose an exit. The land owner sees
a use for a piece of property. The
operator sees a place where advertising
can be sold over time. Their interests
meet at that sign, but their results do
not have to be identical. The landowner
can receive the agreed rent during a
week sales period. The operator can sell
a campaign that disappoints the diner. A
busy diner can still decide another form
of advertising is a better use of its
money. A durable business needs those
relationships to keep working. The site
must remain usable, the advertising must
remain worth buying, and enough of the
payments must remain after costs to
support the operator's investment.
That's how a billboard makes money. It
gives advertisers access to a particular
audience from a particular place, and
the operator keeps what remains after
securing that place and delivering the
service. The traffic passing underneath
supplies the opportunity. Someone still
has to turn it into the next paying
customer.

metadata.title: The Economics of Owning a Billboard Network
metadata.author: Behind The Billions
metadata.shortDescription:
A billboard network is the only business on Earth that rents the same blank rectangle to a different customer every month. You don't make the product. You don't package the product. You don't ship the product. You don't even print the ad. You own a steel pole, a rectangular frame, a lighting system, and a piece of land beneath it. The advertiser does the rest. They design the ad, they pay the printer, they pay the installer, they pay the rent. And you collect a check every single month whether the ad works or not. You are the landlord of a rectangle in the sky.

It sounds like the simplest, most passive income stream in American business. And for the operator who owns the pole, it absolutely is.

But here's the paradox: a billboard network is the only business where the physical asset costs twenty thousand dollars to build, depreciates over forty years, generates fifty thousand dollars a year in revenue, and the owner still manages to lose the land beneath it because the ground lease renews every twenty years and the landlord wants a bigger cut. The billboard is not the business. The billboard is the advertising. The business is the land.

So how does a business that builds a steel pole for the price of a used car generate one of the highest returns in outdoor advertising? And why do the smartest operators in the industry treat the billboard like a legal instrument instead of a physical asset?

In this deep-dive financial breakdown, we tear apart the real economics of owning a billboard network — the three-tier system from a $20,000 single billboard to a $6 billion national operator, the brutal line items inside the annual operating budget, the hidden insider vocabulary like "traffic count" and "ground lease," and the psychological engineering that turns a piece of steel into a monthly revenue machine. We examine two real case studies of catastrophic failure: a private equity firm that bought 300 billboards for $400 million with 75% debt and lost the portfolio when ground leases doubled at renewal, and a family office that spent $30 million on digital conversion but never renegotiated the ground leases. And we end with the tycoon operators who actually mastered the system: Lamar Advertising, Outfront Media, and Clear Channel Outdoor.

The net margin on owning a billboard network is positive and reliable. Sixty to eighty percent at the property level for the best operators. Every year. That is one of the highest net margins in all of commercial real estate. The system is rigged for the operator who owns the billboard and controls the ground lease — never for the small operator who buys a billboard, signs a short ground lease, and hopes the landowner renews at the same rent.

If you want more deep-dives into the hidden economics of massive assets, hit like, drop your thoughts in the comments, and subscribe.

conversion is not just a technology

the physical asset. A billboard that was
worth $200,000 becomes worth $1 million
after conversion. The fatal flaw is not
the advertiser contract. It is the
ground lease and the regulatory
environment. Case study one, the
over-leveraged portfolio. In 2018, a
private equity firm bought a portfolio

stable advertiser demand, growing

unchanged. The company filed for

office bought a portfolio of 100

invest in the ground lease renewal

demanded 40 to 80% rent increases. The
converted billboards could not cover the
higher rent and the debt service
together. The portfolio was sold to a
national operator at a loss in 2023. The
digital conversion was not the problem.
The ground leases were the problem. The
professionals exist because the system
is too complex to improvised. So, here
is the final balance sheet. A billboard
network is a land lease arbitrage
wrapped around a monthly advertiser
contract wrapped around a digital
conversion strategy. The equation is
simple. Revenue per panel times number
of panels minus ground lease rent minus
operating cost minus debt service minus
capital expenditure equals your true
profit. For most billboard portfolios,
that number is between 50% and 70% net
margin at the property level. For the
national operators, that number is
between 30% and 50% after corporate
overhead. The net margin on owning a
billboard network is positive and
reliable. 60% to 80% at the property
level for the best operators. Every
year, that is one of the highest net
margins in all of commercial real
estate. And it is one of the most
underrated. The tycoon who mastered this
system was not a single person. It was
the executive teams at Lamar
Advertising, Outfront Media, and Clear
Channel Outdoor who understood that the
billboard business is not about
advertising. It is about real estate,
ground leases, and digital conversion.
They bought the billboards. They secured
the ground leases. They converted to
digital. They repriced the contracts.
They made money on the rent, the
advertiser fees, the digital upgrades,
and the land appreciation. They never
depended on any single advertiser. The
system is rigged for the operator who
owns the billboard and controls the
ground lease. It is rigged for the
national operator that can convert to
digital at scale. It is rigged for the
REIT that can refinance at investment
grade rates. It is never rigged for the
small operator who buys a billboard,
signs a short ground lease, and hopes
the landowner renews at the same rent.
They did not buy a billboard network.
They bought a land lease arbitrage with
steel poles attached. That is not
advertising. That is a real estate
business that happens to rent rectangles
in the sky. And the driver does not
care. But the ground lease does.

metadata.title: What Does Lamar Really Sell The Dirt Under the Billboard
metadata.author: Plain Sight
metadata.shortDescription:
Some of America's invisible empires do not sit on a screen but on a pole beside the highway, standing on ground few drivers think about. This video follows Lamar Advertising, which says it has operated under the Lamar name since 1902, from a poster shop in Pensacola and a 1908 coin toss to about 159,300 billboard displays in 45 states and Canada, per its 2025 annual report. What does Lamar really sell: the ad, the pole, or the permission to stand there? Along the way: the Highway Beautification Act, an Austin sign case, and about 71,500 leased sites. We stick to filings, statutes and court opinions, and we mark where the company is speaking for itself.

#invisibleempires #plainsight #lamar #billboards

CHAPTERS
0:00 The dirt under the pole
1:25 A coin toss in Pensacola
4:27 Washington steps in
6:26 Just compensation
8:23 What the filing says
10:15 The Austin sign case
12:39 Who owns the ground
14:59 Who rents the space
15:38 Logo signs
16:42 Tobacco and acquisitions
18:16 REIT and the Reilly family
19:21 Lamar today
22:49 Back to the pole

SOURCES
Filings, statutes and court opinions (Tier A):
1. Lamar Advertising Company, Form 10-K for fiscal year ended December 31, 2025: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1090425/000109042526000008/lamr-20251231.htm
2. Lamar Advertising Company, Form 10-Q for quarter ended June 30, 2026: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1090425/000109042526000024/lamr-20260630.htm
3. Highway Beautification Act provisions, 23 U.S.C. 131 (govinfo): https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCODE-2023-title23/html/USCODE-2023-title23-chap1-sec131.htm
4. City of Austin v. Reagan National Advertising of Austin, Supreme Court opinion (No. 20-1029): https://www.law.cornell.edu/supremecourt/text/20-1029
5. Maine Revised Statutes, Title 23, section 1901: https://legislature.maine.gov/statutes/23/title23sec1901.html
Company history (Tier B, attributed in the video):
6. Lamar Advertising Company history, FundingUniverse: https://www.fundinguniverse.com/company-histories/lamar-advertising-history/

DISCLAIMER
This video is for educational and documentary purposes only. It does not constitute investment, legal, or financial advice. Corporate and operational figures are drawn from filings with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, statutes, court opinions and published company history; statements the company makes about itself are described as the company's own statements. Plain Sight is an independent documentary channel and is not affiliated with Lamar Advertising or any company mentioned.

segments.text: Next time you drive out of town, look up at the big billboard with the lawyer, the burger, or the clinic on it.
Now look lower, at the base of the pole, where it meets a small patch of ordinary dirt.
You have passed it more times than you can count, and you have probably not wondered who owns it.
Here is the odd part: the report says bulletin ads generally run four to fifty-two weeks, while site leases run from month-to-month to more than ten years.
Meet Lamar Advertising, a company that says it has operated under the Lamar name since 1902.
Its annual report says it operates about one hundred fifty-nine thousand three hundred billboard displays in forty-five states and Canada.
So is Lamar a sign company, or a company whose real product is the legal right to a patch of ground?
Stay for a coin toss, the opponents who enlisted Lady Bird Johnson, and an Austin rule letting owners keep old signs in place without added light or new technology.
You will not need a finance degree for any of this; you just need to keep one eye on the pole.
And stay for the company's own filing, which says regulations generally pose a significant barrier to entry and expansion in many markets.
The story starts in 1902 in Pensacola, Florida, where a man named J.M. Coe ran a small poster company promoting the coming attractions at the opera house.
Back then, the company's history says, a billboard was nothing more than a town or city wall space used to advertise businesses or, just as often, upcoming public events.
In the early years many billboards were hand-painted right on the display surface, which the same history calls a tedious process.
In 1905, a banker named Charles W. Lamar, Sr., who was president of the American National Bank of Pensacola, became Coe's partner.
You can already guess the problem: the two men owned the opera house and the poster business together.
Then, in 1908, they decided to break up, and they settled it the way two kids settle who gets the last cookie: with a coin toss.
Coe won the more lucrative opera house, while Lamar lost the toss and got the poster business.
If you have ever settled something with a coin, take comfort: so did these two, and the loser still got a business out of it.
After the coin toss split the partnership, Lamar took the poster business and named the new firm Lamar Advertising.
The history says that before the company's first decade ended, it became clear the auto would soon replace the horse and buggy and that roads would be needed.
By 1926, Lamar and his two sons had bought the Baton Rouge Poster Advertising Company and renamed it Lamar Advertising Company of Baton Rouge.
Baton Rouge is still where the company keeps its management headquarters.
But then came the Great Depression, and the company's markets were in states with few paved roads.
Yet the history says the company soon turned roadside advertising into its primary business.
Charles Lamar died in 1944 and left the business to his son Charles, Jr. and his two daughters.
Between 1940 and 1960, the history says, yearly revenue across the whole industry grew from forty-four point seven million dollars to more than two hundred million.
In 1958, a new period of expansion for Lamar began under president and CEO Kevin Reilly, Sr.
Reilly had married Charles Lamar, Sr.'s granddaughter, which made him the third generation of family management.
Over the next fifteen years, the history says, Lamar bought eight more companies in Florida, Alabama, and Louisiana.
Remember that family name, because it comes back later.
So who was angry enough about the signs to ask Washington for help?
Critics felt the industry was cluttering American highways with eyesores and blocking out the natural beauty of the landscape.
The history says that, enlisting the aid of Lady Bird Johnson, the industry's opponents prompted a milestone piece of legislation.
The law was the Highway Beautification Act of 1965, which that history describes as designed to limit and govern outdoor advertising along more than three hundred thousand miles of federal highways.
In the statute's own words, Congress found that signs along the Interstate and primary systems should be controlled to protect the public investment, the safety of travel, and natural beauty.
A state that did not provide effective control faced a ten percent cut in some of its federal highway money.
The company's history says the act ended the indiscriminate erection of billboards along federally funded roads, and that it was a heavy blow to the industry.
It also says the act brought the growth in billboard displays to a virtual standstill.
Along the Interstate and primary systems, signs may go up within six hundred sixty feet of the road's edge in areas zoned industrial or commercial under state law.
State and local zoning rules imposed permit requirements and specified where displays could go and how big they could be.
Picture a pizza shop owner who is told the town will issue no more pizza licenses, ever.
If you have ever tried to build a fence and been told by the town that it is the wrong height, you already know how these rules feel.
What would that do to the shops that already hold licenses?
The law also says just compensation shall be paid when a sign lawfully erected under state law, but not permitted under the federal limits, is removed.
Lamar's annual report says the same about federal-aid primary and interstate highways: a government that compels a lawful billboard off must pay just compensation.
But here is the quiet twist: under that section, no sign has to be removed if the federal share of the compensation is not available.
Imagine you are told to move out, and the money for your moving fee never arrives.
The same section lets states set stricter limits than Washington does on signs along federal-aid highways, subject to the just compensation rule.
Maine's billboard law says the scattering of outdoor advertising throughout the state is detrimental to the preservation of its scenic resources.
It adds that the proliferation in number, size, and manner of outdoor advertising is hazardous to highway users.
Lamar's report puts the pattern in one line: all states have passed billboard control laws at least as restrictive as the federal requirements.
Those laws include removing illegal signs at the owner's expense, without compensation from the state.
Yet the same report says no state where Lamar operates has banned billboards outright.
But what about the towns and counties?

The report says municipal and county governments generally have sign controls in their zoning laws, and some local governments prohibit new billboards or allow new construction only to replace existing structures.
Now imagine you are a company that wants to put up a brand-new billboard in one of those places.
But strip away the poetry, and the filing says net revenues come primarily from renting advertising space on displays the company owns and operates.
The company says it manages its business through three operating segments: billboard, logo, and transit advertising.
The report also says regulations generally restrict the size, spacing, and lighting of structures.
Remember that these statements are the company's own view, because the company wrote them.
But even so, the report says that from time to time governments have required the company to remove signs and billboards legally erected under permit requirements and laws.
It also describes a concept called amortization, where a government asserts that a billboard owner has already earned compensation by continued operation over time.
Under that idea, local governments have attempted to force removal of legal but nonconforming billboards, meaning ones that conformed to the zoning when built but not to the current rules.
The report adds that the legality of amortization is questionable, but that it has been upheld in some instances.
The company says it has generally been able to obtain satisfactory compensation for billboards purchased or removed by government action, though it gives no assurance that this will continue.
States have also used federal transportation money to buy billboards and take them down for beautification, the report says.
And Lamar says it is involved in routine administrative and judicial proceedings over billboard permits, fees, and compensation for condemnations.
To see how this plays out, go to Texas.
As the Supreme Court described it, the Austin sign code prohibited building any new off-premises signs but allowed existing ones to remain as grandfathered non-conforming signs.
Off-premises signs, as the Court described them, advertise things not located on the same premises as the sign.
The owner of a grandfathered sign could change the face of the sign, but could not change the technology used to convey a message or increase its illumination.
Translation: you may keep the grandfathered sign, but you may not upgrade the way it shows its message.
In 2017, Lamar and another company, Reagan National Advertising of Austin, both applied for permits to digitize their existing off-premises signs.
The city applied its sign code and denied the applications.
Reagan sued the city in state court, alleging that the prohibition violated the First Amendment.
The city removed the case to federal court, and Lamar intervened as a plaintiff.
After a bench trial, the district court entered judgment in favor of the city.
But in 2020 the Fifth Circuit reversed and held that the sign code's distinction was content based.
The Supreme Court heard the case in November 2021 and decided it on April 21, 2022.
It held that the city's on-premises and off-premises distinction was facially content neutral under the First Amendment.

metadata.title: The Economics of Owning a Billboard Company
metadata.author: Ned Talks Business
metadata.shortDescription:
A single billboard permit can be worth more than the steel holding it up.

In some cities, you literally cannot build a new one — the legal right to display an ad is frozen in place, and the only way in is to buy someone out.

This is the real economics of owning a billboard company.

Most people assume billboards are passive income: put up a sign, collect a check. But the operators who actually make serious money aren't selling advertising — they're sitting on an appreciating, government-protected monopoly that gets harder to replicate every single year.

We dig into what a 35-board mid-market portfolio actually costs to run, why Lamar Advertising posts 50% EBITDA margins, how the Reagan Outdoor family turned a regional play into a repeated acquisition target, and what the math looks like for a solo operator in year one versus year seven.

Would you rather own a billboard company or just advertise on one? Drop your answer below.

If you enjoyed this, hit like and subscribe for more on the economics behind everything.

📑 VIDEO CHAPTERS
0:00 Intro
1:07 The real cost
4:12 How the money flows
6:45 Hidden costs
9:20 Who's winning
12:03 How people lose
13:35 The profit math

——————————————
SOURCES
——————————————
▸ Lamar Advertising 2023 annual revenue and EBITDA figures: Lamar Advertising Company Annual Report, 2023
▸ Clear Channel Outdoor US revenue 2023: Clear Channel Outdoor Holdings Annual Report, 2023
▸ Outfront Media 2023 revenue: Outfront Media Inc. Annual Report, 2023
▸ Highway Beautification Act billboard regulations: Federal Highway Administration, U.S. Department of Transportation
▸ US outdoor advertising revenue decline during 2008–2009 recession: Outdoor Advertising Association of America (OAAA), industry data
▸ Billboard construction and digital LED conversion costs: OAAA industry benchmarks and operator surveys, 2020–2023
▸ Billboard REIT classification and tax treatment: IRS guidance on REIT qualifying income, real property definitions
▸ Vermont, Maine, Hawaii, Alaska highway billboard bans: Federal Highway Administration state compliance reports

metadata.shortDescription:
So You Want to Own a Cell Tower? The Real Numbers Behind the Rent




Somewhere near you, a steel pole on a tiny patch of land collects rent from some of the biggest corporations on Earth, month after month. In this video we break down the real numbers behind cell towers: build costs, tenant rent, margins, zoning, and the quiet ground-lease buyout business that landowners rarely understand.

CHAPTERS
0:00 The pole that collects rent
0:18 What is a cell tower business?
0:36 The questions we answer
0:48 Misconception #1: carriers own the towers
1:30 Why a tower works like an apartment building
1:42 A real lease: tenants, rent, and escalators
2:00 Why the second tenant is almost pure profit
2:30 What a tower costs to build
3:00 Scenario 1: one tenant
3:12 Scenario 2: two tenants
3:24 The tenancy ratio explained
3:36 Costs: land, permits, terrain
3:54 The ground lease underneath
4:06 Colocation: the cheap path for carriers
4:24 The zoning and permit moat
4:36 FCC shot clocks explained
5:12 Why the delay protects existing towers
5:30 The ground-lease buyout twist
6:30 Risks: carrier mergers, tenants, debt, small cells
7:30 Margins: what the real numbers say
7:54 Returns by number of tenants
8:36 Strategic takeaway
9:00 Lessons for landowners and investors
9:36 Final thoughts

SOURCES USED
American Tower FY2025 10-K and Q4 2025 earnings release, SBA Communications reported figures, FCC tower cost and shot clock materials, and a public New York town tower lease. The two-tenant return model is my own simplified illustration (about $275K build cost, $2,000/month per tenant, 75% margin).

DISCLAIMER
This video is for education and entertainment only. It is not investment, legal, or financial advice. Numbers vary widely by location, tower height, ground rent, and tenants.

Subscribe for more breakdowns of hidden money flows and unit economics. Comment which business you want next: billboards, self-storage, or car washes.
