segments.text: Somewhere near you, there is a tall
steel pole standing on a patch of land
smaller than your backyard. It looks
boring. It makes almost no noise, but
the company that owns it collects rent
from some of the biggest corporations on
Earth every single month and almost
never loses a tenant. That pole is a
cell tower, and while most people see an
ugly piece of infrastructure, American
Tower turned this exact business into
roughly 10 and 1/2 billion dollars in
annual revenue with margins most
software companies would envy. So today,
we are breaking down the real numbers.
What does a tower actually cost to
build? Who pays the rent? How many
tenants does it take to make money? And
why are landowners being quietly offered
cash to sell their lease? Here is the
misconception. Most people assume a cell
tower is owned by the phone company,
like Verizon or T-Mobile, and for a long
time that was true. Carriers built their
own towers, paid for them, and kept them
on their books. But carriers are in the
business of selling wireless service,
not owning steel. So over the years,
they sold or leased their towers to
specialized companies and then rented
space back. Fixed costs became monthly
bills. The second misconception is about
who makes the money.
People think the tower business is about
phone signals. It is not. It is a real
estate business, and the product is
simply space at height in a spot nobody
else can easily get permission to build.
Think of a tower like a landlord who
owns a skinny apartment building with
room for several tenants. One tower can
hold antennas from multiple carriers,
each paying rent for their own spot on
the structure. In one real lease from a
town in New York, Verizon started at
$2,500 a month in 2014, rising 3% every
year.
Later, Dish added its equipment to the
same tower, paying roughly $1,300
monthly, rising 2% annually. Notice what
happened. The tower did not change.
Nobody poured new concrete. The second
tenant simply showed up, and almost all
of that new rent dropped straight
profit. American Towers' own annual
filing says this directly, and these
leases are sticky. Initial terms
typically run five to 10 years with
multiple renewals and built-in annual
increases. American Tower reports more
than $54 billion of contracted future
lease revenue, and customer churn was
only about 2% last year. Now let's build
the math. According to an FCC report, a
new tower costs somewhere between $150
American Towers' own rule of thumb for
the United States was roughly 200 25 to
though that figure is more than a decade
old, so today's number is likely higher.
So let's use a round number, $275,000.
That covers the site work, the permits,
the foundation, the steel, the fencing,
and the power hookup. The carriers bring
their own antennas and radios. Scenario
one, a single tenant paying $2,000 a
month. That is $24,000
a year. Take away costs and a 75%
margin, you keep about 18,000. Payback?
Roughly 15 years. Scenario two, a second
tenant arrives at the same price.
Revenue doubles to 48,000. Profit rises
to about 36,000 and payback drops to
under eight years. Same tower, same
land, one extra phone company. That is
why the whole industry obsesses over one
number, the tenant ratio, which means
average tenants per tower.
SBA Communications, another major tower
company, reported about 1.8 tenants per
site. Every fraction above one is mostly
profit. Of course, nothing is free.
Building from scratch means finding a
site, signing a ground lease with a
landowner, and surviving the permitting
process.
Costs swing widely with height, soil,
and location, so a tall tower in
difficult terrain can cost far more than
our round number.
Then there is the ground lease, the
quiet cost underneath everything.
The tower owner usually pays the
landowner monthly rent, often with
annual increases,
and that rent comes straight out of the
margin we calculated earlier. Here is
where it gets interesting.
Adding a tenant to an existing tower
called co-location costs the carrier
roughly 30 percent of what a new tower
would cost according to that same FCC
report.
So renting space on an existing tower is
the cheap path and that keeps towers
like ours full. Now the real moat. You
cannot just plant a steel tower wherever
you like. Neighbors object, councils
hold hearings and zoning boards worry
about how it looks. Federal rules limit
how long a town can stall, but the
clocks are still long. Under FCC shot
clocks, a town has 150 days to decide on
a brand new tower and 90 days for adding
equipment to an existing one. For
certain simple upgrades under a law
called Section 6409, the clock is just
60 days and if the town misses it, the
request is deemed approved. But for new
towers, a missed deadline does not mean
approval. The builder has to sue and in
practice an FCC commissioner has said a
new macro tower can take about two
years. Once you count hearings, permits,
and construction, that delay is the
moat. A rival who wants to challenge an
existing tower needs two years, a new
landowner, and a fresh approval. A tower
that is already standing, already
permitted, and already full is extremely
hard to copy. Now for the twist most
landowners never see coming. Remember
the ground lease?
The person who owns the land under a
tower collects a modest monthly rent and
a whole industry exists to buy that
income stream from them. Companies like
Landmark Dividend and American Tower run
divisions that offer landowners a lump
sum of cash for the rights to that
future rent.
One landowner was reportedly approached
19 times in three years. Buyout letters
have used valuations of roughly nine to
12 times annual rent according to one
industry publication.
So a landowner earning 15,000 dollars a
year might see an offer between 135 and
180,000 dollars and give up decades of
rent that keeps rising. To be fair, that
money is real and taking it can make
sense for some owners. But consultants
who negotiate these deals claim lease
terms are often weak with no escalator
and no share of revenue from added
tenants. Those are sellers of advice, so
treat their claims as one side of the
story. Now the risks. First, tenant
concentration. A tower's income depends
on a handful of big carriers, and when
carriers merge, they can shut down
duplicate equipment. When two networks
combine, the combined company may no
longer need both sets of antennas.
Second, financial strength. Some tenants
are not as stable as others. If a
carrier struggles, it can try to cancel
or renegotiate its leases. That is why
long contracts matter and why churn near
2% stands out. Third, interest rates and
debt. Towers are often bought with
borrowed money, and American Tower
itself used about $2 billion from an
asset sale to pay down debt and return
to its target leverage. When rates rise,
tower valuations can fall even if rent
keeps growing. Fourth, technology. If
wireless demand shifts towards small
cells and fiber, some of the need for
tall macro towers could change. An FCC
report estimated small cell sites cost
less than half as much per site, which
makes them a real alternative in dense
cities. So what do the real numbers say?
American Tower reported property gross
margin of 75% last year and an adjusted
EBITDA margin of 67%
on more than $10 billion of revenue. SBA
Communications reports a tower cash flow
margin near 80% at the tower level. For
context, many restaurants, retailers,
and manufacturers would be thrilled with
a margin of 10 or 15 % but margin is not
the same as return. Our single tower
earns about $18,000 a year after costs
on $275,000 invested. That is a return
about 6.5% before debt, taxes, and any
rent increases. Add a second tenant and
that return jumps to about 13 %. Add a
third and it approaches 20 %. And
remember, escalators of 2 to 3 % a year
push those numbers higher, even if
nobody new ever arrives. These are
simplified numbers, not investment
advice. Real towers vary by location,
height, ground rent, and who the tenants
are. But the shape of the curve is the
point. The first tenant pays the bills,
and every tenant after that pays you. So
here is the strategic takeaway. The
tower business is not really about steel
or signals. It is about scarcity.
Permission to build is scarce. Good
locations are scarce, and once a tower
stands, every extra tenant is highly
profitable. Whoever owns the pole owns
the toll booth. Whoever owns the land
under it owns a smaller toll booth with
a steady rising check. And whoever buys
that check from a landowner is betting
that the rent grows faster than the
discount. If you are a landowner
approached by a buyer, the lesson is
simple. Know your escalator, know your
tenant count, and get an independent
valuation before you sign anything. If
you are an investor, the lesson is to
ask one question first. How many tenants
does this tower have? Next time you
drive past one of these poles, remember
what you are looking at. It is not just
infrastructure. It is a contract, a
lease, a zoning approval, and a stream
of rent that keeps compounding quietly
while almost nobody looks up. That is
what a hidden money flow looks like in
real life. If this breakdown showed you
something new, subscribe because the
next video covers another business
hiding behind a boring piece of real
estate. Tell me in the comments which
business you want broken down next. A
billboard, a storage facility, or a car
wash. Thanks for watching, and I will
see you in the next one.

metadata.title: How to Negotiate a Cell Tower Lease - Part One
metadata.author: Tower Genius
metadata.shortDescription:
Wondering how to negotiate a cell tower lease and what to do if a cell tower site acquisition company hands you a blank lease without any pricing filled in? Whenever a property owner receives a blank cell tower template without any rental terms such as annual or monthly rent, length of the lease, or rent increases, it's an indicator that the cell tower agent is either lazy or trying to rip you off, or both. NEVER negotiate against yourself. Allow them to make you an offer. It's okay to tell them that you have no idea what the value of a cell tower lease is, ask them to kindly make you some kind of offer. Do not blink first. Do not tell them any kind of price or business terms until they have made you an offer. And even then, do not negotiate back and forth. If you are interested in possibly having a cell tower build on your property, tell them you will consider their offer and get back to them. Any negotiating that you do from your front porch or over the phone on an initial call can only hurt you, not help you.

Have you been presented with a skeleton lease, all bones and no meat? Call Tower Genius at 888-313-9750 or visit https://www.towergenius.com/blog/how-to-negotiate-a-cell-tower-lease-part-one/

metadata.title: POV: The Cell Tower Lot Pays You $2,100 a Month
metadata.author: Time Ticket
metadata.shortDescription:
Your uncle laughed when you paid $4,000 at a county auction for a weedy scrap of land behind a gas station. Then a tower company knocked on your door. In this story you become Ezra, and we go through how cell tower ground leases really work: why a phone company will pay rent for a patch of dirt the size of a garage, what goes into the lease, how the rent grows, why companies offer to buy your lease for one big check, and the day you have to decide: $330,000 today, or $2,100 a month for decades, with the risk that the tower could one day be switched off.

🔑 The money ideas in this story:
1. Land can earn rent even when nothing is built on it, if someone needs that exact spot
2. Read the escalator: how fast the rent rises matters as much as the starting rent
3. A lump-sum offer should be compared with what the future rent is worth today, not with the total of all future payments
4. Every lease can end: merged phone companies switch off towers they no longer need

📊 Numbers in this story (a simple model, not advice): rent $2,100 a month rising 3% a year; 30 years of rent adds up to about $1.2 million, but valued at a 7% discount rate it is worth about $430,000 today; the buyout offer is $330,000. Real tower leases, rents and offers vary widely by location and contract. After the T-Mobile and Sprint merger, T-Mobile said it planned to decommission tens of thousands of overlapping sites (company statements).

💬 Would you take the $330,000 today, or keep the $2,100 a month? 👇

Glossy paper, big friendly logo. A company that specializes in buying tower leases wanted to pay you one lump sum today in exchange for all your future rent. $330,000 right now. No waiting. That's life-changing money. It's more than you've earned in 10 years at the warehouse. So it seems obvious. Take it right. Here's the trap. Most people compare the offer with the total of all the future rent. $1.2 million against $330,000. That makes the offer look terrible, but that's the wrong comparison. A dollar 30 years from now is worth much less than a dollar today. You could invest today's dollar and inflation slowly shrinks tomorrow's. So you have to ask, what is all that future rent worth right now? If you assume you could earn about 7% a year elsewhere, 30 years of your rising rent is worth about $430,000 today, more than the offer. So on paper, the rent wins. But there's one thing the math assumes, that the tower stays. And towers don't always stay. When phone companies merge, they often end up with two towers covering the same area. After T-Mobile merged with Sprint, the company said it planned to shut down tens of thousands of overlapping sites. If your tower is one of the extras, the rent can simply stop. So the lump sum isn't just money. It's insurance. You're selling the risk to someone else. The question is how big that risk is for your tower. You made three phone calls. One to the tower company to ask how many phone companies were on your tower. The answer was three. One to a lawyer and one to a second lease buyer to get another offer. Three carriers on one tower on a busy highway in the only spot with coverage is about as safe as a tower gets. The second buyer offered 370,000 just because someone else was bidding. And in the end, you said no to both. You kept the rent, not because the lump sum was bad, but because your tower looks strong, and because $2,000 a month already covered your rent and then some. The honest part, you might be wrong. In 10 years, a new technology or another merger could switch your tower off, and you'd wish you'd taken the check. Plenty of landowners take the lump sum, and for them, it's the right call, especially if they need the money now or the tower looks weak. The point isn't which choice is right for everyone. It's to compare the offer with what the future rent is worth today. Ask how safe the tower really is, and always get a second offer. At the barbecue this summer, your uncle didn't mention motorcycles. He asked if there were any more land auctions coming up. Most land is just land, but a patch of dirt in exactly the right place can be worth more than a building. So, would you take the 330,000 today or keep the 2,100 a month? Pick one in the comments.

And for the last 15 plus years, we see letters from different companies that go out to property owners all across the United States. They say, "Look, the end is near. If you don't reduce your rent, we're, you know, the cell tower industry is changing and we may have to just take down your tower and you're going to lose your revenue." But I'm here to save you. If you reduce your rent from, let's say, $1,500 to $1,000, we'll save you. But there's two problems with that. There's more than two, but there's two big ones. One is that most of the times they're not going to move the tower. I can't say 100% but I'd say 99 and a half percent they're not moving it. It depends upon the individual situation. So you have to know that. But that's just a tactic. They get paid to get you to reduce your rent. The other thing here is let's say you agree to every term they want you to agree to. You agree to a rent reduction. You agree to other terms that are beneficial to them. You agree to extend your lease out even though they said the end is near. They want more time which is counterintuitive. But you agreed all that. What keeps them from doing these two things? Coming back to a year later and saying, "We're going to take the tower down." Nothing. Because they didn't give you any guarantees. They just got you to pay you less money. The second thing is what keeps them from coming back a year or three years, five years later and say, "Hey, I know back in 2025 or whenever we got you to reduce rent, we need you to do it again and then again and then again and then again." They just keep on playing the same card. So you need to understand your individual situations, but this is just a numbers game. They contact people over and over and over and eventually a certain percentage of those people will agree to that rent reduction. And there's only two parties that benefit from that. And one of them is not you. It's the company that's working for the cell tower company and the cell tower company. Okay. And Chris from Ohio asks, "Is it better to sign a short-term lease with renewals or a longer fixedterm lease?" >> Well, most leases are somewhere when they come out now, it's looking looking like they're asking for 50 years plus. And those are usually broken down to initial five-year term and multiple fiveyear renewals. So, the best way I can explain this is what you're trading when you're negotiating a cell tower lease is you're getting money and you're committing to them. They're not committing to you. You're committing to them for a period of time. So, you want to give them as least amount of time as possible. It's a commodity. Time is a commodity. So, you're trying to get initially or any time through lease. Get get something in exchange, but don't give up too much. So, we try to get people to agree to leases that are far less than 50 years because they will be able to renegotiate sooner than later. So, and what I mean is if you agree to, let's say, a 30-year lease, it's not going to be 30 years before you have to be able to renegotiate because once they get under a certain number of years, that being the cell tower company, they need to think of it like a gas tank you're driving down the road. They need to put more gas in it before they get close to empty. They're not going to wait till the, you know, that tank runs dry. So you have the ability to renegotiate sooner than later. So time is a tricky thing. You need to play it right when you're negotiating a lease, but don't give up too much and not get enough in return. >> Okay. Yeah. Uh Maria from Arizona wants to know uh what is a rent escalator and what is what's a reasonable uh rent escalator today? Well, that's a a good question because we're seeing across the country, especially in the last three, four years when inflation was skyrocketing up to over 9% that cell tower companies were coming in trying to get property owners and still trying to get property owners agree to a 2% 1% half percent or even no escalator at all on the rent. And you have to get an escalator that keeps you of inflation. People think of an escalator as a rent increase. It really isn't because a rent escalator hopefully keeps you up with inflation. That means if you're getting a dollar today, inflation grows 3%, you get a 3% escalator, you're effectively just getting another dollar in spending power. So you have to get an escalator to keep up with inflation. So there's two ways to do that. One is the best way, and the cell tower companies hate it, is a a consumer price index, a CPI, which basically just tracks inflation. And that just means if inflation is 2%, it grows 2%. If it's 9% it goes up 9%. They just don't like it because they have to keep track of it. They want a fixed rate and they want a fixed rate really low. So the other way is historically over the last 25 years the inflation rate's been right around 3%. So if you get a 3% fixed escalator historically you're going to be pretty safe. You may be a little bit below inflation, you may be a little bit above inflation, but historically you're going to be able to do it. The other thing here is you got to make sure you get a yearly escalator, not every five years. Because if you don't get a yearly escalator, it's not compounding. One of the misperceptions, people say, "Well, I get a 15% or a 10% escalator every five years." And they say, "Well, I have a 2% or 3% uh annual increase." No, you don't. Because it's only increasing every five years, so it's not compounding during that little bit of time. And if you start looking at what the difference is between only having a 2% escalator or a 3% escalator over a 20 30-year term, it's tens of thousands if not more, hundreds of thousands of dollars that you lose. That's why the cell tower companies fight for every nickel because they know that nickel turns into a quarter and that quarter turn turns into a dollar and then over years it makes up a whole lot of money on their side of the ledger and not on yours. Great. Uh Ryan from Texas asks, "How much could I how much control do I really have over a tenant adding more equipment or subleasasing space?" >> Well, uh couple thing there. That's a couple different questions, but I'll try to address both of them. With regards to adding equipment, one of the things you have to know when you presented a lease or you have an existing lease, most of the time the lease says they can modify, add equipment, do whatever they want to inside that space they're leasing. And that's a problem because they're trying to add equipment to get more value out of your property and you don't have any control over. You can't renegotiate based upon them getting more value. So you need to have certain controls on that to be able to renegotiate based upon what they're doing on your property, not just how much space they're taking. The other thing is it's for a control issue as well. If you don't have some control over your property, if you think about it, what's on your property? You don't know. You have liability issues. You have other issues with regards to their use. And you're just saying, "Well, I they're in there, but I don't know what they have, and I don't know how I need to address those things from a liability issue or use issue." So you really need to understand that having some oversight over what they have inside that space is important not only from a monetary perspective but also control and liability perspective. From a subleasasing perspective the best answer I can give you there with space is this. The more subtenants they add to the tower the more space they need on the ground. So what you need to do is you're trading space initially and going through the lease. You need to understand the value of that space not only today but going forward. A lot of cell tower companies come out and they ask for 10,000 square feet of space. If they build a tower the next day, you'd see about 7,000 square feet not being used. They're just gathering up as much space they can so they don't have to come back and ask for it later. And they're just going to make money off that space, not doing anything to it. They're just going to take your property and lease it out to somebody else and they're going to make money from it. So, control the space and you'll get more money. >> Great. Yeah. Uh, a Judy from Minnesota asks, "I'm worried about the impact on future development of my land. What relocation rights should I keep in the lease?" >> That's a great question. This is something that's mostly overlooked by property owners because they look at a lease as what's in front of them right now and not what's going to happen 10, 15, 20 years from now. And so, you need to have this one word flexibility. flexibility not with only relocation but flexibility in general because none of us know exactly what the future's going to hold tomorrow more or less 101 15 years from now. So you need to get relocation rights in the lease that state if you need to relocate them and I what I mean by that is not just the cell tower but you think about they're running utilities across your property. They need access roads across your property and if you ever want to sell your property or redevelop it you need to have the ability to maybe relocate those. So it's not just the physical tower. So, you need to get relocation right. So, if you need to have them to move some of those things, there's a pathway already built in the lease, that's a contractual obligation for them to work with you to be able to do that. If not, you are basically at their mercy. And I'm I promise you, they're not going to be very receptive to help you out to try to relocate certain items on the on the property that would only benefit you. >> Right. Yeah. Cindy from North Carolina says, "Uh, are there situations where selling the lease outright makes more sense than holding on to it?" Sandy, that's a great question, but I'll give you a quick answer on this is we get contacted by property owners about selling the leases and 90 plus% we tell them not to. There's only three reasons you should ever sell a cell tower lease. One is you need the money and that's a personal decision. You just have to have it right now. for whatever reasons you may have. The second reason is that you have a great way of taking that money and that you would get from a selling the cell tower lease and reinvesting it. Now, that's again personal to you and we can't answer that, but we can tell you there's very few investments that have a good a return as a cell tower lease based upon the passive income that you're getting from a cell tower agreement. And the third is, and we can't help you with this, is to hedge against risk. you think, well, I think this the rent's going to go away. I think certain things are going to happen and I better sell it now. Now, that is uncommon, but it does happen. There's certain leases that you need to be ahead of before you get behind u and you need to basically liquidate those leases. So, I will tell you nine plus times out of ten, we tell people to hold their lease, don't sell it, but if there's certain situations, we're there to help them try to get the most out of it and also to limit the terms they're agreeing to in exchange for it. People ask us, you know, how much money can I get out of selling this lease? They don't ever ask most of the time, what am I agreeing to to do that? And you need to understand what you're agreeing to. Say, if I came to you and you you think of a figure in your head right now and you say, "This is what I want for that lease." I said, "I'll triple it, but I have three conditions before I give you your money." You'd want to know what those three conditions are. And I've tripled the highest number you thought of. That's what you need to think of when anybody presents a sell tower buyout. You need to get away from the money for a second and understand what you're agreeing to first and then figure out the money is worth it. >> Okay. Yeah. All right. Shifting gear a little bit. Uh, Peter from Kentucky asks, "How can land owners market their property to cell tower company or to sell tower carrier directly or do they just have to wait to be approached by a cell tower company?" >> Well, as I said before, we get contacted by property owners all across the country every day and saying they have a great location. So, usually what we tell people is if you have a great location, they'll come to you. It's not that you can go out and knock on the door of AT&T and say, "Hey, I got a great location. you need to build something here because it's a great location. I think it's a great location. You need to build something. They have to come to you. So, but if you want to increase your odds, you want to narrow that gap just a little bit. What we offer and what I would tell you to do is you need to get your information in front of as many cell tower companies as possible. So, the people that make the decisions so you can actually deter they can actually determine if they're looking in area that if your property meets that criteria. Now, that didn't mean they're going to rush to you the next day, and that doesn't mean you're automatically guaranteed you're going to get a cell tower, but you're trying to increase those odds by doing a couple things. First, you're getting your information of how to contact you, because they can find out who owns the property, but they need to find out how to contact you. And that's sometimes a gap that takes a little bit of time. And if you narrow that gap, they're more apt to go that property because they know that's a they can get in touch with you. Second thing is they know you have an interest already. It's not like they're shooting in the dark and contacting somebody who may or may not have an interest in putting something on their on their property. The third is they know you've kind of researched this already, so you're familiar with the process to some degree and you'll be able to move quickly. This is all about a speed to market play about getting information in front of them, making it readily available and getting them from one, two, three as fast as possible, but also getting you a good lease as well during that process. >> Okay. And uh lastly here uh just add to that uh Sophia from Idaho says, "What can I do to make my property more attractive for a tower site?" Kind of same question. But >> yeah, I mean I I guess it's not to be repetitive, but it's somewhat the same answer. It's the way you can make there's no way you can go out and you know level the ground, you know, trim up the trees or whatever and make it more beautiful. It really depends upon, as I started the conversation way back ago, it depends upon how the need for the network. But if you get your information out there, the best way you can get a cell tower on your property or have a better odds is getting it out there. And it's kind of like if you get information out to the the tower companies, it's kind of like having a virtual full rent sign in your front yard or on your property. It tells them that you're available and how to contact you. If not, they're just driving around saying, "I wonder who owns that property. I'm interested in it." And so again, getting your information to the right cell tower companies, we do that. We provide a few plans to do that. And it does a few things. It gets them to them, but it saves you time because you'd have to go through dozens upon dozens of cell tower companies, find out who you have to contact, get their information, and write individual uh emails and such to those companies to get it out there. So, for a nominal fee, we we get that out and instantaneously for you. >> Okay. Yeah. Just one last thing here. uh might be useful for people. Uh Ron from Michigan says, "Uh, I've been asked to modify my lease. What's the difference between a lease extension and a modification and why does that matter?" >> Well, there's a different a lease extension is basically taking the back end of the lease and adding time to it. So, they're asking for additional fiveyear terms. That could be 15, 20, 30 years additionally. A modification may mean one of of a few things. One, it may mean that you are being asked to modify your lease to add certain provisions in it that just modify the language to it. Or more particularly, modification means that they have to get your approval to get certain equipment on the on the property within the current premises area, what land you're leasing, or they need to expand what they're leasing. And either of those situations, an extension or a modification provides you an opportunity. that doors opening gives you an opportunity to renegotiate and get better not only financial terms but better overall terms as well. >> All right. Well, I think that just about wraps up our questions for the day. Thanks for all the helpful answers and um I mean hopefully that you know a lot of valuable information there just to help property owners make some better better decisions. Uh you is there anything like you'd like to add with that? Yeah, I mean, we're just trying to get you, as I mentioned earlier, as Ethan said, we're trying to get you some information that answers questions that we get basically almost every day from property owners all across the country just like you who either have an existing lease or been proposed a lease. And we're going to try to answer these as best we can, give you quick answers, and try to give get you the first step of getting a better cell tower lease. We're here always via you can email us, go to our website at selltowwerleaseexperts.com. Again, that's celltowwerleaseexperts.com and you can contact us via that website or you can contact us via our 1-800 numbers at the bottom of this podcast. We're here always to answer your questions. There's always a free consultation. Uh, and we're trying to give you very quick to direct, truthful, blunt answers to your questions. And we're trying to get you to think bigger than what the cell towers are trying to do. We're trying to get you to think about how to make more money today, make more money going forward, and as important, protect you and your property. >> All right, thanks a lot, Hugh. Um, guess we'll wrap it up here and we'll see you on the next episode. >> One more thing, get more money, get a better lease, get vertical.

metadata.title: What’s Inside a Cell Tower Antenna? | Cellular Antennas Explained
metadata.author: Telecom Training
metadata.shortDescription:
Most people see cell tower antennas every day…

But very few understand what’s actually inside those tall white panels.

In this video, we break down how modern cellular antennas really work — including:

• Cellular sectors
• Antenna arrays
• Polarization
• Slant polarization (+45° / -45°)
• Beamforming basics
• Phased-array concepts
• How modern towers support massive numbers of users

You’ll also learn why modern cellular antennas are far more advanced than simple single antennas — and how they precisely control radio signals across an entire coverage area.

This video is the beginning of a new deep-dive series on modern wireless communication systems and cellular antenna technology.

Upcoming videos will cover:
• Sectorization
• MIMO
• Beamforming
• Massive MIMO
• Phased arrays
• Frequency reuse
• 4G / 5G antenna systems
• RF propagation
• And much more.

If you enjoy telecommunications, RF engineering, wireless systems, or antenna technology, this series is for you.

#celltower #5G #RFengineering #telecommunications #wireless

cellular networks start making a lot
more sense.

up, there's something important to

signal.

don't realize.
One tower usually doesn't cover every

into sectors.

metadata.title: How TxDOT uses Address Points and Land Parcel Data For Billboard Regulation
metadata.author: Texas Geographic Information Office
metadata.shortDescription: John Miner, with the Texas Department of Transportation (TxDOT) Right of Way Highway Beautification Program, shares how they uses the statewide land parcel dataset to save time and effort in the billboard permitting process to examine land use, determine access rights, and remove illegal signs.

segments.text: [ Intro Music ]
>> So I'm John Miner.
I'm a right of way agent inside Texas DOT in our Right of Way Division.
And I work specifically with our Hi-Beautification Program.
And we regulate the billboards on the side of the road.
We're dealing with almost entirely private property and private assets
for the permitting and control of these signs.
So for us it's very important to know who owns the land and what those boundaries are,
because we're going on someone else's property and we have to have permission.
So we use this state-wide parcel data in three major ways.
First, when we're issuing the permits for these sign locations, one of the things we have
to look at from the federal and state level is actual land use.
And while it's not the only determinant, knowing the delineations of that property let's us kind
of determine if the land is being used in a commercial or industrial way
or if it's being developed like that.
Which is something we have to look at before we can issue a permit.
Because those signs are supposed to be kind of constrained to those areas by law.
The second way we use it is, because all these signs are private property and they're located
on private parcels, we have to make sure that we have actual access rights to the land.
We rely on those sign companies to get us permission.
And we need to make sure that who signs the paper is who actually owns the land,
so we can get on there, we're not trespassing on someone else's property.
The third way we use it is in illegal signs and getting rid of them.
For the most part, when someone puts up an illegal sign, they don't write their name
on the sign for us to find out who owns them.
So we rely heavily on the ownership information that we currently get
from the CAD to see who owns the land.
That way we can contact the person who is maintaining these signs presumably,
and either have them remove them or get a permit if it's appropriate.
Using the state-wide land parcel data can save us a lot of time, because currently what we have
to do is go to each individual CAD and we're asking them for information.
And there's going to one CAD for every inspection for who owns what parcel.
It takes a lot of time for our inspectors from what they could be doing
in the field, or processing more signs.
We only have 60 days to turn around every inspection for a new sign.
So they need all the time they can get to look through everything
and make sure everything is air tight before they approve or deny an inspection.

metadata.title: The Real Economics of Owning a Billboard
metadata.author: Business Breakdown
metadata.shortDescription:
First two lines: A billboard looks like a simple advertising business — a big sign you rent to advertisers. So why is a cheap steel sign on land you don't even own worth many times what it cost to build?

This documentary follows Elena Marchetti, who spent $85,000 to put up a single billboard beside a highway outside Columbus, Ohio, and spent two years believing she was in the advertising business. We break down the real economics of owning a billboard: the $85,000 structure, a ground lease of about $9,000 a year on a tiny patch of a farmer's field, and two faces renting for roughly $3,500 a month each — about $84,000 a year at full occupancy, at a margin north of 80%. It looked like a good little advertising business. Then two things happened. A competitor tried to build a billboard half a mile down the same highway and was flatly refused — and a national outdoor-advertising giant offered to buy Elena's single sign for many times its construction cost. The reason is the Highway Beautification Act of 1965, which, along with state and local rules, effectively froze the issuing of new billboard permits along regulated roads. Existing signs were grandfathered in as "nonconforming" — legal, protected, and impossible to reproduce. The real asset, Elena realized, was never the steel or the advertising. It was the permit: a government-created scarcity, a legal monopoly on a sliver of the public's attention that no competitor could ever be allowed to reproduce. That's why permitted billboards trade at values bearing no relationship to their build cost. We cover how she used that pricing power, converted one face to digital (multiplying the income of a protected slot), and nearly destroyed everything when a storm tempted her to rebuild — because a reconstruction over half the sign's value would have extinguished the grandfathered permit forever. You'll learn why a billboard isn't really in the advertising business at all — it's in the business of owning a scarcity the government created and will never allow again. No hype.

Financial disclaimer: Figures are a researched documentary model, not a verified single business, and vary by location, permit status, and format. This is educational, not investment advice. permanently off-limits.

they would not be allowed today, they
could not be reproduced. No one could
build another one beside them. No one
could add to the supply.

endless number that could always be
built. It was one of a fixed, frozen,
and slowly This was the true engine, and
it reframed everything Elena thought she
owned.

advertising business, competing on skill
and hustle to sell space.
In fact, she owned something far rarer
and far more valuable, a legal monopoly
on a sliver of the public's attention,
protected and guaranteed by a government
that would not allow anyone at any price
to build a competitor beside her on that
stretch of road. The permit, that
unremarkable sheet of paper she had
filed away years ago without a second

not the advertising contracts, not even

right to occupy it that could never be
granted again. Because that permit could
never be reissued, her billboard had a

company's offer had seemed so absurd

rational.

structure that could be welded together
by anyone. He was purchasing a permanent
position in a market where the supply
was, by the force of law, frozen
forever, and demand for human attention
beside a busy highway only grew. The
construction cost measured the steel. It
could not begin to measure the scarcity.

logic of her business inverted. The

of as the asset, was almost worthless, a

$85,000. The advertising revenue, which
she had obsessed over, was merely the
income the asset happened to throw off.

the legally enforced impossibility of
anyone building a competing sign nearby.
She owned a piece of a fixed supply in a
market of endless demand, and the
government itself was the guarantor of
that scarcity.
It was in a strange way one of the most
powerful competitive positions in all of
business. A moat dug and maintained not
by her, but by the law.

decision she made from that day forward.
She stopped thinking of herself as an
advertising saleswoman scrambling to
fill space and started thinking of
herself as the owner of an irreplaceable
license, a landlord of a monopoly.

she understood at last that she held
real and durable pricing power, the
rarest thing in business.
Because an advertiser who wanted to
reach the 100,000 cars that streamed
past her sign every single day had
nowhere else on that road to go. There
was no competing billboard and by the
force of federal and local law, there
never could be one.

that traffic, those eyes, it had to come
to Elena and it had to pay what Elena
asked.

longer as a frightening gamble, but as a
way to multiply the income of a
protected monopoly many times over.

rotate six or eight different
advertisers in the time a static face
held just one.

slot into many streams of rent from the
very same irreplaceable sliver of
protected space. The scarcity stayed

understand it with a jolt of fear when

non-conforming status, was also
astonishingly fragile and it could be
destroyed permanently and irreversibly
by a single careless act.

grandfather's sign also in the same
breath, forbade her from ever truly
rebuilding it. She was allowed to keep
what already stood. She was not allowed
to build it new.

she was no longer legally allowed to use
at all.

endlessly, from the owner's own
understandable temptation to improve.

first instinct, the instinct of the

have been a disaster. It was only
because she had finally, painfully, come
to understand what she truly owned that
she caught herself and stopped.
To rebuild too much of the sign would be
to kill the permit that was the sign's
entire reason for being valuable.

be a new billboard and a new billboard
could not exist there at all.

the thing that only made sense once you
understood the hidden engine. She

safely below the fatal threshold that
would have stripped away her
grandfather's status.

improve. She was no longer protecting a
sign at all. She was protecting a piece
of paper in a government file, and the
invisible, irreplaceable scarcity that
piece of paper represented.

the national company, though the offers

she actually held.

carefully protected the invisible
license that was its beating heart. She

saleswoman and become something rarer,
the deliberate owner of a
government-made monopoly.

beside the road. Those were the visible

anyone could enter.

permission granted once and never again,

in the business of selling advertising.

metadata.shortDescription:
Who really gets paid when a giant billboard towers over an American highway?

You’ve driven past thousands of billboards, but have you ever wondered who owns them? In this video, we follow the money from the roadside to the bank account and break down the economics of the billboard business in America.

We cover how landowners, billboard companies, and advertisers split the roles. We look at what a static billboard earns compared to a digital one, and why the permit can be worth more than the steel. We also show why revenue is not the same as profit once leases, construction, electricity, insurance, financing, and empty ad space take their cut. Finally, we compare who actually comes out ahead: the landowner, the independent operator, or the giant outdoor advertising company.

In this video:
0:00 – Who owns the billboard beside the highway?
2:00 – How the billboard business works
5:00 – The real money: rates, occupancy, and profit
8:30 – The hidden costs and risks
11:30 – Who actually gets rich?
Sources and notes:
Industry figures come from the Out of Home Advertising Association of America (OAAA) 2025 revenue and display reports and from Lamar Advertising’s fourth quarter and full-year 2025 results. Example revenue, rate, and cost figures in this video are illustrative estimates only. Actual billboard pricing, construction costs, and profits vary widely by market, location, and contract.

Disclaimer: This video is for educational and entertainment purposes only and is not financial, legal, or investment advice.

Next on Voltonomics: Which business should we break down next? Tell us in the comments.

If you enjoy learning how America’s businesses really make their money, subscribe to Voltonomics and turn on notifications.

Add insurance, because a very tall structure over a public road is a liability magnet. Add property taxes. Add sales commissions to the people who actually find advertisers. Add the cost of the sales people, the accountants, the technicians, and the guy who drives around checking signs. Then comes financing. Most people don't pay cash for a hundred thousand dollar structure. They borrow. Which means interest. And when interest rates rise, the math that worked last year can stop working this year. Now, the big one. Empty space. Billboards don't earn money when they're blank. A vacant face earns zero while the lease, the insurance, and the loan payment keep ticking. The ad industry also follows the economy. When businesses cut marketing budgets in a downturn, billboards feel it. Out-of-home advertising dropped sharply in 2020 when the pandemic emptied the roads, and it took time to recover. And that gets at an important point. Advertiser demand isn't guaranteed. Political ad money can surge in election years and fade afterward. A big local advertiser can leave and take thousands of dollars a month with them. Competition is the next problem. Other billboards in the same area, digital screens that rotate more advertisers, plus the elephant in the room, the entire internet, where an advertiser can target a person by age, location, and interests, and measure every click. Billboards fight that battle with something the internet doesn't have. You can't skip them. You can't block them. And you can't scroll past them. Finally, the government can change your fortunes overnight. A highway gets widened. A city changes its zoning. A new law restricts digital signs. In some cases, owners are compensated for removal, but compensation isn't the same as making money. So now look at the real picture. A billboard looks like pure revenue because the sign itself has no moving parts. But under the surface are leases, loans, power bills, permits, repairs, commissions, insurance, taxes, and empty months. Revenue is just the number on the contract. Profit is what's left after everyone else gets paid. And in this business, a lot of people get paid before you do. So who comes out ahead? That's next. Let's compare the three people who profit from the same sign: landowner, independent operator, large outdoor company. Same pole, completely different economics. First, the landowner. This is the lowest risk seat at the table. You own the dirt. You sign a lease. Someone else pays for the permit, the construction, the maintenance, and the insurance. You collect rent. The downside is that the rent is limited. You won't get rich from a lease check, but a good location can mean a steady, quiet income stream that asks almost nothing of you. The smart move is reading the lease carefully, how long it lasts, whether rent rises over time, and who's responsible for removing the structure when it ends. It's simple money, and sometimes simple is just fine. Second, the independent billboard owner. This is the most exciting seat, and also the riskiest. You're the one hunting down locations, negotiating leases, fighting for permits, borrowing money, and selling ads. If you pick a great location and fill it consistently, the returns can be strong because once the sign is built and paid off, much of what comes in can flow to you. But, you carry the load. If your sign sits empty, you pay. If a permit falls through, you pay. If interest rates climb, you pay. The independent's best weapon is local knowledge, knowing which corners are about to boom, knowing which business owners want to advertise, knowing which landowner might sign a lease today. That's an edge a giant company can't easily copy. And many small operators eventually sell to bigger companies that are hungry for permitted locations. Third, the large outdoor advertising company. This is the scale player, and scale is where this business gets interesting. A company like Lamar owns a huge portfolio of signs. It can sell national advertisers across multiple markets. It has big sales teams, long-standing relationships with agencies, access to cheaper financing, and the muscle to buy smaller operators. It spreads risk across thousands of locations, so one empty sign hardly matters. We saw earlier that Lamar posted a roughly 47% adjusted EBITDA margin. That's what scale and good locations can do. And here's the part that really matters. Billboards are scalable in an unusual way. Once you have a permitted location, adding a new advertiser doesn't cost you another sign. The structure stays the same. Digital takes this further because one structure can sell many slots. A good board can sell the same space again and again without building anything new. Few businesses can say that. But the risks are real and they rank something like this. Regulation, because the permit is the foundation of everything. Ad cycles, because marketing budgets shrink in bad times. Debt, because borrowed money magnifies both profits and losses. Technology, because digital screens are expensive and don't last forever. And competition from digital media that can target people with a precision that no sign on a pole can match. So can owning billboards be a profitable long-term business? Yes, but not for the reasons most people think. It's not because the sign is cheap and it's not because ads sell themselves. It's because the right locations are scarce, the permits are hard to get, and the people who already hold them benefit every time an advertiser needs to reach drivers. The profit doesn't come from the pole, it comes from the permission, the location, and the relationships. So think back to that billboard you passed this morning. The lawyer's face, the cheeseburger, the fireworks store. The advertiser rented it, the landowner leased it, the operator built it. But the ones who really control the roadside are the ones who hold the permits and the best locations and they've held them for decades. If you enjoyed this breakdown, hit subscribe to Voltanomics and tell me in the comments which business you want me to take apart next. Because the next time you see a billboard, don't ask who's on it. Ask who holds the permit. Because on the American roadside, the ads are rented. The empire is the location.

metadata.title: How Billboards Make Money From a Steel Pole
metadata.author: How They Make Money
metadata.shortDescription:
That billboard on the highway does almost nothing — no staff, no stock, no product to ship — yet the largest billboard company in America brings in about $2.27 billion a year, mostly from steel poles and printed faces. This video follows the money at scale (US out-of-home advertising hit a record $9.1 billion in 2024; one major operator averaged about $3,036 per billboard face per month in late 2025), explains why the permit is the real asset — federal law has restricted new signs within 660 feet of major highways since 1965, so prime faces barely grow while traffic keeps rising — shows how one digital conversion lets a single permitted face sell six to eight advertisers at once, and covers what the owner does not keep: ground leases of about $447 million against about $1.39 billion in billboard revenue at one operator in 2025, plus storms, sign codes and ad cycles.

This channel explains how businesses make money. It is education, not financial advice.

CHAPTERS
0:00 The hook: rent on empty air
0:22 What everyone assumes
1:04 The money machine: $9.1B and $3,036 a face
2:02 The secret: the permit is the asset
3:00 The costs and risks
3:40 The lesson: supply capped by permission
4:20 The close

SOURCES
Out of Home Advertising Association of America (OAAA), 2024 full-year revenue release (reported Mar 2025): US out-of-home revenue reached a record $9.1 billion in 2024, up 4.5%; digital OOH accounted for 34% of total OOH spend. Lamar Advertising, Form 10-K / FY2025 results: total net revenues of $2,266.2 million in 2025, of which billboard advertising was $2,013.9 million; company materials describe a network of more than 360,000 displays. Billboard Insider, reporting OUTFRONT Media's Q3 2025 earnings: billboard yield (revenue per average display per month) of $3,036 in Q3 2025. OUTFRONT Media, Form 10-K / annual report FY2025: billboard revenues of $1,391.4 million and billboard property lease expense of $446.6 million in 2025. Highway Beautification Act of 1965, 23 U.S.C. § 131; OAAA "HBA Primer": federal control of signs within 660 feet of interstate and primary highways, largely limited to commercial and industrial areas meeting state permit rules; lawfully erected nonconforming signs may remain, and removal requires just compensation. OAAA digital billboard guidance (as summarised in OAAA-citing operator and platform guides): a digital billboard typically rotates about 6–8 advertisers per loop, each displayed for about 6–8 seconds.

Every video on this channel starts as a human idea — researched, written and directed by a person. AI tools help execute the animation and narration.

Cars drive past and the owner collects

Yet, the largest billboard company in
America brings in more than $2 billion a
year, mostly from steel poles and
printed faces like this one. The pole is
not the asset, the permission is. Here's
how it works.
Most people assume a billboard is simple
rent. An advertiser pays for space, the

easiest money on the road. So, the

not just build more of them. That

nobody can skip a 40-ft sign. In most

somewhere between very hard and flatly
illegal. Federal law has controlled
signs near major highways since 1965.
Local zoning decides much of the rest
and the boards that already stand in the
right places are protected by the very
rules that block their replacements.
Follow the money at scale. Out of home
advertising, the category billboards

the United States in 2024. Lamar, the
largest American outdoor company,
reported about $2.27 billion in total
revenue in 2025 and about 2 billion of
that came from billboards alone.
Now, zoom in on one face. Outfront,
another major operator, reported an
average billboard yield of about $3,036
per display per month in the third
quarter of 2025. That is one face on one
pole in an average month. Multiply a
yield like that across hundreds of
thousands of permitted faces on
contracts that renew year after year and
a sleepy roadside sign becomes a
national rent roll. The advertiser
changes, the traffic does not. Lamar
alone operates more than 360,000
displays and digital boards already took

The secret is scarcity written into law.
The Highway Beautification Act of 1965
restricted new signs within 660 ft of
interstate and primary highways, largely
to commercial and industrial areas that
meet state permit rules.
Signs that were already legal but no
longer fit later rules could often stay
as grandfathered non-conforming boards.
Removing one can require paying just
compensation. So the supply of prime
faces barely grows while traffic and
advertiser demand keep rising. Then
digital made each scarce face worth
more. A printed board sells one
advertiser at a time. A digital board
rotates about six to eight advertisers
in a loop, each showing for a few
seconds, sold and swapped remotely. Same
pole, same permit, several rent checks.
It also explains why old boards change
hands like property, not equipment.
Buyers pay for the permitted position
and the traffic in front of it, not for
steel anyone could weld.
The owner does not keep it all. The
biggest cost is the ground itself. Most
operators lease the land under the pole.
An Outfront reported about $447 million
in billboard property lease costs in
2025 against about $1.39 billion in
billboard revenue. Add steel, power,
lighting, insurance, permits, and the
crews who hang vinyl in all weather.
Digital faces cost far more to build and
maintain than printed ones, and the
risks are regulatory and cyclical. A
city can tighten its sign code. A lease
can be lost to a new building. And when
the economy dips, advertising is one of
the first budgets cut. Storms bend
poles, and a dark board earns nothing
while the ground rent still leaves every
month. The lesson is to look for assets
where supply is capped by permission,
not by effort. A permit, a license, a
grandfathered location.
When nobody can simply build a competing
copy next door, an ordinary asset can
charge extraordinary rent.
Ask the same question of any business
idea.
What stops a rival opening beside it
tomorrow?
If the honest answer is nothing, the
margin will eventually be competed away.
If the answer is a rule, a lease, or a
scarce location,
the economics can last for decades.
Scarcity you did not create can still be
scarcity you benefit from as long as you
understand the rules protecting it.
So, the billboard is not really selling
advertising space. It is selling a legal
right to stand in the one spot every
driver has to pass. Be honest.
What is the one billboard on your
regular drive that you could describe
from memory? Tell me in the comments.
And next, a business with no permit mode
at all, where the money is pure hustle.
Pressure washing.

metadata.title: Synthesis: Develop Outdoor Advertising Control Reference Manual for TxDOT 0-7085
metadata.author: TxDOT
metadata.shortDescription:
Regulating billboards along Texas roadways is a complicated, time consuming process, and TxDOT knows that process can be improved. States that do not comply with the federal mandate of billboard regulation face a penalty of 10 percent of its federal funding being withheld. Experts say the findings of this study will help other states as well.

For more information on research project 0-7085, check out the TxDOT Research Library project record here: 
TxDOT Research Library - TxDOT Research Project (utexas.edu)

For access to all TxDOT research, please visit the TxDOT Research Library at https://ctr.utexas.edu/library/

Today, I sat down with Evan Shelley, the brains behind Truck Parking Club.

Evan took a unique path in real estate, spotting a big opportunity in truck parking. He used his experience in land investing and civil engineering to build a tech startup that's changing the way truckers find parking across the U.S. We talked about how he went from zero bookings to thousands of reservations every day—a testament to his hard work and vision.

We also discuss the potential of industrial outdoor storage, the challenges of building a marketplace for truckers and parking lot owners, and how real estate investors can profit from this growing trend. Evan shares great insights about the market, the importance of solving real problems, and how focusing on a clear goal can lead to tremendous growth.

Whether you're a seasoned investor or just starting out, this episode will give you a new perspective on finding opportunities in unexpected places and how technology is changing the game in real estate.

metadata.title: How a BESS Site Works: Batteries to Grid | BESS Decoded Ep. 1
metadata.author: BESS Engineer
metadata.shortDescription:
Take a visual tour of a battery energy storage system (BESS) and see how its main parts connect—from battery containers to the grid.
Explore practical BESS training: https://bess.courses/

Welcome to Episode 1 of BESS Decoded: complex battery storage concepts explained through clear, simple visualizations.

We start with the solar “duck curve” and show how charging and discharging a battery changes the power the grid needs to supply. Then we explore the equipment around an illustrated BESS site:

• Battery containers: where energy is stored
• PCS / MV skid: power conversion and the move to medium voltage
• Energy stations: repeating the same building block across the site
• MV switchgear, the main step-up transformer and the HV switchyard
• The point of interconnection: where the plant meets the grid
• The control building: coordinating charging and discharging
• The reverse charging path: from the grid back to the batteries

See how the equipment works together as one complete system.

CHAPTERS
00:00 The duck curve—and how BESS helps
00:41 Inside a BESS site: battery containers
01:02 PCS, MV skids and energy stations
01:29 MV switchgear and the step-up transformer
01:49 HV switchyard and grid connection
02:02 The control building and EMS
02:16 Charging: from the grid back to the batteries

ABOUT BESS DECODED
Short visual explanations that make battery energy storage easier to understand. Subscribe and follow the BESS Decoded playlist for new episodes.
Watch the series: https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLKHzaqG6DNvQ

GO DEEPER
Build your knowledge with structured courses and practical learning resources at https://bess.courses/

#BESS #BatteryEnergyStorage #BESSDecoded

cells.
At sunset, [music]
it flows back out.

connect. [music] One path repeated at
scale, keeping the lights on after the
sun goes down.

metadata.title: Inside India's Biggest Utility-Scale BESS | The Energy Storage | IndiGrid × National Geographic
metadata.author: IndiGrid Infrastructure Trust
metadata.shortDescription:
What does it take to store sunlight and use it after dark?

The Energy Storage, an IndiGrid × National Geographic documentary, takes you inside India's biggest utility-scale battery energy storage system (BESS) at Sanand, Gujarat.

At 180 MW / 360 MWh, this is where clean energy is captured when it's plentiful and released when the country needs it most. Behind the long rows of battery units are the engineers, planners and crews who designed, built and powered up a project at a scale India hadn't seen before.

The film follows their story, and the bigger question it answers: how can India keep renewable energy flowing round the clock and make clean power something the grid can count on, day and night?

Developed by IndiGrid and EnerGrid, the Sanand project offers a real glimpse of what India's energy transition will look like.

🌐 Want to know more about IndiGrid? Visit www.indigrid.co.in

#TheEnergyStorage #IndiGrid #NationalGeographic #EnergyStorage #BESS #EnergyTransition

metadata.title: Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) Explained | Layout, PCS, EMS, BMS & Working Principle
metadata.author: Circuit Masterclass
metadata.shortDescription:
Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) is becoming one of the most important components of modern power systems. With the rapid growth of renewable energy sources such as solar and wind, maintaining grid stability has become a major challenge. BESS helps store excess renewable energy and supply it during peak demand hours.

In this video, we explain the complete conceptual architecture of a Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) in a simple classroom style. You will understand how different components of BESS work together to stabilize the power grid.

Topics covered in this video:
• What is Battery Energy Storage System (BESS)
• Why BESS is required in modern power grids
• Renewable energy fluctuation problem
• Peak demand vs solar generation problem
• Storage battery and battery bank
• Power Conversion System (PCS)
• Rectifier and inverter operation
• Role of Energy Management System (EMS)
• Battery Management System (BMS)
• Transformer connection between PCS and grid
• Fire protection and cooling system in BESS
• Switchgear and protection system in BESS

#BESS
#BatteryEnergyStorageSystem
#RenewableEnergy
#ElectricalEngineering
#EnergyStorageSystem

This video is especially useful for:
Electrical engineering students
Power system engineers
Substation engineers
Renewable energy professionals
Competitive exam aspirants (GATE / PSU / Engineering exams)

If this video helps you understand the Battery Energy Storage System, please subscribe to the channel for more electrical engineering tutorials.

Link of our website :
https://circuitmasterclass.com/

segments.text: Let us have a discussion on BESS.
The full form of BES is battery energy
storage system. It is one of the most
modern elements of the power grid used
to stabilize the power demand and supply
of the system. Nowadays, renewable
energy sources are being added to the
grid day by day and governments all over
the world are trying to reduce the use
of conventional fuel-based power
generating stations. Even in India, the
target is 500 gawatt of renewable energy
by 2030. However, renewable sources of
energy are not very stable sources of
energy. The generation capacity of these
sources fluctuates greatly. For example,
a solar power plant generates maximum
energy during a sunny afternoon, but it
produces almost zero energy after
sunset. Likewise, a wind power mill
produces maximum energy when the wind
speed is high. But the wind speed is not
constant. It varies with the time of day
and even throughout the year. Therefore,
windmills also produce fluctuating
power. Let us take a practical example
so that our idea becomes clear. Do you
know during which interval of the 24
hours the power demand reaches its peak?
Obviously, it is during the evening time
after sunset. usually from 6 p.m. to
around 10 p.m. Now, think about a solar
power plant. A solar plant does not
generate any electricity during this
peak demand time. However, when the
solar plant generates the maximum
energy, that is during a sunny
afternoon, the actual power demand is
quite low. Therefore, there must be some
means to utilize this unused power
generated during the peak period of
renewable power generation. Here the
battery energy storage system BESS comes
into the picture. That means we need a
system to store the excess energy
generated during the non- peak hours of
the grid and that energy can be utilized
on the grid during the peak hours. The
battery energy storage system has
several advantages. For example, it can
also help stabilize the voltage of the
grid system. A battery storage system
mainly has three primary components.
Obviously the most important component
is the storage battery itself. Next, as
these battery cells are rechargeable
cells, there must be some means by which
the battery can be charged from the
grid. Therefore, there should be a
battery charger which converts
alternating current to direct current to
charge the battery. But when the load
demand increases, the stored energy of
the battery has to be supplied to the
grid. However, the battery produces only
DC power. Therefore, there must be some
means to convert this DC into
synchronized three-phase alternating
power. For this purpose, an inverter is
used. It converts the stored DC into
synchronized three-phase alternating
power so that it can be fed into the
grid. The combination of the charger and
inverter together is called PCS or power
conversion system. Whenever charging is
required, the battery is charged through
the rectifier which converts the grid
three-phase AC power into DC power. When
the grid demands power, the stored DC
energy of the battery is converted into
synchronized three-phase AC by the
inverter and supplied to the grid. In
modern PCS systems, IGBT devices are
used to build both the rectifier and
inverter circuits because their
switching speed is very fast allowing
efficient control of power conversion.
Now the question is who controls the
PCS? How does the system know when to
charge the battery and when to discharge
it? This is done by the energy
management system EMS. The EMS
continuously monitors the grid
conditions such as voltage, frequency,
and phase angle. Based on these
measurements, it sends commands to the
PCS to operate either in charging mode
or discharging mode. So the storage
battery PCS and EMS together form the
basic structure of a battery energy
storage system. In addition to these,
several auxiliary systems are also used.
A battery management system BMS monitors
the voltage, current and temperature of
each battery cell. It helps monitor
every cell individually and improves the
operational performance of the battery
bank. Another important component is the
fire protection system because batteries
store a large amount of energy and there
is always a potential risk of fire
hazards. The cooling system is also very
important. During charging and
discharging, batteries generate heat.
Generally, lithium ion batteries are
used because of their high energy
density. However, lithium ion batteries
perform efficiently only within a
temperature range of 20° C to 40°.
Therefore, cooling systems are required
to maintain the battery temperature
within this range. The battery bank
produces DC at a relatively low voltage
level. This DC is converted into low
voltage three-phase AC by the PCS.
However, the grid voltage is much
higher. Therefore, a transformer is used
to step up the PCS output voltage to the
grid voltage level. Similarly, the
transformer also steps down the grid
voltage when power is taken from the
grid to charge the battery. So, a
transformer is connected between the PCS
and the grid. Switch gear and protection
systems are also applied to protect the
transformer from faults and also to
protect the entire BESS system. So
finally a BESS system consists of a
storage battery, PCS, EMS, transformer,
BMS, fire protection system and cooling
system. And this forms the overall
conceptual architecture of a battery
energy storage system. Hope you got a
clear picture. If this video is really
helpful for you, please don't forget to
subscribe to our channel so that we can
continue making such videos for you
again and

Unlock the full financial potential of your Solar PV + Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) project! 🔋☀️

This video provides a complete walk-through of the Solar BESS Financial Model Template in MS Excel from eFinancialModels. This powerful spreadsheet is essential for analyzing the project feasibility and profitability of microgrids, as well as Commercial and Industrial (C&I) solar projects, especially those leveraging fluctuating electricity prices and price arbitrage opportunities.

💰 Key Benefits of the Solar BESS Financial Model:
-  Calculate Expected Savings: Accurately estimate reductions in electricity costs.
- Optimize Configuration: Determine how your PV and Battery setup impacts profitability.
- Advanced Modeling: Includes features for hourly consumption/production, battery fading and replacement schedules, charging/discharging speeds, and loading cycles.
- Detailed Financials: Calculate resulting financials and run countless scenarios to stress-test your investment.


💡 Why Combine Solar PV with BESS?
A Photovoltaic (PV) project combined with BESS enables price arbitrage—charging the battery when market prices drop and discharging when prices peak. This is crucial for:

- Load Shifting: Moving produced electricity from afternoon to evening hours for better use.
- Solving the Duck Curve: Stabilizing solar-heavy microgrids that face profitability issues due to low/negative midday electricity prices caused by excess solar production.
- Enhancing Project Economics: Turning potential excess generation into a revenue stream.

⬇️ Download the Solar BESS Financial Model Template:
Get the exact Excel template demonstrated in the video and start your analysis today:

metadata.shortDescription:
This video provides a comprehensive overview of Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) and their critical role in India's clean energy transition. Here is a summary of the key sections:

The Renewable Energy Challenge (1:02 - 1:58): India’s power grid faces a mismatch between peak solar generation (mid-afternoon) and peak human demand (7:00 p.m.). BESS acts as a 'time machine' for electricity, using peak shaving and load shifting to store daytime solar power for evening use.
Regulatory Mandates (1:59 - 2:34): Governments are actively driving adoption. For example, Rajasthan’s 2025 green open access rules mandate energy storage for large renewable projects while providing significant transmission charge exemptions to incentivize developers.
Battery Chemistry (2:35 - 3:16): While Lithium Iron Phosphate (LFP) dominates due to high energy density and efficiency, the industry is exploring alternatives like Sodium-ion and Flow batteries to reduce reliance on imported materials and address fire safety concerns.
Anatomy of a BESS (3:17 - 5:35): These systems are modular, built from cells grouped into modules, packs, and racks within industrial shipping containers. They feature advanced HVAC, fire suppression, and a multi-layered Battery Management System (BMS) to ensure safety and prevent catastrophic failure.
Application Strategies (5:36 - 6:15): Corporations like Tata Communications face a strategic choice between 'consumer-end' storage (backup at office sites) or 'plant-end' storage (large-scale batteries at solar farms), which offers cheaper power but requires complex grid coordination.
Future Challenges (6:16 - 7:29): The shift to 500 gigawatts of renewable energy by 2030 faces hurdles, including high upfront capital costs, limited local manufacturing, and a lack of standardized integration policies.

metadata.title: How We Choose Battery Storage Projects: The Investment Case for BESS
metadata.author: Gore Street Capital
metadata.shortDescription:
How do you decide which battery storage projects are worth investing in?

Before a battery energy storage system (BESS) is built, connected to the grid and begins operating, a critical question must be answered: is it a project worth investing in?

In this video, members of Gore Street Capital's Investment Team explain how they identify, assess and select battery storage projects across multiple energy markets.

Featuring:
• John Cheshire, Managing Director
• Rutwij Hoshing, Senior Investment Manager
• Will Coffey, Investment Manager

From evaluating market fundamentals and grid requirements to conducting extensive due diligence and managing investment risk, successful battery storage investing requires far more than finding promising projects.

Topics covered:

00:33 What makes a good battery storage project
01:43 How we assess different markets and grids
02:42 What "investment-ready" really means
03:30 How we conduct due diligence
04:35 The biggest risks in battery storage investing
05:33 Gore Street Capital's value-add as an investor

Battery storage plays a vital role in supporting renewable energy integration, grid flexibility, and the wider energy transition. Understanding how projects are selected is a key part of understanding the investment case for BESS.

Discover how Gore Street Capital approaches battery storage investment and the expertise required to identify opportunities that can deliver long-term value.

Learn more about Gore Street Capital: https://www.gorestreetcap.com

#batterystorage  #BESS #EnergyStorage #EnergyTransition #RenewableEnergy #InfrastructureInvesting #EnergyMarkets #EnergyInfrastructure #BatteryEnergyStorage #GoreStreetCapital

metadata.title: What Is BESS? Battery Energy Storage System Explained Simply
metadata.author: Learn Solar & BESS
metadata.shortDescription:
Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) are becoming one of the most important technologies for the future of solar, wind and modern power grids. But how does a BESS actually work?

In this video, we explain BESS from the battery cell all the way to the electrical grid using simple visual explanations.

You will understand why energy storage is needed, how small battery cells become large battery systems, how stored DC energy reaches the grid through power conversion equipment, and how safety, monitoring and intelligent control help protect the system.

⚡ In this video, you'll learn:

0:00 The Challenge of Renewable Energy Reliability
1:52 Building a Mega Battery from Micro to Macro
2:50 From Container to Grid: The Energy Journey
3:44 Safety, AI, and Protecting the Grid

🔋 BESS explained simply

A Battery Energy Storage System is much more than a battery. It combines battery cells, modules, racks, containers, power conversion, monitoring, control and safety systems to store electrical energy and deliver it when needed.

BESS can help integrate renewable energy, shift energy across time, support grid reliability and create a more flexible electricity system.

If you're learning Solar PV, BESS, Electrical Engineering or Renewable Energy, this video gives you the big-picture foundation you need before going deeper into BESS design and engineering.

Subscribe to Learn Solar & BESS for practical explanations of Solar PV, BESS design, electrical engineering, renewable energy technology and engineering careers.

#BESS #BatteryEnergyStorage #EnergyStorage

metadata.shortDescription:
Tower Genius Managing Partner Steve Kazella responds to a reader's questions about an American Tower cell tower lease perpetual easement that a deceased relative signed with the cell tower company. They are faced with receiving discounted purchase offers on an inherited house where a perpetual easement for a cell tower exists. 

If you were buying a house with a cell tower in the backyard, but could not get any rent for it, would a reasonable person want to have the selling price  reduced? 

The only exceptions that I can imagine is if there are some other uses or qualities to the property that outweigh the negatives of having to give access to American Tower for zero dollars. For example, is there some recreational use like a stream for fishing on there property or is there a barn where you can keep horses, or does it have a nice view of the sunrise or sunset?
