videos.full_text: So you want to own a cell tower. Find a piece of land, put up some steel, and watch the wireless carriers pay you every single month. Simple enough, right? Here's the thing, every time you make a phone call, send a text, or load a video on your phone, that signal travels through a physical structure sitting somewhere out in the world. Usually something you've driven past a thousand times without ever thinking about it. Millions of people depend on these towers every single day, and almost none of them have any idea who actually owns them. That's not an accident. The tower business is designed to be invisible to the people who need it most, and that invisibility is exactly what makes it one of the most interesting infrastructure businesses in the world, because the money isn't made at the consumer level at all. The money is made several steps behind the scenes in a structure most people have never even heard of. So let's start at the beginning. You're not in the phone business, you're not selling data plans or $5 unlimited text packages. What you're actually selling, if you own a tower, is a specific location in space. A spot on the map where wireless can travel from a metal structure through the air and into someone's phone. That's it. The product is geography, and geography, once secured, is almost impossible to replicate. Now, the first question most people ask is the obvious one. If the phone companies need these towers to run their entire business, why don't they just own them all themselves? Why would AT&T or Verizon or T-Mobile hand over rent money every single month to someone else? The answer goes back to the 1980s and 90s, when the major wireless carriers were building out their networks from scratch. Back then, they did own the towers themselves. Every carrier built its own infrastructure, sometimes duplicating structures within a few miles of each other, because neither wanted to share with a competitor. But by the late 90s and early 2000s, something changed. Carriers started realizing that owning and managing thousands of steel structures across the country was an enormous distraction from their actual business, which was selling mobile service to customers. So, they started doing what became one of the defining business moves of that era. They sold their tower portfolios to independent companies and immediately signed long-term leases to keep using those same towers. This created two entirely separate industries from what had been one. The carrier handles the customer, the tower company handles the ground, and that separation is the foundation of everything that makes this business work. Now, let's talk about what you're actually buying when you buy a tower, because the steel frame is the least interesting part of the asset when a tower company acquires or builds a site. It's really buying five things at once. First, there's the land itself, either purchased outright or secured through a long-term ground lease. In the United States, ground leases for tower sites typically run anywhere from 30 to 99 years, which means the tower operator has the right to occupy that specific point on the map for decades. Second, there's the physical structure, the metal tower itself, engineered to hold significant weight under wind and weather. Third, there's the power infrastructure, the electrical connections, backup generators, and battery systems that keep the site running even during power outages. Fourth, there's the equipment shelter, the locked compound at the base of the tower where the wireless carriers store their electronics. And fifth, and most critically, there are the permits. Getting permission to build a telecom tower in the United States is not simple. You need zoning approvals from the local municipality. You need clearance from the Federal Aviation Administration if the tower is tall enough to be a hazard to aircraft. You need environmental impact reviews. You need historical preservation reviews if the site is near anything protected. This process can take anywhere from 6 months to several years, cost tens of thousands of dollars in legal and engineering fees, and still end in rejection. So, what you are really buying when you buy an established tower is not steel. You are buying a permitted, approved, legally protected location that another carrier has already proven they need. That is the scarce asset. The steel is just the thing holding it up. Now, let's talk about how the money actually flows, because this is where most people's mental model of the tower business falls completely apart. You pay your wireless carrier, let's say around $60 a month for a standard plan. That carrier takes a portion of your money and pays rent to a tower company for every single site their equipment sits on. In the United States, a basic lease for space on a macro tower typically runs between 1,000 and 3,000 dollars per month per carrier. In dense urban markets, it can go significantly higher. Those lease payments arrive every month whether network traffic is up or down, whether the carrier had a good quarter or a terrible one. The tower company then pays ground rent to whoever owns the land under the tower, which might be a farmer, a municipality, or a private landowner. That ground rent typically runs somewhere between 300 and 800 dollars per month for rural sites, though urban ground rents can be dramatically higher. After that comes maintenance, insurance, property taxes, and basic site management. What's left after all of that is the site's gross profit. And here is where the numbers start to get genuinely interesting. A tower with a single wireless carrier paying $1,500 per month in rent might generate around 12 to 15,000 dollars per year in gross site profit after ground rent and basic operating costs. That is not remarkable. At that rate, if you spent $250,000 building the tower, you'd be looking at a payback period of 17 to 20 years. That is a long time to wait. But here is where everything changes. What if you could add a second wireless carrier to that same tower? The tower is already built, the land is already secured, the foundation is already poured, the power is already connected. Adding a second carrier doesn't require you to build another tower. It requires some additional structural engineering, some equipment installation, and some negotiation. But the incremental cost of adding that second tenant is a fraction of what the original tower cost to build. So now you have two carriers paying rent on the same structure. Your annual revenue roughly doubles, your operating cost barely move. The ground rent doesn't increase, the insurance doesn't double, the property tax doesn't jump significantly. That second tenant's monthly payment flows through to your bottom line at something like 90 cents on the dollar. This is called collocation. And it is the single most important economic concept in the tower business. Add a third carrier, and the math gets even more compelling. American Tower, which is one of the largest tower companies in the world with over 200,000 towers across multiple continents, has built its entire business around this concept. The company reported revenues of approximately 10.1 billion dollars in its fiscal year 2023. That is not from selling phone service, that is from renting space on steel structures to the same carriers that spend billions advertising to you on television. Crown Castle, another major American tower operator, has focused primarily on the domestic United States market and reported revenues of around 6.9 billion dollars in 2023. SBA Communications, the third major American independent tower company, operates across the United States and Latin America and has built a business model almost entirely around the needs of its customers. What these companies figured out is something that sounds almost too simple. One physical asset in the right location can generate revenue from multiple competing customers simultaneously. And those customers, once they're installed, almost never leave. That last part deserves a closer look because it is one of the most powerful features of this business, and most people don't fully appreciate it. When a wireless carrier installs its equipment on a tower, that installation is not trivial. The engineers have to mount antenna arrays, run fiber cables, configure backup power connections, and integrate that specific location into the carrier's broader network. The site gets mapped, optimized, and tested as part of the regional grid of hundreds or thousands of other sites that collectively provide coverage. Moving that installation, physically dis connecting the equipment, transporting it, remounting it somewhere else, and reintegrating the new site into the network costs anywhere from $20,000 to $50,000 in engineering and labor costs alone. And that's before accounting for the potential coverage gaps, small interference problems, and network headaches that come with any major site change. The master lease agreements that carriers sign with tower companies reflect this reality. These are not short-term deals. In the United States, the standard initial lease term for a major carrier on a macro tower is 10 years, with multiple automatic renewal options of 5 years each. So, a carrier that signs a lease today could realistically be paying rent on that same site for 25 or 30 years. The lease also typically includes an automatic annual rent escalator, usually around 3% per year, which means even without adding a single new tenant, a tower's revenue grows steadily every year just from the existing contract over a 10-year lease means the carrier is paying roughly 34% more in rent at the end of the term than at the beginning. That built-in growth requires zero additional capital from the tower company. No new tow dot ears, no new tenants, just the passage of time and the math of compounding European tower markets work slightly differently on this point. Companies like Cellnex Telecom, one of the largest independent tower operators in Europe with sites across Spain, France, Italy, the United Kingdom and others typically structure their leases with rent escalators tied directly to the consumer price index, essentially local inflation. During the inflationary period of 2022 through 2024, those CPI-linked escalators translated into meaningfully higher rent increases than the fixed 3% common in American leases, providing a real inflation hedge to European tower operators. And the churn rate, the percentage of tenants who actually leave in any given year, is historically somewhere between 1 and 2% under normal market conditions. To put that another way, if you own 100 towers and your tenants leave at the industry average rate, you might lose one or two tenants per year. That is an extraordinary level of stability for any business. If you're finding this interesting as I do, go ahead and subscribe to the channel and hit the like button. It genuinely helps more people find this kind of content. There is one more layer to how tower companies make money that doesn't get discussed as often as it should, and it matters when you're trying to understand why the business is significantly more complex than it looks from the outside. Beyond the basic structural lease, the monthly rent for space on the tower itself, carriers also pay for ground space within the compound to house their electronic equipment, for power services, and for amendments when they modify their installation. That last category matters. When a carrier upgrades from a standard 4G antenna to a heavier 5G massive MIMO array, they add significantly more weight and wind resistance to the structure. The tower company charges an amendment fee often thousands of dollars up front plus a permanent increase in monthly rent. So, ongoing technology evolution in the wireless industry isn't a neutral event for tower owners. It's a recurring revenue opportunity built directly into the existing lease structure. Now, let's talk about locations because not all towers are and the difference between a great tower and a mediocre one almost always comes down to where it sits. A tower in a rural area might cost similar amounts to build as a tower on the edge of a major city, but the economics are dramatically different. In dense urban markets, Manhattan, downtown Chicago, Central Los Angeles, the demand for network capacity is intense. Millions of people in a small geographic area generating constant mobile traffic means carriers absolutely need multiple overlapping sites. Real estate in those areas is expensive and scarce. Getting a permit for a new structure in a dense city neighborhood can take years and involve community opposition, historical review boards, and complicated zoning variance hearings. That means existing permitted sites in urban areas are extraordinarily difficult to replace. A carrier that needs coverage in a specific block of Midtown Manhattan has very few alternatives if they lose access to an existing site. That gives the tower owner significant pricing power. Rural towers face the opposite problem. The population density is low, which means the number of potential wireless carrier tenants is limited. Often in rural America, only one or two carriers have built out coverage at all, which caps the colocation potential of any given site. A rural tower might sit for years with a single tenant generating modest cash flow, but never achieving the multi-tenant economics that make urban sites so valuable. This is one of the reasons the government has historically provided subsidies and grants for rural telecommunications infrastructure. Programs through the Federal Communications Commission's Universal Service Fund have provided billions of dollars to support network build-out in areas where the private economics alone don't justify the investment. Without these programs, large stretches of rural America would have little or no service. Now, let's talk about what happens when you actually try to build one of these things because the upfront costs are not trivial. A standard greenfield macro tower in the United States, meaning a brand new tower built from scratch on undeveloped land, typically costs somewhere between $200,000 and $500,000 to complete depending on soil conditions, tower design, local permit requirements, and power infrastructure complexity. Here's roughly how that breaks down. Getting the land rights, whether through purchase or a long-term lease option, along with the legal fees, boundary surveys, and environ- mental assessments typically run somewhere between 10% and 15% of total project cost. The actual civil work, excavation, soil testing, and pouring the reinforced concrete foundation adds another 20% to 25% and the steel structure itself, fabrication and erection, accounts for another 25% to 30%. Electrical infrastructure, getting power to the site, installing generators and battery backup, running the necessary cabling adds roughly 15% to 20% and permits, engineering review, FAA clearances, and project management consume the final 10% to 15%. At $250,000 in total development cost with a single tenant paying $14,000 per year in net site profit, the payback period is nearly 18 years. That number alone tells you everything about why this business lives and dies on colocation. The moment you add that second tenant, a net site profit jumps to something closer $40,000 per year, the same investment pays back in roughly 6 years. Add a third tenant and you might be looking at $65,000 in annual net profit from a single site. That is a roughly 26% unlevered return on the original investment. That is not a bad piece of dirt with some steel on it. That is a cash generating machine. This is also why large tower companies don't primarily grow by building new towers. They grow by adding tenants to existing towers. Every new colocation lease on an existing structure goes straight to the bottom line at margins that most businesses can only dream about. Tower cash flow margins, which is the site level profit before corporate overhead, regularly reach 70% to 85% on mature multi-tenant sites. Now, all of this sounds almost impossibly attractive, and it is with some very specific and very important caveats. The tower business requires large amounts of money up front long before any revenue arrives. Building or acquiring towers means deploying capital today in exchange for lease payments that come in over 10, 20, or 30 years. To fund this kind of expansion, tower companies borrow heavily. American Tower, for instance, carried approximately $36 billion of long-term debt as of the end of 2023. Crown Castle carried approximately 21 billion. These are enormous debt loads secured against the predictable cash flows of their lease portfolios. The logic is straightforward. If you know with high confidence that you'll collect $100 million in lease payments over the next 10 years, you can borrow against that income stream today to fund more tower construction. This works beautifully when interest rates are low and tenant contracts are stable. It becomes significantly more stressful when interest rates rise sharply, which is exactly what happened across the entire global economy starting in 2022 and running through 2023 and beyond. As the Federal Reserve raised the federal funds rate from near zero to over 5%, the financing costs for tower companies rose meaningfully. Companies with large floating rate debt exposure faced rising interest expenses, which compressed the margins that make this business attractive. This is the double edge of the leverage that tower companies use. On the way up, borrowing cheaply to fund high-yielding tower assets amplifies returns to shareholders. On the way down, that same debt can turn a stable infrastructure business into a company primarily focused on servicing its obligations rather than growing. The other risk in this business, and it's a significant one, is carrier consolidation. Think about what happens when two major wireless carriers merge. They now share a single combined network. And in many cases, that combined network has two sets of equipment sitting on the same towers because both carriers were previously paying rent as independent companies. The merged carrier looks at the map and identifies every location where it's paying rent twice for coverage it now only needs once. Then it starts canceling the duplicate leases. This played out in the United States in concrete terms following the 2020 merger of T-Mobile and Sprint. T-Mobile acquired Sprint for approximately $26 billion and immediately began rationalizing the combined network. Thousands of former Sprint tower leases were canceled as T-Mobile transitioned traffic to its own preferred sites. SBA Communications specifically flagged the impact of Sprint lease cancellations as a material headwind to its domestic revenue growth in its 2025 fiscal year reporting. American Tower and Crown Castle both reported meaningful organic growth headwinds from the same consolidation wave with the added complication of Dish Network, later rebranded as Dish Wireless, dramatically scaling back its original ambitious build-out plans, which had been expected to be a major source of new tower leasing demand. The math on carrier consolidation is brutal for tower owners. A merger that creates a larger, more financially powerful carrier customer can simultaneously reduce the total number of paying tenants on your existing portfolio. You get a bigger customer who pays less overall. Now, let's talk about the technology angle because 5G has been a constant topic of conversation in this industry for the better part of a decade, and the reality is more nuanced than the headline suggests. 5G is not just a marketing term. It represents a genuine shift in the physical equipment.

Almost every tower lease includes a built-in annual rent increase called an escalator. In the United States, the standard is a fixed 3% increase every single year. In parts of Europe, leases are instead tied to the official inflation rate, so the rent rises automatically with the cost of living. Take a tenant paying $30,000 a year with that standard 3% annual bump. After 10 years, without a single renegotiation, without adding a single new tenant, that same lease paying out over $39,000 a year. After 20 years, it's passed $51,000. After 30 years, it's crossed $66,000, more than double where it started. Nobody had to go find a new customer. Nobody had to sell anything. The contract did the work by itself year after year, compounding quietly in the background. But here's the catch, and it's an important one. Revenue growing on paper is not the same thing as profit landing in a bank account. Between the number a tenant pays and the number a tower company actually keeps, there's a whole chain of deductions. First comes ground rent, taxes, insurance, and basic site upkeep. Subtract those and what's left is called tower cash flow. and on a mature multi-tenant site that typically runs 70 to 85% of total revenue. Then comes corporate overhead, the staff, the offices, the administrative cost of running a company with tens of thousands of these sites, which eats another 5 to 10%. What survives that becomes adjusted earnings. And from there, you still have to pay interest on whatever debt was used to build or buy the towers in the first place. fund ongoing maintenance and cover tax before you ever reach the actual cash that gets paid out to owners. Revenue is the headline number. What you actually keep is a much smaller, much more carefully guarded figure. This is the exact same trap that shows up in almost every capital heavy business from apartment buildings to airlines. The topline number is the one that gets printed in the press release. And the number that actually matters to an owner is buried four or five line items further down the page. Anyone evaluating one of these companies who stops at total revenue is looking at the least useful number on the entire page. Location changes everything about this business and not in a small way. A tower sitting in the middle of a dense city mounted on a rooftop might command monthly rent of $2.5 to $6,000 per carrier because space is scarce and every carrier desperately needs capacity there. A suburban tower typically brings in1 to $3,000 a month per tenant. But a tall rural tower built along a highway corridor to cover a wide stretch of open land might only pull in $500 to $1,800 a month because there's plenty of empty land and no particular scarcity forcing carriers to compete for that spot. The steel might look identical. The economics are not even close. This is also where the industry's biggest trap lives. Picture a tower built in a rural area with a single tenant, minimal population growth nearby, and a ground lease with aggressive built-in rent increases. That tower may never attract a second tenant. It sits there for years, generating just enough to barely cover its own costs, and it never earns back what was spent building it. The industry has a name for this. They call it a stranded asset, a tower that exists, that's fully built, and fully functional. And that will simply never make anyone real money because nobody built enough demand into the location before putting steel in the ground. Now, let's talk about the risk that keeps tower company executives awake at night, because it isn't the one most people would guess. The biggest threat to a tower's revenue isn't people using their phones less. It's carrier consolidation. What happens when two big wireless companies merge into one? When that happens, the combined company suddenly owns two overlapping networks covering the exact same geography with duplicate equipment sitting on separate nearby towers. The obvious move, the one that saves the merged company enormous amounts of money, is to shut down the redundant sites and consolidate everyone onto one. This actually happened and at a massive scale. When one major American carrier merged with a smaller rival a few years ago, the combined company identified roughly 35,000 overlapping towers across the country that no longer needed to exist separately out of a combined footprint of around 110,000 sites. Over the following two to three years, those redundant leases were systematically terminated. One of the largest tower companies in the country reported that this single wave of decommissioning cut about 4 percentage points off its annual organic growth rate in its core American and Canadian business. 4 percentage points doesn't sound dramatic until you remember that this is an industry whose entire pitch to investors is stability and predictability. A single merger on the other side of the country in an industry the tower owner has no control over can quietly erase years of steady growth. And here's why that risk is so dangerous specifically for this business. The costs on a tower don't disappear just because a tenant leaves. Ground rent still has to be paid. Property taxes still come due. Insurance premiums don't shrink. Picture a two tenant tower generating $50,000 a year in revenue and $37,000 a year in profit. Now the anchor tenant leaves. revenue falls to $20,000, a drop of 60%. But because operating costs barely move, profit collapses all the way down to $8,000 a year, a drop of nearly 78%. The same operating leverage that made adding a second tenant so wildly profitable works in exact reverse when a tenant walks away. It amplifies the good years. It also amplifies the bad ones. There's a second kind of risk that's subtler, and it involves technology itself. Every time wireless networks upgrade from 4G to 5G, for example, carriers don't necessarily add brand new towers, often they simply swap out older antennas for heavier, more powerful equipment on the towers they're already using. That new equipment weighs more and catches more wind, which means the tower's structural engineering has to be checked and sometimes reinforced to handle it. When that happens, the tower company typically renegotiates the lease and charges an amendment fee, usually raising the tenants's rent by 10 to 15%. It's a genuine opportunity, but it also means towers need continual structural attention, inspection, and occasional expensive reinforcement work just to keep pace with the equipment sitting on top of them. So given all of that, the slow payback on a single tenant, the explosive upside from collocation, the very real risk of carrier consolidation, how do professional investors actually decide what a tower portfolio is worth? They generally don't value towers one at a time the way you'd value a house. They value entire portfolios using a multiple of a specific number called tower cash flow. Essentially revenue minus the direct costs of running the site. Highquality tower portfolios in major markets have historically traded at 20 to 30 times that cash flow figure. Sometimes more, reflecting just how durable and how inflation protected that income stream is considered to be. Meanwhile, when a company wants to buy out the underlying ground lease itself, converting it into a permanent easement, the going rate is typically a capitalization rate of 4 to 6%. Which in plain terms means the buyer is willing to pay a very high price for a very safe, very long-lasting stream of rent. Now, let's walk through what this actually looks like from the perspective of somebody deciding whether to put money into this business because the honest answer depends heavily on which version of the story you end up living. In the optimistic version, you build or acquire a tower in a location where demand keeps growing. You land a second tenant within a year or two of opening and a third not long after that. Your annual escalators keep compounding quietly in the background. Ground lease costs stay under control because you've locked in a long-term or permanent agreement. Under those conditions, a tower that cost you around $355,000 to build and upgrade could be generating something in the neighborhood of $66,000 a year in profit within just a few years, recovering your entire investment in roughly 5 to 6 years, and then continuing to pay out for decades afterward with the rent still rising every single year. In the realistic version, at least one of two things goes wrong. Either your location turns out to be weaker than you hoped and you never land that second tenant, leaving you stuck earning $8,000 a year against a $275,000 investment, a payback period stretching past three decades. Or worse, you do land multiple tenants, the economics look wonderful for several years and then two of your major carrier tenants merge with each other. Suddenly, you're looking at losing 60% of your revenue and nearly 80% of your profit on that specific site with no warning and absolutely no ability to stop it because the decision was made in a boardroom that has nothing to do with you. The difference between those two outcomes on a single tower can be the difference between $37,000 a year in profit and $8,000 a year in profit. Multiply that gap across a portfolio of tens of thousands of towers and you start to understand why the largest players in this industry spend so much energy and capital on exactly two things. Picking locations carefully before they build and locking tenants into leases that are as difficult and as expense as possible to walk away from. Before we get to what actually determines a tower's value, it's worth addressing the threat that most people assume is coming because it's almost always the first objection anyone raises about this industry. Won't new technology simply make towers unnecessary? There are three specific technologies usually mentioned. The first is small cells, little low power radio boxes mounted on street lights and utility poles in busy downtown areas designed to add extra capacity exactly where a crowd of people happens to be standing. The assumption is that small cells will eventually replace the big macro tower altogether. In practice, they don't because of basic physics. The higher frequency signals that make small cells useful for adding capacity travel only a short distance and struggle to pass through walls or glass. They're a local supplement, filling in gap in a dense area, not a replacement for the tall structure that provides continuous wide area coverage across an entire region. The second is satellite internet, the kind beam down from low orbit satellite constellations. These systems are genuinely useful in remote places where no tower will ever be economical to build. But they simply don't carry enough total capacity to serve a city or even a midsized town the way a fiberconnected ground tower can. They fill gaps in coverage maps. They don't replace the backbone. The third is a shift in how carriers build their internal network software, sometimes called open radio access networks, which allows carriers to mix and match equipment from different vendors instead of relying on one supplier for everything. That change affects which company sells the electronics. It changes nothing about the physical requirement to mount an antenna somewhere elevated with a clear line of sight over the surrounding area. None of these three technologies eliminates the need for height, location, or for the specific spot the tower already occupies. Now, let's zoom out from a single tower to the scale that the largest players in this industry actually operate at. Because the biggest companies aren't managing hundreds of sites, they're managing tens of thousands. The largest American tower company operates roughly 150,000 communication sites across the world with about 42,000 of those inside the United States alone. Its closest domestic rival operates over 40,000 sites concentrated mostly in the United States and Latin America. A major European operator runs well over 138,000 sites across Western Europe. At that scale, a handful of structural advantages kick in that simply don't exist for a company with a few dozen towers. The biggest companies sign master lease agreements directly with national carriers, covering their entire tower portfolio under one standardized contract instead of negotiating sight by sight. That alone saves enormous amounts of administrative time and legal expense. Scale also brings cheaper access to debt. A company managing thousands of towers with reliable, contracted, escalating rent can borrow money at lower interest rates than a small operator with a handful of sites and no track record. because lenders can see in black and white exactly how predictable that income stream is. And in the United States, the largest tower companies structure themselves as a special type of company called a real estate investment trust, which requires them to pay out at least 90% of their taxable income directly to shareholders as dividends in exchange for not paying corporate income tax themselves. That structure exists specifically because towers behave like real estate, steady, contracted, long duration income rather than like a typical fast growing technology business. Which brings us to the idea that actually explains this entire business once you strip away everything else. The tower itself, the steel is not really the asset. Steel is a commodity. Anyone with enough money can pour a foundation and bolt together a lattice structure. What can't be easily replicated is the permission to put that steel exactly where it's standing. the zoning approval that a city may never grant again nearby, the radio engineering that ties that specific spot into a much larger coverage grid, and the long-term legal control over the small patch of land underneath it. Those three things together are the real moat. They're the reason a company will pay 20 or 30 times a tower's annual cash flow to acquire it rather than simply building a new one down the street for a fraction of the price. So, if you ever hear someone describe this as the business of owning cell towers, that description is a little bit misleading. It's really the business of owning a specific hard toreplace location at a specific height, connected into a specific network that a handful of enormous companies have no realistic alternative, but keep renting from you year after year for decades at a time. The tower is just the part you can see. Notice how every piece of this fits together. The entry cost is high enough to keep casual competitors out. The location itself is protected by zoning boards that actively discourage new towers nearby. The tenants are enormous, creditworthy companies that almost never default, and once installed, they almost never leave voluntarily either because moving an antenna even a short distance can create coverage gaps across their entire network. And the one real threat, carrier consolidation, arrives so rarely and takes so many years to fully play out that a well-run portfolio can absorb it and keep growing regardless. That combination of high barriers, durable tenants, and rising contracted rent is precisely why this unglamorous piece of steel in a field commands the kind of valuation multiples usually reserved for far more exciting businesses. That's the full picture of how this industry actually works. The upside and the downside, both included. If you found this breakdown useful, do the channel a favor. Hit that like button, subscribe if you haven't already, and share it with someone who'd find this as interesting as you just did. Thanks so much for watching.

metadata.shortDescription:
Cell towers aren't technology assets—they are specialized real estate. While most people assume tower owners sell cell service or data plans, tower companies actually operate as landlords
. They rent steel capacity (30 to 150 feet in the air) to major telecom carriers like Verizon, AT&T, and T-Mobile, as well as emergency services and broadcasters
.
In this video, we break down the exact financial engineering, construction costs, lease math, and hidden risks behind cell tower ownership:
What You'll Learn:
🏗️ Greenfield Build Costs: Why a single monopole costs $200,000 to $470,000 (average $275,000) to build, with legal, permitting, and foundation work taking up most of the budget
.
📈 The Power of Collocation: How adding a 2nd tenant increases profit from $8,000 to $37,000 per year (a 97% profit conversion rate on new rent), slashing the payback period from 34 years to under 9 years
.
📜 Ground Leases & Escalators: How 30- to 50-year land agreements with built-in 3% annual escalators allow single-site rent to double over 20 to 30 years without finding new customers
.
📍 Location Economics: Why urban rooftop sites yield $2,500–$6,000/month per carrier, while rural highway sites pull in just $500–$1,800/month
.
⚠️ Major Industry Risks: The danger of stranded assets and how carrier consolidation (such as major mergers cancelling ~35,000 overlapping leases) can reverse collocation profits
.
💼 Valuation & Scale: Why institutional investors pay 20x to 30x Tower Cash Flow to buy entire portfolios
.
TIMESTAMPS:
00:00 - The Landlord Model: Rents, Not Phone Bills
02:15 - Greenfield Build Breakdown: Where Does $275k Go?
05:40 - Collocation Math: How 1 Pole Reaches 24%+ ROIC
08:30 - Ground Leases & Compounding Rent Escalators
11:10 - Urban vs. Rural Rates & The "Stranded Asset" Trap
14:25 - Carrier Mergers & 5G Equipment Upgrades
17:00 -

bare steel pole planted in a field,
topped with some blinking lights, and
protected by a locked chain-link fence.
On the surface, it looks like the most
uninteresting object in the entire
modern economy. But this tower does not
sell phone service. It never has. It
does not care whether you have five bars
of reception or a dropped call, and it
certainly does not touch your monthly
data plan.
The company that owns this steel takes
no part in connecting your calls. They
are landlords. The massive telecom
carriers whose names appear on your
phone bill are simply tenants.
And those different antenna arrays
bolted on at staggered heights, those
are essentially vertical apartments,
rented out space by space on a steel
structure.
Once you strip away the blinking lights
and the illusion of telecommunications
technology, you are left with a vertical
apartment building. Seeing the tower
through that lens is the only way to
understand how it actually makes money.
Getting into this business requires
serious upfront capital. Building a
single new site from the ground up costs
an average of $275,000.
This chart shows the budget. The steel
is surprisingly cheap. The majority goes
to soft costs like engineering and
permits. An anchor tenant pays $20,000,
but operating costs eat up $12,000,
leaving just $8,000 in profit. On a
investment, that 3% return takes 34
years to break even. A single tenant
tower barely beats the return of a
standard high-yield savings account. On
paper, it looks like a disastrous
financial trap. Nobody spends that kind
of money to wait three decades to break
even. They do it to set up a completely
different strategy. The secret to this
entire industry revolves around a single
concept called colocation. A tower built
for one tenant is almost always
engineered from day one to hold two or
three. That extra structural capacity
sits there, unused, waiting. When a
second carrier decides they need to
mount their equipment on that same pole,
you do not need new land. You skip fresh
concrete foundations or battle through
zoning hearings. You just reinforce
mounting points. Because fixed costs
were already paid by the first tenant,
97% of the second tenant's rent drops to
the bottom line, returning 12%. Add a
third tenant, returns jump above 24%.
The 34-year payback collapses to 5
years. Then the compounding engine kicks
in. Almost every commercial lease has an
escalator clause, a built-in 3% annual
rent increase. Without adding a single
new customer and without renegotiating a
single contract, that automatic yearly
bump quietly doubles the value of a
lease over a 30-year time frame. The
business model here has absolutely
nothing to do with telecommunications.
It is an exercise in extreme operating
leverage. This zero-cost expansion,
combined with continuously compounding
rent, turns a thin initial investment
into a high-margin cash engine.
You might ask why telecom giants don't
simply build their own towers.
They prefer not to tie up their capital
in concrete and steel when they need it
to purchase wireless spectrum licenses.
Furthermore, local zoning boards
actively block duplicate towers from
being built nearby to avoid cluttering
the landscape.
But the landlord's model carries a
distinct set of risks.
If you build a tower in a sparsely
populated rural area with minimal
demand, you might never attract a second
tenant. The industry calls this a
stranded asset. The owner is permanently
stuck with bad math, barely covering
costs. Yet even a fully leased, highly
profitable tower faces one massive
existential threat, carrier
consolidation.
When two major telecom companies merge
into one, they suddenly control
overlapping networks. They
systematically identify duplicate sites
covering the identical geography, and
terminate those redundant leases,
instantly wiping out years of organic
growth for the tower owner. This is
where that incredible operating leverage
works in reverse. When a tenant walks
away, the revenue disappears
immediately, but the ground rent and
property taxes do not. The fixed costs
remain identical, which causes the
actual profit from the site to collapse
completely out of proportion to the lost
rent. Investors in this sector value
predictable stability above almost
everything else. The identical financial
mechanics that generate 24% returns
during periods of expansion can
systematically hollow out a portfolio
during a wave of corporate mergers.
The most frequent objection raised about
this industry is technological. Won't
new innovations, like small cells or
satellite internet, eventually make
giant steel structures unnecessary?
Take small cells. Because of the basic
physics of high-frequency signals, they
have a very short range and struggle to
pass through solid walls. They act as
highly effective local supplements for
dense crowds, but they cannot replace
the wide area continuous coverage
provided by a tall macro tower.
Low-orbit satellites are excellent for
remote areas, but they physically cannot
carry the total data capacity required
to serve a mid-size town.
And while carriers frequently update
their internal network software, like
shifting to open radio access networks,
they still require an elevated position
to mount their antennas.
Software protocols and electronics are
replaced every few years, but the
requirement to mount a transmitter at a
specific height with a clear line of
sight over the surrounding landscape is
a fixed law of physics. The physical
infrastructure remains permanent.
To grasp the true scale of this
industry, you have to zoom out from a
single structure to the massive
corporations that operate global
portfolios of over 150,000
sites.
Scaling to this degree creates
structural advantages.
These corporations negotiate
standardized master leases directly with
national carriers. In the United States,
they structure themselves as real estate
investment trusts, legally requiring
them to pay out the majority of their
income as dividends in exchange for
paying zero corporate income tax.
Look closely at these massive operations
and a surprising truth emerges. The
physical steel pole is just a cheap
replaceable commodity. Anyone with
enough cash can pour a concrete pad and
bolt a lattice structure together. The
true moat protecting the business is
invisible. It is the unreplicable
geographic coordinates tied into a wider
network. It is the zoning permission
that a local city council will likely
never grant to a competitor nearby.
And it is the long-term legal control
over the 30-x-30 foot patch of dirt
underneath it all.
That unglamorous pole in a field
represents a highly regulated localized
real estate monopoly, quietly
compounding cash in the sky.

metadata.title: The Economics of Owning a Cell Tower
metadata.author: Selina Gonzales
metadata.shortDescription:
Owning the dirt under a cell tower looks like the ultimate passive income. You own the space everyone needs, the tenant can't move the steel mast, and the rent checks just show up for decades. The reality is much meaner. You are simply the cheapest line item on a massive corporate spreadsheet.

This breakdown covers the true balance sheet of cell tower economics. We map out the three distinct businesses stacked on one hole in the ground: the landowner, the tower company, and the telecom carrier. We explain how the real money is made when a tower company secures a second or third tenant on the same steel, and why the landowner's ground lease is heavily capped by slow escalators and 50-year options that outlive the original owner.

Then, we look at the quiet risks that destroy this asset. We explain exactly how to read a massive lump-sum buyout offer, why tower companies are spending hundreds of millions of dollars to buy out ground leases and kill the 3 percent escalators, and the catastrophic risk of telecom mergers. When two networks become one, duplicate sites get deleted, leaving landowners with an empty steel mast, a terminated lease, and a massive demolition bill.

If you want more of these breakdowns, subscribe to the channel.

Let us know in the comments which business or asset we should cover next.

metadata.title: The Economics of Owning Telecom Towers
metadata.author: Mr. Finance Pro
metadata.shortDescription:
What does it really take to own a telecom tower—and how does a single tower generate thousands of dollars in recurring revenue?

Telecom towers are one of the most overlooked businesses in the world. They don't sell phones, data plans, or internet subscriptions. Instead, they own the infrastructure that wireless networks depend on—and rent space to multiple telecom companies.

In this documentary, we break down the economics of owning telecom towers, from the initial investment and construction costs to rental income, operating expenses, maintenance, financing, and long-term profitability.

We explore how tower owners make money, why multiple tenants can dramatically increase profits, how long-term contracts create predictable cash flow, and why telecom infrastructure can become a powerful business model.

But owning a tower isn't as simple as collecting rent. Land leases, electricity, maintenance, debt, regulations, and expensive construction all play a role in determining whether a tower becomes a profitable asset.

So, how much money can a telecom tower actually make? And why are infrastructure investors so interested in this business?

Let's break down the economics of owning telecom towers.

Subscribe to Mr. Finance Pro for more business documentaries exploring the real economics behind companies, industries, and assets.

#TelecomTowers #BusinessDocumentary #BusinessEconomics #Infrastructure #MrFinancePro
keywords: the economics of owning telecom towers

segments.text: Okay, so you want to own a cell tower.
Picture it. A steel pole a couple of
hundred feet tall rising above a quiet
field. At the top, antennas from the
biggest phone companies on Earth. Every
call, every video, every ride you order
on your phone passes through that one
piece of metal. And every month, those
companies send you a check just for
letting them bolt equipment to it. You
don't run the network. You don't answer
customer complaints. You don't pay for
spectrum or advertising. You own the
pole and the pole gets paid. It sounds
like the closest thing to free money
that capitalism has ever invented. And
for some people, it has been. Companies
that own towers are worth hundreds of
billions of dollars. And some of their
investors have made fortunes by doing
almost nothing but waiting. But here's
the problem. For every person who has
gotten rich from a tower, there is
someone who bought into the dream at the
wrong price with the wrong tenant on the
wrong piece of land and watched it
slowly turn into an expensive steel
sculpture. So, what separates a tower
that prints money from a tower that
quietly drains it? And why do the
biggest players in the world keep buying
more of them even at prices that look
insane? To answer that, we have to start
with something much simpler. Why does a
phone company need a tower in the first
place? Your phone is basically a tiny
radio. When you call someone, your voice
becomes radio waves that travel through
the air to the nearest antenna. That
antenna passes the signal into a network
and the network passes it to the person
you're calling. The trick is that radio
waves are weak and easily blocked.
Buildings stop them, hills stop them,
even trees and rain weaken them. So to
cover a city, a phone company needs
antennas placed high above the clutter
in a pattern that overlaps like the
circles on a honeycomb. Think of it like
a coffee chain. You can't serve a whole
city from one shop. You need a location
every few blocks, each covering its own
neighborhood, or customers give up and
go somewhere else. In the phone
business, each of those locations is a
cell. And the cell sits at the top of a
tower. Now, here's the question that
built an entire industry. Who should own
the tower? In the early days, the answer
was obvious. The phone company. If
you're a carrier like AT&T, you build
the network, you build the towers, you
own everything. Simple. But there was a
catch, and it's the same catch that
exists in every business that needs real
estate. Towers are expensive. Building a
single new tower in the United States
typically costs somewhere between
That covers the steel, the foundation,
the fencing, the power connection, the
permits, and the crews. And that's
before the ongoing costs of rent and
maintenance. Now, multiply that by tens
of thousands. A big carrier might need
40,000 towers just to cover one country.
Suddenly, you're looking at tens of
billions of dollars of concrete and
steel that doesn't make a single phone
call better than a rented one would.
Here's the analogy that makes it click.
Imagine you run a bakery chain. You
could buy the building for every shop or
you could rent. Buying ties up enormous
amounts of cash in something that isn't
your core skill, which is baking.
Renting lets you spend that cash on

Prices collapsed. Several carriers couldn't survive the price war and shut down or merged. One of them, Vodafone Idea, spent years struggling under crushing government dues and debt. Indis Towers had to chase payments from Vodafone Idea for years, sometimes carrying large unpaid bills and at times threatened to cut service to towers that kept the network alive. Radius Global Infrastructure bought thousands upon thousands of small ground leases from land owners around the world in the United States, across Europe, and in Latin America. metadata.title: The Economics of Owning a Single Digital Billboard
metadata.author: Ekoniq
metadata.shortDescription:
Digital billboard economics look simple—buy a screen, sell ads, collect revenue. But what actually determines whether one billboard becomes a profitable business or an expensive trap?

You’ll discover how a digital billboard really makes money, why location and permits can matter more than the screen itself, and how occupancy, advertising demand, land costs, electricity, maintenance, and financing affect your returns. This economics explained breakdown explores the business model behind outdoor advertising and what it really costs to own a digital billboard. If you’ve ever searched how much money a digital billboard can make or whether owning a billboard is profitable, this analysis will show you the risks and opportunities. A practical business case study reveals how one permit decision can change the entire investment.

0:00 - The Digital Billboard Business
2:00 - Location, Permits & Scarcity
3:23 - How Billboard Revenue Works
6:00 - The Real Economics
8:43 - Hidden Risk
12:14 - How much money can make?

If you found this analysis useful, like the video and subscribe for more economics explained and business breakdowns.
What matters more: the billboard screen or the location? Share your answer below.

#DigitalBillboard #EconomicsExplained #Business #BillboardBusiness #Ekoniq
keywords: how much money a digital billboard can make
whether owning a billboard is profitable

Your screen didn't break, your economics did. Mistake three, development risk. Somebody builds in front of you. Congratulations again. You still own the board. Drivers just don't. Mistake four, competition. The first digital in a corridor is exciting. The third digital in a mile is a pricing discussion. The fifth is a market problem because digital inventory is amazing until everybody else installs some too. Cell Tower Lease Buyouts: Smart Evaluation Tips for Investors

In this episode of the Furlo Capital Real Estate Podcast, we dive into the fascinating world of cell tower leases. We explore the intricacies and potential benefits of selling cell tower leases, likening it to selling the roof of your home while keeping the rest. We touch on my current experience with cell tower lease discussions, examine the financial implications, and discuss various strategic considerations. This episode aims to equip you with the knowledge to invest wisely, build wealth, and improve housing. Join us for a unique and informative exploration of real estate investing!

// Key Moments
00:00 Intro
01:58 Understanding Cell Tower Lease Deals

13:14 Understanding Payment Structures
15:31 Comparing Business Leases
16:40 Navigating Letters of Intent
22:52 The Role of Brokers in Cell Tower Deals

// 8 Key Lessons
Lesson 1: Use lump-sum payments as strategic leverage: Selling a cell tower lease can provide capital that reduces how much funding you need to raise, and sometimes that's the smarter move.

Lesson 2: Don't just listen—demand documents: Verbal offers sound nice, but until you see that Letter of Intent and easement sample, you don’t really know what you're agreeing to.

Lesson 3: Treat lease negotiations like real estate deals: Yes, you can and should negotiate these offers. Think of it like selling a house—just with antennas on top.

Lesson 4: Watch the fine print on “higher offers”: A company may pitch a high number but then claw back several months of payment. It’s the cell tower equivalent of airline pricing games.

Lesson 5: Factor in future tech shifts: Starlink and satellite-based services could shrink the long-term value of ground-based cell towers—don't ignore this possibility in your analysis.

Lesson 6: Don’t give away your roof without a plan: Selling an easement means you lose long-term control. Know whether you're okay with that—especially if you’re giving up future cash flow and property value.

Lesson 7: More towers, more power (maybe): Some deals include 50/50 revenue sharing if new carriers come in. That could be a silver lining if an existing lease goes dark.

Lesson 8: Small players flip to big players: Easement buyers may package your deal into a larger portfolio and resell it—understanding their playbook helps you know what kind of negotiation power you have.

metadata.title: How Profitable Is the Billboard Business? Industry Experts Share Their Advice
metadata.author: The Bell Board Podcast
metadata.shortDescription:
What does it really take to start and grow a billboard business? From finding the right locations and securing financing to navigating permits, building relationships, and understanding the future of digital advertising, successful billboard ownership takes more than putting up a sign.

In this episode of The Billboard Podcast, Neil Bell brings together experienced billboard owners and industry professionals at the IBO Conference in Phoenix, Arizona, to share their experiences, biggest lessons, and advice for anyone looking to enter the outdoor advertising industry.

You'll hear real stories about unexpected billboard setbacks, difficult financing, land leases, storm damage, digital billboard opportunities, and the challenges of building a successful outdoor advertising company.

Whether you're considering buying your first billboard, starting an independent billboard company, expanding your existing inventory, or exploring outdoor advertising as an investment, these conversations offer an inside look at what it takes to succeed.

**WHAT YOU'LL LEARN:**

- How experienced operators got started in the billboard business
- What to know about billboard locations, traffic patterns, and land leases
- The challenges of financing your first billboard structure
- Why permits, zoning, and local regulations can make or break a project
- How digital billboards are creating new opportunities for operators
- Where AI and technology could impact the outdoor advertising industry
- How to build relationships with local businesses and advertisers
- Why patience, research, and disciplined growth matter
- How to increase revenue and expand an independent billboard operation
- What experienced billboard owners would tell someone entering the industry today

**CHAPTERS**

00:00 The Right Mindset for Selling Billboard Advertising
00:42 Inside the IBO Conference: Conversations With Billboard Operators
01:26 The Craziest Stories From the Billboard Business
04:25 Billboard Storm Damage, Repairs & Unexpected Expenses
06:40 The Entrepreneurial Side of Billboard Ownership
07:53 Developing Billboard Locations vs. Operating a Company
09:56 What Experienced Operators Wish They Knew
10:05 How Technology Changed the Billboard Industry
11:16 From Yellow Pages to Outdoor Advertising
12:01 The Reality of Billboard Financing
13:27 Learning the Billboard Business From Scratch
14:19 Billboard Permits, Zoning & Government Regulations
15:01 The Biggest Opportunities in Outdoor Advertising
15:05 Programmatic Advertising, AI & Digital Billboard Technology
16:34 How Technology Is Changing Billboard Sales
16:51 The Opportunity to Convert Traditional Billboards to Digital
17:12 Creating Additional Revenue Through Local Marketing
17:50 Billboard Inventory Management & Business Software
19:01 Advice for Starting Your Own Billboard Company
19:22 Why Patience Is Critical When Building a Billboard Business
20:26 Finding Profitable Billboard Locations Through Traffic Research
20:51 Why Relationships Matter in the Billboard Industry
21:31 The Secret to Better Billboard Sales
22:16 Building Systems Before Hiring and Scaling
22:43 Why Industry Networking and the IBO Conference Matter
23:10 Managing Overhead and Operating Costs
23:27 Why Billboard Owners Shouldn't Undervalue Their Inventory

**ABOUT THE BILLBOARD PODCAST**

The Billboard Podcast brings you conversations with billboard owners, outdoor advertising entrepreneurs, industry experts, and the people shaping the future of the billboard industry.

We cover billboard ownership, outdoor advertising, digital displays, industry trends, business growth, and the opportunities behind one of the most visible forms of advertising.

Subscribe for more real conversations and insights from the people building the outdoor advertising industry.

metadata.title: The Secret Billboard Business Nobody Talks About
metadata.author: Finpulse
metadata.shortDescription:
Billboards are everywhere, but have you ever wondered who owns them and how they make money?

In this FINPULSE documentary, we uncover the business behind billboard advertising — from renting advertising space and digital billboards to land leases, maintenance costs, permits, and recurring revenue.

Discover how billboard companies earn money, why location matters, how advertisers pay for visibility, and what risks can affect profitability.

The revenue figures discussed are illustrative examples, not guaranteed earnings. Actual results depend on location, demand, expenses, and operating conditions.

Subscribe to FINPULSE for more hidden business models, surprising money mechanisms, and real-world business breakdowns.

What do you think — would you invest in a billboard business? Share your thoughts in the comments!


#FINPULSE #BillboardBusiness #BusinessExplained #OutdoorAdvertising #DigitalBillboards #BusinessDocumentary #HowBusinessesMakeMoney #AdvertisingBusiness

segments.text: Every single day, millions of people
drive past giant billboards without
giving them a second thought. A
restaurant advertises its latest burger.
A lawyer promises to fight for your
rights. A real estate company wants you
to buy a house.
And sometimes, a giant digital screen
displays a completely different ad just
minutes later.
But here is the interesting part. The
company paying for that advertisement
might be spending thousands of dollars
to rent a space that already exists. And
the company collecting that money, they
might not even own the land beneath it.
Welcome to one of the most overlooked
businesses in American advertising, the
billboard business.
In 2025, the United States out-of-home
advertising industry generated
approximately 9.46
billion dollars in revenue.
Now, that includes billboards alongside
other outdoor formats. So, it's not
billboard revenue alone, but still, it
shows just how much money businesses
spend reaching people outside their
homes. And billboards remain a massive
piece of that pie.
So, how does this business actually
work?
Imagine driving down a busy highway.
Beside the road stands a massive steel
structure with a large advertising
panel. Thousands of drivers pass it
every hour, and a company wants those
drivers to notice their brand.
The advertiser pays to display its
message. The billboard operator provides
the space, manages the location, and
collects the payment. Simple enough,
right?
But here's the catch. The operator does
not necessarily own the ground beneath
the structure. They might simply lease a
small piece of land from a farmer, a
property owner, or a local business.
That creates an unusual arrangement. The
landowner receives passive rent. The
billboard operator earns money by
selling ad space
and the advertiser pays to access to an
audience moving through that exact
location.
Three separate parties benefiting from
one roadside structure.
Of course, none of them is guaranteed to
make a profit. The landowner needs a
suitable lease. The operator must cover
heavy expenses and the advertiser needs
results.
The real opportunity lies in finding a
location that advertisers desperately
want and that brings us to the ultimate
secret of this business. A billboard is
not valuable simply because it is large.
It is valuable because of where it
stands, who sees it and how hard it is
to reach that audience anywhere else. To
understand the economics, imagine a
billboard operator leasing land beside a
busy highway.
The operator negotiates a contract with
the landowner and obtains the necessary
approvals before building or installing
a billboard.
The landowner might receive a fixed
monthly payment. Alternatively, the
agreement could include rent based
partly on advertising revenue. The exact
arrangement depends on the location and
the contract.
Now, the operator has a different
problem. It needs advertisers. A local
car dealership might want to promote a
weekend sale. A personal injury law firm
might want its phone number displayed to
thousands of commuters. A national brand
might want to reach customers across an
entire region.
Each advertiser has different goals,
budgets and expectations.
The operator sells advertising space for
an agreed period, often measured in
weeks. Some campaigns occupy a single
location while others form part of a
larger network of billboards. Revenue
depends on several key factors. Location
matters because a highly visible sign on
a busy route is far more attractive than
one on a quiet road. Audience matters
because the number of people passing a
billboard is only part of the story.
Advertisers also care about who those
people are and whether they are likely
to become customers. Competition matters
because advertisers can compare
different locations and alternative
forms of marketing.
And occupancy matters because an empty
advertising space generates zero
revenue.
Let's use a hypothetical example.
Suppose an operator sells one billboard
advertising face for $4,000 over a
4-week period. If the space is sold
continuously at that rate, 12 4-week
periods would generate $48,000 in annual
revenue. But that is revenue, not
profit. The operator may still need to
pay land rent, insurance, maintenance,
electricity, sales commissions,
financing costs, and other operating
expenses. If the billboard sits empty
for several weeks, the numbers change
drastically.
This is why a billboard that looks
impressive from the highway may not
actually be a profitable investment. The
operator must keep the space occupied at
prices that cover all these costs.
Larger companies have another major
advantage, scale.
A company managing hundreds or thousands
of advertising displays can share sales
teams, technology, maintenance
operations, and administrative expenses
across its entire network.
An independent operator with only one or
two billboards may not have those same
advantages.
However, a smaller operator can still
succeed if it controls a valuable
location and manages costs carefully.
The central lesson is simple. The
billboard business does not make money
merely by putting steel in the ground.
It makes money by repeatedly selling
access to a valuable advertising
location. Traditional billboards have
one obvious limitation. Once an
advertisement is installed, that
advertising face generally displays the
exact same campaign until the creative
is replaced.
Digital billboards change the equation
entirely. Instead of printing and
manually installing a new advertisement
for every campaign, a digital screen can
rotate multiple advertisements according
to a programmed schedule.
One advertiser might promote a
restaurant. Another might advertise a
new vehicle. A third might promote a
streaming service. The exact same
physical screen can serve several paying
customers during a single day. That is
the digital billboard multiplier.
The operator is no longer limited to
selling one advertiser the entire
display. They can sell individual
advertising slots within a continuous
rotation.
However, there is an important
distinction.
Eight advertisements rotating on one
screen do not automatically generate
eight times the profit of a traditional
billboard.
Each advertiser receives only a portion
of the screen's overall display time.
The operator must find enough customers
willing to pay for those slots, and the
total revenue must justify the higher
investment and expenses.
Digital screens also require specialized
hardware, electrical infrastructure,
software, connectivity, and constant
maintenance.
The initial investment can be
substantial.
A digital display that attracts strong
demand may generate considerably more
revenue than a static display.
But a poorly located screen with weak
demand, it may struggle to ever recover
its costs.
Consider another hypothetical example.
Suppose a digital billboard sells six
advertising slots for $1,500 each over a
4-week period. If every slot is sold,
the screen generates $9,000 in revenue
for that period. But if only three slots
sell, that revenue cuts in half, falling
And neither figure tells us how much
money the operator actually keeps.
Electricity, repairs, land rent,
insurance, software, financing, those
costs still have to be paid.
Digital technology does give operators

But here is the interesting part. The company paying for that advertisement might be spending thousands of dollars to rent a space that already exists. And the company collecting that money, they might not even own the land beneath it. Welcome to one of the most overlooked businesses in American advertising, the billboard business. In 2025, the United States out-of-home advertising industry generated approximately 9.46 billion dollars in revenue. Now, that includes billboards alongside other outdoor formats. So, it's not billboard revenue alone, but still, it shows just how much money businesses spend reaching people outside their homes. And billboards remain a massive piece of that pie. So, how does this business actually work? Imagine driving down a busy highway. Beside the road stands a massive steel structure with a large advertising panel. Thousands of drivers pass it every hour, and a company wants those drivers to notice their brand. The advertiser pays to display its message. The billboard operator provides the space, manages the location, and collects the payment. Simple enough, right? But here's the catch. The operator does not necessarily own the ground beneath the structure. They might simply lease a small piece of land from a farmer, a property owner, or a local business. That creates an unusual arrangement. The landowner receives passive rent. The billboard operator earns money by selling ad space and the advertiser pays to access to an audience moving through that exact location. Three separate parties benefiting from one roadside structure. Of course, none of them is guaranteed to make a profit. The landowner needs a suitable lease. The operator must cover heavy expenses and the advertiser needs results. The real opportunity lies in finding a location that advertisers desperately want and that brings us to the ultimate secret of this business. A billboard is not valuable simply because it is large. It is valuable because of where it stands, who sees it and how hard it is to reach that audience anywhere else. To understand the economics, imagine a billboard operator leasing land beside a busy highway. The operator negotiates a contract with the landowner and obtains the necessary approvals before building or installing a billboard. The landowner might receive a fixed monthly payment. Alternatively, the agreement could include rent based partly on advertising revenue. The exact arrangement depends on the location and the contract. Now, the operator has a different problem. It needs advertisers. A local car dealership might want to promote a weekend sale. A personal injury law firm might want its phone number displayed to thousands of commuters. A national brand might want to reach customers across an entire region. Each advertiser has different goals, budgets and expectations. The operator sells advertising space for an agreed period, often measured in weeks. Some campaigns occupy a single location while others form part of a larger network of billboards. Audience matters because the number of people passing a billboard is only part of the story. Advertisers also care about who those people are and whether they are likely to become customers. Competition matters because advertisers can compare different locations and alternative forms of marketing. And occupancy matters because an empty advertising space generates zero revenue. Let's use a hypothetical example. Suppose an operator sells one billboard advertising face for $4,000 over a 4-week period. If the space is sold continuously at that rate, 12 4-week periods would generate $48,000 in annual revenue. But that is revenue, not profit. The operator may still need to pay land rent, insurance, maintenance, electricity, sales commissions, financing costs, and other operating expenses. If the billboard sits empty for several weeks, the numbers change drastically. This is why a billboard that looks impressive from the highway may not actually be a profitable investment. The operator must keep the space occupied at prices that cover all these costs. Larger companies have another major advantage, scale. A company managing hundreds or thousands of advertising displays can share sales teams, technology, maintenance operations, and administrative expenses across its entire network. An independent operator with only one or two billboards may not have those same advantages. The billboard business does not make money merely by putting steel in the ground. It makes money by repeatedly selling access to a valuable advertising location. Traditional billboards have one obvious limitation. Once an advertisement is installed, that advertising face generally displays the exact same campaign until the creative is replaced. metadata.title: How to Buy, Build & Grow a Billboard Business | Dan Franklin
metadata.author: The Bell Board Podcast
metadata.shortDescription:
How do you grow a billboard business when you’re up against companies many times your size?

Dan Franklin of Franklin Outdoor joins Neil Bell on the Bell Board Podcast to share what three generations in outdoor advertising have taught his family about land, acquisitions and running a lean operation.

More from SignDash: cloud-based billboard sales and inventory software built for independent outdoor advertising companies. Learn more at https://signdash.com/

With roughly 500 billboard sites, Franklin Outdoor grew through strategic land ownership, smart acquisitions, operational efficiency and long-term landowner relationships. Dan explains how he evaluates underperforming billboard assets, why owning the land and easements matters, and how to navigate local ordinances and permits. He also covers running an in-house print shop, managing install crews, upgrading to LED lighting with remote monitoring, and what traffic counts and programmatic advertising mean for independent operators.

If you’re an independent billboard operator, an outdoor advertising investor or thinking about starting a billboard business, this conversation is a practical playbook.

GUEST BIO & LINKS
About Dan Franklin: Third-generation operator at Franklin Outdoor Advertising, Minnesota’s billboard partner for 50+ years, serving Minnesota and Western Wisconsin.
Franklin Outdoor: https://franklinoutdoor.com/
LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/dan-franklin-4b4123148

KEY TAKEAWAYS

Owning the land under your billboards protects your business for the long term.
Underperforming billboards can be your best acquisitions.
LED lighting and remote monitoring cut costs and downtime.
A print shop and install crew add revenue and control.
Independent operators win on relationships, not size.

metadata.title: 30 Years in Billboard Advertising: Sales, AI & Growth with Jonathan Graviss
metadata.author: The Bell Board Podcast
metadata.shortDescription:
Want to grow your billboard business? Discover billboard sales strategies, pricing insights, and AI marketing tools that can help independent outdoor advertising operators improve performance and generate more revenue.

On this episode of the Bell Board Podcast, host Neil Bell welcomes Jonathan Graviss of Graviss Marketing, who brings 30 years of billboard industry experience to a conversation about sales leadership, outdoor advertising, and the future of the industry.
Jonathan shares lessons from his time working with major outdoor advertising companies, including Lamar and Clear Channel, and explains why independent billboard operators often struggle to develop effective sales systems, train employees, and market their own businesses.

Neil and Jonathan also explore the ongoing debate between billboard pricing and occupancy, how AI can improve customer research and landowner outreach, and why audience-based selling is becoming increasingly important in out-of-home advertising.
Whether you're an independent billboard operator, sales manager, or outdoor advertising professional, this conversation offers practical perspectives on building a more efficient, scalable billboard business.

Guest: https://www.linkedin.com/in/jpgraviss
