metadata.title: How a Cell Tower Actually Works: A Phone Call, Ground to Sky
metadata.author: Buildrightacademy
metadata.shortDescription:
Every cell call crosses about a dozen pieces of equipment, and once it is connected your voice makes the trip in a fraction of a second. We follow one call from your phone through the antenna, the RRU, the fiber, the BBU, the backhaul and the core network, and we build the site from the ground up: foundation and grounding, shelter and batteries, cable and ice bridge, tower types, sectors, tilt, backhaul, FAA lights, handoffs, 4G vs 5G and small cells, and the crews who keep it running.

Chapters
0:00 Cold open
0:35 Start in the dirt: foundation and grounding
2:39 The shelter and the cable
4:43 The steel: four tower types
6:34 The top: sectors, antennas, RRU
9:01 The dish, the fiber, and the lights
10:47 One phone call, start to finish
12:40 Handoffs
14:07 4G, 5G, and small cells
16:07 The people on the tower
18:15 How a site stays up

Want to work on sites like this, or lead the crews that do? Courses for tower and construction crews: https://buildrightacademy.com

Sources: 14 CFR 77.9 and AC 70/7460-1 (FAA), 47 CFR Part 17 and 1.1310 (FCC), 29 CFR 1926.501 and OSHA 3877 Communication Tower Best Practices, ANSI/ASSP A10.48-2023, ANSI/TIA-222, CTIA annual survey (cell sites, small cells), FCC Auction 107 (C-band), 3GPP TS 23.401 / 23.501 / 36.300 / 38.300. Photos: FEMA (public domain) and National Weather Service (public domain). Illustrations: BuildRight Academy.

Educational overview, not a work procedure: follow your employer's site plan, the manufacturer's instructions and OSHA rules.

segments.text: You press call. Once the call is up,
every word you say turns into radio in a
blink. It's a panel about as tall as a
door, 150 feet in the air, and drops
down a cable to a box on the ground.
Then it leaves the site as light through
a strand of glass.
There are about 450,000
cell sites in this country.
Almost nobody looks at one.
Today we climb one from the dirt to the
top and follow a single phone call all
the way through.
This is how a cell tower actually works.
Start where nobody looks, the ground.
A tower is a tall, thin piece of steel
standing in an open field.
It will see wind, ice, and lightning, so
it has to be anchored like it means it.
A monopole usually sits on a concrete
pier.
Think of a drilled shaft several feet
across going down 20, 30, 40 feet or
more. A lattice tower sits on three or
four footings. A guyed tower sits on a
small base and leans on steel cables out
to anchors in the ground. The soil
report decides the design. Same pole,
different dirt, different foundation.
Now the part that matters most on a
stormy night, grounding. A tower is the
tallest thing around, so lightning wants
it. The goal is not to stop lightning. A
lightning rod at the top gives a strike
a place to land. The rest of the system
gives it an easy road into the earth and
makes everything on the site rise and
fall in voltage together. So the crew
buries a ring of heavy bare copper
around the base. Ground rods are driven
into the soil along that ring, often 8
feet long, sometimes much deeper. The
tower, the fence, the shelter, and the
cable ladder all to the ring. Inside the
shelter, a copper ground bar collects
the bonds and ties [music] back to the
ring. One copper path, no gaps.
How good is good enough? Owners test it.
They measure the resistance of the
ground system to the earth. 5 ohms or
less is a common target. In dry, rocky
soil that can take extra rods or long
copper radials running out across the
lot.
Remember that copper ring. Every wire we
meet higher up connects back to it.
And the next stop is the busiest box on
the site. If the tower is the body, this
is the heart.
At the foot of the tower sits the
equipment. Sometimes it is a small
walk-in shelter. Sometimes it is a row
of outdoor cabinets on a slab. Same job
either way. Open the door and you find
four things. First, the power.
Utility power comes in and goes to
rectifiers. A rectifier turns the
alternating current from the grid into
direct current, usually 48 volts.
Telecom runs on that and the same plant
charges the batteries.
Second, the batteries. A rack of them
sits on the floor and when the grid
drops, they carry the site without a
flicker. For how long depends on the
owner, but think hours, not days.
Third, the brain of the site. [music] It
is called the BBU, the baseband unit. It
takes the digital stream that comes down
from the radios and turns it into data
the network understands.
Fourth, outside the building, the
generator. On many sites, when the grid
stays down, a transfer switch starts it
on its own while the batteries bridge
the gap. Diesel, propane, or natural
gas. Some sites have no generator, just
a plug for a portable one.
That's the ground floor. Now, how do the
antennas up top talk to the brain down
here?
through the cable. Years ago, thick
coaxial lines ran up the tower, one for
each antenna. They were heavy and they
lost signal on the way. Today, many
sites use a hybrid cable. It carries two
things in one jacket, fiber for the data
and copper conductors for the 48-volt
power. Others run fiber and power as
separate cables. Either way, the cable's
metal shield is grounded where it leaves
the tower and surge protection sits at
the power end.
At the base, the cable crosses the gap
from shelter to tower on a steel ladder
called an ice bridge. It holds the cable
up and its canopy keeps ice falling from
the tower off it.
Now look up.
Which kind of tower is it? There are
four you will see.
The monopole is a single tapered steel
tube, hollow, clean, and small
footprint. It is the choice in towns, on
highways, and wherever land is tight.
Heights run from a few dozen feet to
around 200.
Why that tall?
Higher means farther, but too high and
the site starts covering ground that
belongs to the next one. Height is a
design choice, not a bragging right.
The self-support lattice tower is a
triangle or square of steel legs and
braces. It is stiff and strong and it
can carry heavy loads for a lot of
antennas. It needs more ground and a
bigger foundation.
The guide tower is a thin mast held up
by steel cables, called guys, in three
directions. It is the cheapest way to go
very tall if you have a lot of land. The
tallest guide masts in the country,
[music] TV towers in North Dakota, stand
about 2,000 feet. A cell tower is a
small fraction of that.
Then there is the stealth tower, a pole
dressed as a tree, a flag pole, a clock
tower, a church steeple. The radios are
the same. The disguise is a local zoning
decision, not an engineering one.
Here is something you can use on any
site. Whatever the type, a US tower is
designed to a national standard,
ANSI/TIA-222,
usually through the local building code.
It says how much antenna weight and wind
and ice the steel must carry. Add an
antenna and the tower might not have the
room for it. We will come back to that
because someone has to check.
At the top, you find the first real
piece of the radio system.
First a mount, then the antennas. A
platform or a sector frame bolts to the
tower.
Its job is to hold antennas steady,
pointing exactly the way the engineers
planned. A tower may carry three arms or
a ring around the pole. Everything up
here is sized for the wind.
Here is the design that most sites are
built on. Three sectors. Each antenna is
aimed at one slice of the circle, 120°
from its neighbor. Three slices make
360. One tower, three directions, three
groups of phones.
Each antenna looks like a tall, flat
panel a few feet high. Inside, many
small elements are stacked in a column.
That stack makes the energy go out in a
flat fan, not in a ball. So the signal
goes out toward the ground you want to
cover, not up into the sky.
Most panels are really several antennas
in one case. Several connections go to
each one. That lets the site listen on
more than one path and send more than
one stream at the same time. Two paths
beat one when a signal bounces off a
building. Engineers call it MIMO. For
you, it means a steadier call and faster
data.
The antenna is also tilted down toward
the ground in degrees. That is down
tilt. Too much down tilt and the site
covers less. Too little and the beam
overshoots into the next site and causes
interference. Tilt comes in two kinds.
Mechanical tilt is the physical angle of
the antenna on its bracket, and the crew
sets it on the tower with a digital
level. Electrical [music] tilt is built
into the panel, and on most modern
antennas a small motor changes it
remotely, so engineers can adjust it
without a climb. The two add together.
Behind many antennas you will see a
small box. It is the RRU, the remote
radio unit. On older sites the radio
lived in the shelter. Now it sits right
behind the antenna, so the radio signal
only travels a few feet in coax jumpers.
Then it becomes a digital signal in the
fiber for the long trip down. Shorter
run, less loss, less wasted power.
So the call is at the bottom in the BBU.
Where does it go next? Out of the site.
That's called backhaul. And here is the
part most people never think about. The
tower is only the front door. The real
network is what's behind it. Today most
backhaul is fiber, buried in conduit
straight to a switching building.
[music] Fiber carries far more than any
radio link, and it does not care about
rain. But not every site has fiber at
the road. Fiber is a trench, a permit,
and a landowner. Where it isn't there a
microwave dish on the tower shoots a
narrow beam to another tower within
sight, sometimes many miles away. That
beam has to land on a dish a few feet
across. A degree or two off and the link
can fail.
Now look at the very top of a taller
tower. A red light. On some towers a
white strobe in the day. This is not for
decoration. It is for aircraft. Under
FAA rules a structure more than 200 feet
above ground must be reported to the FAA
before it is built, and the FAA decides
if it needs marking and lighting. The
FCC registers the structure and enforces
the lights. Our 150-ft pole is below
that line, but a shorter tower near an
airport can get lights too. The detailed
rules are in an advisory circular,
Hold on to that rule. If a light on one
of these towers goes out, pilots lose a
warning, so the owner has to report it
and fix it fast. We'll see who catches
that and how near the end.
You've seen the parts. Now we run a call
through them.
Your phone is a radio. Even when you are
doing nothing, it keeps listening to the
nearest towers, and it checks in now and
then so the network knows roughly where
to find you. When you dial, the phone
picks the strongest sector and asks it
for a connection. Your voice is turned
into digital data, packaged, and sent on
a certain frequency to the antenna. The
phone sends a fraction of a watt, far
less than a flashlight bulb. The antenna
is built to hear that from a mile away
or more. The signal hits the antenna and
goes through a few feet of cable into
the RRU. The RRU cleans it up and turns
it into a digital stream. Then that
stream runs as light down the fiber at
about two-thirds the speed of light in a
vacuum. In the shelter, the fiber
reaches the BBU. The BBU decodes your
voice and hands it off to the transport
network through fiber or the microwave
dish. At the other end of that line sits
the carrier's core network, a set of
servers in a secure building. The core
checks who you are, looks up the number
you dialed, finds the other phone, and
has it paged through the tower it is
near. Then the whole thing runs in
reverse. Other tower, other BBU, other
RRU, other
other phone. Your friend hears you.

your voice makes the whole trip phone to
phone in a fraction of a second. And
there was a lot of road in there.

core, and back again. It takes about a
dozen separate pieces of equipment that
all have to work. Now picture the same
call from a moving car.
You drive down the highway. You are
talking.
You pass a tower and the call doesn't
drop. How?
The phone keeps measuring the signal
from nearby sectors all the time and
reports to the network.
When a neighbor sector gets stronger
than your current one by a set margin,
the network prepares the next one first.

phone moves and your voice never stops.

blink. You never feel it. But if you
ever lose a call in the same spot every
day, that is usually a handoff that
failed, a gap in coverage, or a neighbor
that was never set up to take the call.

with test gear to find exactly where it
breaks. There are two kinds. One is
between sectors on the same tower, which
happens inside the same site. The other
is from one tower to the next. In the
second case, the two towers usually talk
to each other directly. The network
moves the call path in the core once the
new tower has taken over, so the data
keeps flowing during the move. Handoffs
also tell you something about how sites
are planned. The sectors must overlap a
little at the edges. Too little and the
call drops in the gap. Too much and
phones jump back and forth.

5G changes some of it.
It comes in three flavors, and the
difference [music]
is the radio frequency.

below 1 GHz travel far and go through
walls. Great for covering whole
counties. Speed is not much better than
Midband is the sweet spot. The C-band,
3.7 to 3.98 GHz is a big one. The FCC
sold it in a record auction that raised
about $81 billion.
It reaches a good distance and carries a
lot of data.
The third is millimeter wave or
millimeter wave. Frequencies from about
24 GHz and up. The speeds are huge, but
the range is short. Trees, glass, rain,
a hand over the phone can block it. So
it usually needs small cells.

a backpack. It hangs on a street pole or
a building close to the street. [music]
One tower can cover miles. A small cell
covers a block or two. Small cells are
now nearly 40% of all US cell sites.

can steer. Instead of a wide fan, many
tiny elements shape a narrow beam and
aim it at your phone. Same tower, same
pole, different panel up top and a
bigger radio behind it. That panel is
often heavier. More wind load, more
weight. So a 5G upgrade is also a
structural job.
Back to that ANSI/TIA-222.
Someone has to check the steel before
the new panel goes up. An engineer runs
a structural analysis. Sometimes the
answer is yes. Sometimes the answer is
reinforce the pole first. Either way,
the check comes before the climb.
So who actually does this work?
Four groups, and every one of them
matters. The climbers go up. They mount
the antennas, run the cable, bolt the
platform, change the light. They climb
in a full body harness with two lanyards
or a safety climb sleeve and stay tied
off 100% of the time from the first rung
to the last. OSHA's fall protection
rules apply above 6 ft and the OSHA and
FCC tower guide calls for 100% tie off.
It is the standard on every professional
site and falls are the reason it exists.
The RF techs commission the radios. They
connect, test, [music] and tune. They
check the tilt, the signal, and the
cable with an analyzer.
They also look after the energy. Close
in front of an active antenna, the radio
energy can exceed the limits. The FCC
sets those limits with stricter ones for
the public than for trained workers.
Workers use meters and power down a
sector when they have to be close.
Then the riggers. When the load is
heavy, steel sections, big antennas, a
new mount, they use a gin pole and a
hoist. A gin pole is a lifting boom that
attaches to the tower.
Riggers know how to read a load, set the
lines, and keep everyone out from under
it.
And the crew on the ground. They run the
winch, watch the hoist line, keep the
tagline, make the radio calls, and keep
the drop zone clear. When a climber has
a problem, they are the ones who call it
in and start the rescue plan. A good
ground crew sets the tempo for the whole
day. Nothing leaves the ground until
they say so.
One more piece. OSHA and the FCC publish
a guide called Communication Tower Best
Practices. There is also an industry
standard, A10.48
that covers planning, fall protection
and rescue, rigging, and training.
Read them and then you know what good
looks like.
So the site is built, tuned, lit, and
carrying calls.
How does it stay that way for years?
Walk it. Crews visit on a schedule. They
check the shelter, test the batteries,
run the generator, inspect the fence and
the lights. Then comes the tower itself.
Climbers look at bolts, welds, guy
tension, cable clamps, [music]
and anything that is loose or rusting.
Towers are inspected on a schedule, and
a tower that gets new antennas gets
analyzed again. And the light. If a top
light fails, the owner has to tell the
FAA and fix it. Many sites have remote
alarms that report the light, the power,
the door, the batteries, and the
temperature. Most of the time, the
network operations center sees the
problem before the neighbors do. Then
the audits. Climbing gear is inspected
before every use and again on a schedule
by a competent person. Crews run rescue
drills because the plan to get a hurt
climber down has to exist before the
climb. Then the paperwork, photos,
torque marks, [music] a report for the
owner. Then the storms, wind, ice,
lightning, flood, [music]
wildfire. Before a hurricane, crews fuel
the generators and check the batteries.
After it, they go back one site at a
time. Power and fiber first, then the
radios. Often a mobile cell site on a
trailer comes in while the real one is
repaired. So that is the whole thing.
Ground ring and rebar, rectifiers and
batteries, a cable up the pole, three
sectors, an RRU behind each, and fiber
going down. Back haul out, the core, and
back again. Every piece has a job and a
person whose job is to keep it working.
[music] If you want to work on these
sites or lead the crews that do, Build
Right Academy has courses built for it.
Learn the work, learn the rules, and go
home at the end of the day.

metadata.title: What a Highway Billboard Actually Makes Full Accounting
metadata.author: Walt Runs The Numbers
metadata.shortDescription:
What does owning a commercial highway billboard actually make after landowner ground leases, DOT permits, steel loan debt, and electricity bills? We run the real math.

THE REAL NUMBERS (SINGLE-FACE STATIC MONOPOLE PRO-FORMA):
Baseline Model: 14' x 48' Steel Monopole Billboard (50,000 Daily Vehicles @ $3,500/Month Advertising Rate)
Total Construction & Permitting Capital: $115,000
Commercial Financing: $85,000 @ 9.5% (10-Year Amortization = $1,098/month)
Equity Down Payment: $30,000

GROSS REVENUE (90% OCCUPANCY MODEL):
- Gross Advertising Rate: $3,500/month ($42,000/year at 100%)
- Effective Revenue at 90% Occupancy: $3,150/month ($37,800/year)

MONTHLY OPERATING EXPENSES (OPEX):
- Private Landowner Ground Lease (20% of Gross): $630
- Commercial Illumination Electricity (Night Lighting): $220
- Vinyl Installation, Crane & Climber Labor: $280
- Commercial Property, Liability & Wind Insurance: $180
- Municipal Sign Permit & Property Tax: $140
- Dedicated Structural Maintenance Reserve: $200
Total Monthly Operating Expenses: $1,650/month

NET OPERATING INCOME (NOI): $1,500/month ($18,000/year)
DEBT SERVICE: $1,098/month ($13,176/year)
NET MONTHLY CASH FLOW (Years 1-10): $402/month ($4,824/year)
Net Cash Flow After Debt Payoff (Month 121+): $1,500/month ($18,000/year)

BREAK-EVEN & OPERATOR HEURISTICS:
- Operator Heuristic: The 85% Occupancy Rule (44 paid weeks/year minimum)
- Below 75% Occupancy: Negative cash flow (-$158/month loss)
- The Landowner Ground Lease Trap: Automatic 15% escalation clauses

PRIMARY SOURCING REFERENCES & BENCHMARKS:
- Outdoor Advertising Association of America (OAAA) Industry Benchmarks
- Federal Highway Administration (FHWA) Billboard Regulations
- State DOT Outdoor Advertising Division Guidelines
- ASCE 7 Structural Wind Load Engineering Standards
- IRS Code Section 179 & MACRS Depreciation

ABOUT WALT RUNS THE NUMBERS:
Walt Runs The Numbers breaks down the real operating economics of income-producing assets ordinary people actually buy — storage units, rental property, laundromats, mobile home parks, and micro-cash-flow businesses. We analyze entry capital, real monthly cash flow, hidden maintenance traps, and multi-year pro-formas. Descriptive economic analysis and financial accounting only — not investment or financial advice.

#Billboard #SmallBusiness #WaltRunsTheNumbers

segments.text: A 14-x-48 foot steel billboard standing
60 feet above a freeway looks like the
ultimate set-it-and-forget-it asset. No
tenants to evict, no toilets to repair,
no employees to manage. An outdoor
advertising broker will tell you that a
single highway face renting for $4,000 a
month generates $48,000 a year in gross
revenue from one steel pole and a sheet
of vinyl.
The pitch works because billboards feel
permanent. They've been standing beside
American highways since the 1920s. And
unlike a rental property, they never
call you at midnight about a broken
water heater. But what the broker will
never volunteer is the single financial
structure that controls the entire
economics of billboard ownership, the
ground lease. You do not own the dirt
your billboard stands on.
A private landowner does. And that
landowner's lease terms silently consume
15 to 25% of every dollar your board
earns before you touch a cent. When you
add the ground lease to permitting risk,
structural maintenance, seasonal
vacancy, and the capital cost of the
steel itself, the actual net return on a
highway billboard looks nothing like the
gross rental figure on the broker's
listing sheet.
Today, we are running the full
accounting on highway billboard

Highway billboards turn a scarce roadside structure into a long-lived advertising asset. Federal controls restrict where signs can stand, while grandfathered permissions can preserve structures that new rules would not allow. The land is commonly leased rather than owned, leaving operators to monetise visibility without buying the ground beneath it. This episode traces how regulation, spacing, digital screens and land contracts shape the money flowing through outdoor advertising.

Sources:
- Federal outdoor-advertising controls apply to signs located within 660 feet of the nearest edge of a highway right-of-way and visible from the highway — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-23/chapter-I/subchapter-H/part-750/subpart-A/section-750.102
- The Highway Beautification Act created the federal framework governing roadside outdoor advertising in 1965 — https://www.fhwa.dot.gov/real_estate/policy_guidance/beautification_act/
- Federal rules allow a legally established nonconforming sign to remain even after later regulations would prohibit a new sign of the same type — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-23/chapter-I/subchapter-H/part-750/subpart-A/section-750.107
- The federal spacing standard generally requires at least 500 feet between signs on the same side of an Interstate or other controlled highway — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-23/chapter-I/subchapter-H/part-750/subpart-A/section-750.105
- The federal outdoor-advertising program requires states to inventory and control signs along covered highways as a condition of maintaining federal-aid compliance — https://www.fhwa.dot.gov/real_estate/policy_guidance/beautification_act/
- U.S. out-of-home advertising revenue reached approximately 9.1 billion dollars in 2023 — https://oaaa.org/industry/industry-facts/
- Digital formats accounted for roughly 32 percent of U.S. out-of-home advertising revenue in 2023 — https://oaaa.org/industry/industry-facts/
- Lamar Advertising reported more than 3,000 digital billboard faces in its U.S. and Canadian network in its 2023 annual report — https://www.lamar.com/about/investors/financial-information/annual-reports
- Lamar Advertising describes its billboard land leases as commonly running for five to twenty years, creating a long-lived revenue asset without land ownership — https://www.lamar.com/about/investors/financial-information/annual-reports
- Lamar Advertising reported approximately 155,000 billboard displays in its 2023 annual report — https://www.lamar.com/about/investors/financial-information/annual-reports

controls access to a small piece of
moving attention. And the next question
is who gets paid for that access?
The landowner collects rent. The
billboard operator collects the
advertising revenue. An advertiser pays
to place a message on a structure facing
passing traffic while the operator pays
for the right to keep that structure on
the property. The arrangement separates
land value from visibility value.

owner may hold the ground. The sign
company holds the commercial
relationship and the physical asset
above it.

horizontal space beneath it.

155,000 billboard displays. The

sold. The roadside does not need to be
purchased again. Maintenance,
electricity, sales, labor, insurance,

beside the road. Sales labor turns
available views into contracts. Printing
or digital display delivers the message.
The traveling public supplies the
attention without buying anything at the
sign itself. Money enters from

owners, maintenance crews, utilities,
production suppliers, and regulators.

scarcity of legal positions.

outdoor advertising is not truly scarce
anymore. Digital screens can rotate
messages and advertisers can choose many
formats across a broad market.

of US out of home revenue in 2023.
If flexibility is expanding, perhaps the
old roadside structure loses its power.
That argument has not yet removed the
bottleneck. Digital still requires a
physical face in a regulated location.
The screen must be visible from the
road, supported, powered, and
maintained. Federal spacing standards
still limit how closely signs can sit
together, and state inventories still
govern the covered network. Lamar

billboard displays, indicating that the

metadata.title: Why a Billboard Is Worth More Than the Ad on It
metadata.author: What They Really Sell
metadata.shortDescription:
The billboard business is less about the sign and more about who controls the land beneath it. Learn why location matters.

While most people see a steel pole and an advertisement, the real competition in the billboard business happens before the sign is even installed. It is a game of securing rights, navigating local zoning laws, and managing land control to ensure a steady return on investment. The physical structure of outdoor advertising is often the simplest part of the equation.

Success in this industry relies on a precise mix of owned and leased sites. Operators must balance the financial requirements of net permits with the need for high-traffic locations to maximize the value of their advertising space. We break down the economic model that keeps these signs profitable long after the initial build.

Subscribe to What They Really Sell for more business breakdowns, and tell us in the comments what industry we should look at next.

0:00 The Hidden Complexity of Roadside Advertising
0:55 The Economics of Land and Leases
2:34 Navigating the Regulatory Maze
6:32 The Digital Transformation
9:10 The True Nature of the Asset

segments.text: Every day, millions of people drive past
these. A steel pole, a giant sign, an
advertisement somebody paid to put in
front of traffic. So, this looks like a
pretty straightforward advertising
business. Build the billboard, find an
advertiser, sell the space. Except the
billboard itself may be the easiest
part. Because before anyone can sell
this space, they need control of the
land underneath it. They need the right
location, the right sighteline, enough
traffic, and most importantly, they need
to be allowed to put a billboard there.
That is the business hiding underneath
the sign. Billboard companies aren't
just selling advertisements. They're
assembling portfolios of scarce
locations where attention can be rented
again and again. And once you understand
that, even the billboard starts to look
different. The advertiser is obvious.
The structure is obvious. What you don't
see is everything underneath it. The
billboard company may own the property,
but often it doesn't. Lamar Advertising,
one of the largest outdoor advertising
companies in the United States, reported
owning about 11,200
parcels beneath its advertising displays
at the end of 2025, but at least roughly
outdoor sites. Those site leases
represented about $348 million in
annualized lease expense, roughly 17% of
Lamar's billboard advertising revenue.
So before Lamar rents the billboard to
an advertiser, Lamar may already be
renting the location from somebody else.
And that tells us something important.
The land owner has land. The billboard
operator needs something more specific.
It needs a piece of that land with
access, visibility, traffic, and the
legal ability to operate an advertising
structure there. A vacant parcel next to
a road is just a vacant parcel. A
controlled parcel with a legal billboard
facing heavy traffic is something else
entirely. It has become advertising
inventory.
And location doesn't simply mean next to
a lot of cars. Think about what actually
has to work. Drivers need enough time to
see the board. The face has to point
toward useful traffic. Trees, buildings,
curves, and elevation can affect the
sighteline. The road has to carry an
audience advertisers care about. And
then there is the problem you can't
solve with better engineering.
Permission. Outdoor advertising in the
United States is regulated at the
federal, state, and local levels. Along
interstate, and certain other federally
controlled highway corridors, federal
law require states to control things
like billboard location, size, lighting,
and spacing. States and local
governments can impose additional
restrictions through zoning, permitting,
and sign ordinances. Which means you
cannot necessarily look at a busy
highway, find an empty patch of ground,
and decide that would be a great place
for a billboard. It might be, but you
still may not be able to put one there.
Lamar describes these regulations in its
own annual report as a significant
barrier to entry and expansion in many
markets. Some local governments restrict
new construction heavily. Some permit
new billboards only under specific
circumstances. Some existing boards
become legally non-conforming when
regulations change but may be allowed to
remain and suddenly the billboard that
is already standing there becomes much
more interesting because somebody
already solved the hard part. Here is
where this gets wonderfully strange.
Look at the balance sheet of another
major outdoor advertising company, Clear
Channel Outdoor. At the end of 2025,
Clear Channel reported about $548
million of billboard permits net as
intangible assets. Not the steel, not
the electronic screen permits.
That doesn't mean every billboard permit
is worth a fortune. And a permit by
itself is not the entire business, but
it shows what these companies are
actually assembling. A useful billboard
location is a package. There may be land
ownership or a site lease. There may be
an easement. There is the physical
structure. There are regulatory rights.
There is the audience moving past it.
And there is the ability to keep selling
advertising from that location. Take
away the sign and you still have a
potentially valuable location. Take away
the right to operate the sign and the
billboard business at that location can
disappear.
Which is why the scarce part isn't
necessarily the steel in the air. It can
be the collection of rights underneath
it. Now multiply this. Lamar operated
about 159,300
billboard advertising displays at the
end of 2025. Different cities, different
highways, different traffic patterns,
different landlords, different leases,
different permits, different
advertisers.
This is no longer one billboard. It's a
portfolio and managing that portfolio is
a major part of the business. Lamar says
that managing site leases and
negotiating renewals and extensions is
an important management activity. Those
leases can range from month-to-month
arrangements to terms longer than 10
years, often with renewal options.
Outfront Media shows the same mechanism
from another direction. It describes
itself as a real estate investment
trust, a REIT providing advertising
space on outdoor structures and sites.
And in 2025, its billboard property
lease expense alone represented about
24% of total company revenue. Lamar is
also organized as a REIT. That doesn't
mean billboard companies are simply
landlords with signs. Advertising sales
still matter enormously. Occupancy
matters. Pricing matters. The audience
matters. But the corporate structure is
a useful clue. Behind the advertising
operation is a giant location control
operation. Thousands of small rights to
put something in exactly the right
place.
And now we get to the part that makes
this business much more interesting. A
traditional billboard has a physical
limitation. There is one face. Put one
advertiser on it and that advertiser
occupies the face until the creative
changes. But convert a suitable location
to digital and the location stays
exactly where it was. Same road, same
traffic, same sight line, same piece of
ground, but now the screen can rotate
through multiple advertisements. Lamar
says its digital boards typically rotate
advertising approximately every 6 to 8
seconds. So, the location didn't
multiply, the sellable inventory did,
and the financial effect is enormous. At
the end of 2025, Lamar had about 5,500
digital billboard displays against
roughly 159,300
total billboard displays. That is only
around 3 and 12% of the display count.
Yet those digital billboards generated
approximately 33% of Lamar's billboard
advertising revenue. Think about that. A
relatively small part of the physical
billboard network was producing roughly
onethird of billboard advertising
revenue. Not because Lamar suddenly
found 10 times more highway. Not because
it duplicated the land. The company
found a way to sell more advertising
through some of the locations it already
controlled. The real estate stayed
scarce. The inventory became flexible.
And that may be the most important
change in the modern billboard business.
Because once you see that the billboard
stops looking like the product, it
starts looking like a platform attached
to a location. The original job was
already difficult. control the site,
secure the rights, build the structure,
maintain it, and sell access to the
audience moving past it. Digital adds
another layer. Now the creative can
change without somebody physically
replacing a printed face. Different
advertisers can occupy the same
sighteline at different moments.
Available inventory can be managed more
dynamically. A premium site can support
more advertising opportunities without
creating another premium site. That
doesn't make digital conversion
automatic. The company still faces
regulation, capital costs, local
restrictions, and the economics of the
individual location. But where
conversion makes sense, technology can
increase what an already scarce location
is capable of selling. That is a very
different business from simply
manufacturing signs. So, go back to that
first billboard. It still looks like an
advertisement on a pole. And
technically, that's what the customer is
buying, advertising space. But look
underneath the transaction. Somebody had
to control the land. Somebody had to
secure or maintain the legal right to
operate there. Somebody had to choose a
useful sighteline. Somebody had to
manage the lease. Somebody had to
preserve the location. And then somebody
had to turn the traffic already passing
that location into something advertisers
could rent again and again and again.
Digital just makes the underlying logic
easier to see because once the billboard
becomes a screen, you can watch the
advertisements change while everything
valuable underneath them stays exactly
where it is. The traffic is still there.
The sighteline is still there. The land
is still there. [music]
The permission is still there. The
billboard is the storefront. The
location [music] rights are the asset.
And that's what billboard companies
really sell. [music] Repeatable access
to attention
from places where that attention can
legally be sold.
>> [music]

metadata.title: The Highway Landlord Nobody Notices
metadata.author: Old School Financials
metadata.shortDescription:
You drive past it every day and never think about it. But that rectangle by the highway is rented land — and the permit underneath it may be worth more than the business it advertises.

In this episode of Old School Financials, we price the billboard business: the 1965 law that made old permits scarce, Lamar Advertising's 363,000 displays, the digital conversion that turns one tenant into eight, and the 55% margin the landlord keeps.

03:38 What the Landlord Keeps

05:37 Own the View, Not the Poster

the same rectangles and never pay them a
thought. They rise over highways, above
rooftops, beside the exits you take
without thinking.
Here's the judgement up front. A
billboard company is not in advertising.
It is in landlording. It rents a
permitted view by the month, by the
year. The poster changes, the pole
stays, the rent keeps coming.
That is why a rectangle by the road can
be worth more than the shop beneath it.
Today we price that rectangle and meet
the landlord who owns the view.
Because the billboard's real product was
never the ad you saw.
It was the ground, the permit, and the
right to be seen.
Start with the permit because without
it, there is no business at all.
In 1965, Congress passed the Highway
Beautification Act. It set a control
zone 660 ft from the highway's edge.
Inside that zone, new billboards face
strict rules on size, spacing, and
zoning.
A nationwide count in 1966 found 1.1
million roadside signs.
About 840,000 were illegal or did not
conform to the new rules.
But the law carried a twist that made
old signs valuable.
A lawfully built sign could not simply
be torn down for free. The government
had to pay just compensation to remove
it.
So the old permits became scarce,
protected, and very hard to replace.
New rivals could not just plant a bigger
board next door.
Scarcity was written into law and
scarcity is what landlords love most. No
company used that scarcity better than
Lamar Advertising.
Lamar was founded in 1902 when cars were
still a curiosity. Today it runs about
363,000 displays across America and
Canada.
About 5,000 of them are digital, the
largest digital network in the country.
That scale did not come from better
posters, It came from buying permits one
by one.
Small operators sold out. Lamar rolled
them up, town by town, highway by
highway. Each acquisition added not just
a board, but a grandfathered right to
stand there. A right that a newcomer
facing today's zoning often cannot get
at any price.
The company's billboard revenue in 2024
was $1.96 billion.
That is nearly $2 billion for renting
views, mostly to local businesses.
Local shops, restaurants, and services
remain the industry's biggest customers.
The national brands get the headlines,
the local dentist pays the rent. Now,
run the numbers on a single pole,
because this is where the model turns
clever.
A traditional static board, 14 ft by 48,
holds one advertiser at a time. Suppose
it rents for $2,000 a month, a plain
mid-market rate.
That is $24,000 a year from one tenant
on one permit. Now, convert that same
pole to a digital screen, and the
arithmetic changes completely. A digital
face rotates its advertisers every 6 to
8 seconds. Eight different businesses
can share one screen, each buying a
slice of the loop. Suppose each slot
rents for $1,000 a month, half the old
static rate. Eight slots bring $8,000 a
month, or 96,000 a year.
Four times the rent from the same pole
under the same single permit. That is
the whole trick. The permit did not
multiply.
The tenants did.
No new land, no new zoning fight, just
eight rents where one used to stand.
So, what does the landlord actually keep
after paying for the ground? Lamar's
billboard earnings before interest and
tax were $1.09 billion in 2024 against
$1.96 billion in billboard revenue. That
is a margin near 55%
Divide that revenue by 363,000 displays
and you get the average.
About $5,400
per display per year across the whole
fleet. That average hides the spread.
A rural poster rents for hundreds.
A city digital face for thousands a
month. The landlord's costs are the land
lease, the structure, the lights and the
crew. But there's no inventory to stock.
No staff on a sales floor. No goods to
spoil. America's whole outdoor industry
took in 9.1 billion dollars in 2024.
It was the first year the median ever
passed 9 billion. Digital already
supplies about 35% of that total. And it
is still growing.
The old poster is not dying. It is being
converted. One pole at a time.
Every landlord has a risk and this one
is written into the same law. Cities can
tighten zoning, ban new digital boards,
or dim the lights at night. A board that
loses its permit loses everything.
Because the view was the asset.
Attention is the second risk. Drivers
now carry a brighter screen in their
pockets.
A billboard cannot be clicked, skipped,
or targeted at one person.
Its defense is blunt and old-fashioned.
It cannot be blocked, muted, or scrolled
past. Advertisers still pay $2 to $18
per thousand impressions. Among the
cheapest reach in media.
Cheap, unavoidable, and always on.
That is a hard combination to kill.
But the landlord who overpays for a
permit or borrows too much to buy one
still fails.
So, here's the verdict. Back where we
started.
The billboard business was never about
the cleverest poster. It was about
owning a view that the law would not let
anyone else copy. The poster is rented
attention. The permit is owned scarcity.
That is the old school lesson and it
travels far beyond the highway. In any
business, ask what cannot be duplicated.
Not what looks impressive.
Find the permitted corner, the
grandfathered right, the view no rival
can buy.
Own the view, not the poster, and the
rent will follow. That is the highway
landlord's quiet fortune standing in
plain sight.

metadata.title: Who Really Owns the Billboard You Drive Past? (The Real Math)
metadata.author: The Wealth Script
metadata.shortDescription:
Who owns billboards? How the billboard business makes money, how much a billboard land lease pays, and why one digital billboard earns 13 times a regular one.

A billboard usually has three owners: the landowner, the billboard company and the advertiser. The land under it might earn about $400 a month. The screen on top can bring in more than $100,000 a year.

In this video: who really owns the sign, how it makes money, the one thing that makes billboards so valuable, and why the screen version earns about 13 times as much as the paper one.

Chapters
0:00 Intro
0:49 Who owns the billboard
1:58 How the money comes in
2:49 The permit is the asset
4:09 Who wins at scale
4:47 How people lose
5:21 Two people, one spot
6:28 What this business really is

Which boring business should we break down next? Tell us in the comments.

Sources (selection)
Lamar Advertising 10-K, fiscal 2025: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1090425/000109042526000008/lamr-20251231.htm
Highway Beautification Act, Public Law 89-285 (1965): https://usc-cdn.house.gov/statutes/pl/89/285.pdf
23 U.S.C. 131: control of outdoor advertising: https://openjurist.org/23/usc/131
Scenic America: Vermont billboard ban: https://www.scenic.org/take-action/resources/case-studies/case-study-vermonts-billboard-ban/
Anchorage Daily News: why Alaska doesn't have billboards: https://www.adn.com/alaska-news/2022/01/23/curious-alaska-why-dont-we-have-billboards-in-alaska
Billboard Insider: digital billboard slots and flips: https://billboardinsider.com/daktronics-on-digital-sign-flips/
Full fact-check table: every number in this video is sourced.

The 20-year lease and the paper-vs-screen comparison (based on Lamar's averages) are hypothetical illustrations with rounded numbers, not real businesses. Market figures vary by location and change over time.

This video is for education and entertainment only. It is not financial, investment, tax or legal advice. Do your own research and talk to a qualified professional before buying any business.

segments.text: Okay, so you drive past a billboard
every day.
A giant sign on two steel legs next to
the highway selling lawyers, burgers,
and phone plans. Who owns it? Usually
not one person. Three. Someone owns the
land. Someone else owns the sign. And
someone else rents the space on it a
month at a time. And here's the strange
part. The land under the sign might earn
its owner about $400 a month. The sign
above it, if it's digital, can bring in
more than $100,000 a year. So who gets
the money? And why doesn't everybody put
up a billboard? By the end of this
video, you'll know who really owns that
sign, how it makes money, the one thing
that makes billboards so valuable, and
why the screen version earns about 13
times as much as the paper one. So who
owns the billboard? One of the biggest
billboard companies in the country is
Lamar Advertising.
At the end of 2025, it ran about 159,000
billboard displays in 45 states and
Canada.
But most of those signs stand on land
Lamar doesn't own. It leases about
sites from landowners, farmers, gas
stations, warehouse owners, anyone with
a patch of ground next to a busy road.
Lamar pays about $348
million a
per site on average. About $400 a month.
Some of those leases run month to month.
Some run for more than 10 years. Lamar
owns the land under only about 11,200 of
its signs. And the third owner is the
advertiser, who doesn't own anything at
all. They rent the face of the sign for
weeks or months at a time. If you like
knowing how these boring businesses
really work, subscribe. We break down
new ones every week. Now, how does the
money actually come in? The formula fits
on one line. Faces times the price of
each face times how much of the year
they're rented minus the land rent, the
power, and the upkeep. In 2025, Lamar's
billboards brought in about $2 billion.
About $1.38 billion came from ordinary
signs, printed or painted, spread across
about 154,000
of them. That's about $9,000 per sign
per year. Then there are the screens.
Lamar runs about 5,500 digital
billboards. They brought in about $632
million.
That's about $115,000
per screen per year, about 13 times as
much as a paper sign from the same kind
of spot by the same kind of road. Here's
the part most people never think about.
The steel isn't the asset. The
permission is. In 1965, President Lyndon
Johnson signed the Highway
Beautification Act to control billboards
along major highways. Today, four states
don't allow billboards at all, Alaska,
Hawaii, Maine, and Vermont. And many
cities and counties ban new ones or only
allow a new billboard to replace an old
one. Lamar says it plainly in its own
annual report, "These rules are a
significant barrier to entry." If nobody
can build a new sign next to your sign,
your sign has almost no competition. And
the same law protects the signs that are
already there. If a government forces a
lawful billboard to come down, it
generally has to pay the owner just
compensation. So, an old billboard in
the right spot isn't just a sign. It's a
permit that's very hard to get and very
expensive to take away. That's why the
screens make so much money. A digital
board is usually an old permitted sign
with a new face. Instead of one
advertiser for a month, it shows six to
eight ads in a loop, each for about
eight seconds, all day and all night.
Same steel, same permit, six to eight
customers instead of one. So, who wins
at scale? The company that holds the
most permits.
Lamar's digital screens are only about
three or four out of every hundred of
its billboards, but they bring in about
a third of its billboard revenue. That's
where the money goes. The big operators
look for their best located signs, the
ones by the busiest roads, and turn them
into screens where the local rules allow
it. Lamar notes that some places
restrict or ban digital billboards, too.
So, a permit for a digital screen is the
rarest thing of all. And the small
landowner, they're often the last to
find out what their corner is worth. So,
how do people lose money on billboards?
The first way is signing a long lease
too cheaply. A sign that sits on your
land for decades at the same rent can
end up earning someone else far more
than it pays you.
The second way is the rules changing. A
city can ban new signs, restrict digital
screens, or try to phase out old ones.
Billboard companies spend a lot of time
and money fighting that. The third way
is the empty face. A paper billboard
with no advertiser earns nothing that
month, but the rent is still due. So,
let's put it together. One spot by a
busy road and the two people who share
it. These are round, simple numbers
based on Lamar's averages just to show
how it works. The landowner signs a
20-year lease at about $4,900
a year. Over 20 years, that's about
for doing nothing but owning the ground.
The billboard company puts up an
ordinary sign.
On Lamar's averages, that sign brings in
about $9,000 a year. Take off the rent,
and there isn't a lot left for the
steel, the printing, and the crews. Now,
the company turns that sign into a
screen. Same land, same rent if the
lease allows it.
On Lamar's averages, the screen brings
in about $115,000
a year.
The landowner's rent is now about 4
cents of every dollar the sign earns.
The screen costs money to build and to
run, so this isn't all profit. But the
point holds. The money in billboards
goes to whoever controls the permit and
the screen, not to whoever owns the
dirt. So, here's what a billboard really
is. It isn't an advertising business.
It's a permit business with a sign on
top. The land is cheap. The steel is
ordinary. The rare thing is the right to
have a sign there at all. That's why the
billboard companies guard their permits,
buy up the best spots, and turn the
busiest ones into screens. So, the next
time you drive past a billboard,
remember, three people own it, and the
one with the permit gets paid the most.
If you want more breakdowns like this,
subscribe. And tell us in the comments,
which boring business should we break
down next?

If you're running a truck parking yard or thinking about starting one, this is the most honest video I can make for you.

Hut. Today, we'll do a quick video on
what we wish we knew before managing our
first truck parking yard.
Before we built Rig Hut, my partner and
I, as we've shared in other videos, were
in the yards physically every day.
We were essentially running a
multi-truck parking property portfolio
around a major port city in South
Florida.
We learned this business under someone
who was doing it for 30-plus years.
He had a major fuel distribution
business, and he liked to accommodate
his own fleet with a lot of these yards,
but also help welcome a lot of the
port-related and just general industrial
fleet, container, trailer,
etc. type businesses that that need
space in South Florida. Eventually, we
were help start managing them for him.
This involved collecting rent, fixing
the gates, kicking people out who didn't
pay, filling up spaces. At peak, I think
we were doing close to about 1,000
vehicles a month. So, we learned a ton,
and most of it the hard way. What we
wish we Here's what we wish someone
would have told us before we started.
Number one, the drivers will normally
always have a reason why they didn't
pay.
There's always a story. The check is in
the mail. He paid for the guy next to
him last month, so that guy now owes him
this month. I paid that guy. I thought
my wife called you. The wife doesn't
speak English. You'll hear every version
of this. The operators who survived this
are the ones who have a system that
doesn't require them to remember who
paid and who didn't.
If it's in your head, the driver knows
that, too, usually. If you don't show a
presence, they probably talk and will
and will share that as well. But,
getting it in writing, getting into a
system, and have a process that runs
automatically, that is the best way that
leakage does not happen.
Number two, speaking of leakage, your
gate code is not a gate. The moment you
give someone a code, they give it to
their own guys, their cousin, their
dispatcher, their buddy who needs
parking for one night, you name it. You
don't know who's in your yard.
You think you have 40 trucks paying, you
might have 50 in there. Three of them
haven't paid in 2 months. Gate codes are
not access control, they get shared. And
real access control is tied to payment.
If someone owes, they shouldn't be able
to get in. That's it. Have access
control that marries that discipline.
Number three, speed to lead is
everything. So, when a driver calls, no
matter what time, and if they ask for
parking, usually they are have they have
the highest conversion rates. So,
they're calling you and they're calling
three other yards at the same time.
Whoever answers gets them booked first,
and they get the paid.
We lost bookings many times because we
called back 20 minutes later, they're
already somewhere else. Remember, these
are drivers, they're driving. If you
don't answer, they're going to keep
going. If someone reaches out, get them
in the system in that moment, not later.
Number four, the monthly guys are your
business. Treat Treat them like it. The
daily traffic feels exciting. Yes, the
the money is better, but the transients,
the walk-ins, the one-nighters, those
usually involve the highest management
and the highest intensity for
management. Usually, they also can click
gates much more naturally. They can hit
other guys that park there. The real
business is the predictable revenue. At
least getting a foundation that way if
the location welcomes it. The thing that
lets you sleep at night is that monthly
tenant who pays you three to $400 or,
you know, 250, we'll call it. Doesn't
think about it. Build your yard around
those relationships. Get to know those
guys. Get to know their businesses. Know
their names. Know their equipment. Know
when their anniversary billing hits,
etc. These people are your business.
Number five, know your numbers. Sounds
obvious, but most operators we talk to
don't actually know what their average
revenue per space is. They don't know
what they charge. They're probably
leaking the bottom line. And while yes,
you know, they say it's been in their
head for years, if you look back every
12 months, there's usually a lot of
dollars on the floor that were left.
They don't know what their net after bed
They don't know what they net after bed
debt. Vacancies hit that as well. Late
payments, you name it. You can't improve
what you don't measure, obviously. And
